conflicts.summary: Council members exchanged views on requiring contractor visibility during work sessions on pulled MWBE items (Item 12) and how to coordinate objective COVID-19 thresholds across City Hall and Durham County before reverting to virtual sessions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Seek prompt data-driven COVID-19 positivity guidelines from Public Health Director Rod Jenkins and improve contractor accountability.
side_a_arguments: Positivity near 5% before holidays requires pre-set thresholds so future shifts to virtual meetings are non-arbitrary.
Contractors should appear virtually to answer questions about equity and MWBE participation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Involve County officials alongside staff briefings while new members complete orientation.
side_b_arguments: Mayor O'Neal and Council Member Williams emphasized learning briefings before setting policies and looping in County leadership.
conflicts.resolution: Jillian Johnson agreed to coordinate an informational email inquiry with Public Health Director Rod Jenkins, City Manager Page, and County leadership.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting March 23, 2023 10 a.m.
conflicts.issue: City of Durham Mentoring Alliance Collaborative Pilot Program ($200,000 / FTE vs. Referral List or Matching Seed Fund)
conflicts.summary: Council members differed on whether to advance a $200,000 pilot with a dedicated FTE or pursue a smaller, multi-agency coordination model.
conflicts.side_a_position: Establish a City-funded Mentoring Alliance Collaborative pilot to coordinate youth mentoring partners and combat crisis-level youth violence.
side_a_arguments: Youth gun violence demands proactive prevention and a centralized one-stop shop connecting families to mentoring organizations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid committing $200,000 or an FTE that alters Office on Youth workflows before identifying specific gaps; use a simpler directory or a small County/DPS matching seed.
side_b_arguments: Ambiguity remains around where the FTE would sit and whether a referral menu/link from the Office on Youth already achieves a one-stop information hub.
A smaller seed allocation (such as $10,000) could test gaps and invite matching funds from Durham County and Durham Public Schools rather than carrying the full $200,000 cost alone.
conflicts.resolution: Time was called at 00:18:59 for workshop categorization, with discussion of scaling down to a smaller matching seed amount before deciding on an FTE.

conflicts.issue: HEART Team Expansion Framing and Comparisons Between Durham PD and Memphis PD
conflicts.summary: During council announcements, members clashed over how Durham's HEART alternative crisis response expansion and local policing oversight were framed in light of the police killing in Memphis and the tasing death of Darryl Tyree Williams in Raleigh.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advocate expanding the HEART crisis response program to 24/7 citywide coverage in the upcoming budget and highlight alternative response amid national scrutiny of policing.
side_a_arguments: HEART has demonstrated success and should be funded to operate 24/7 across the entire city.

Community rallies with Durham Beyond Policing underscore public demand for non-police crisis response, heightened by national attention following the police killing in Memphis where Durham's former chief serves.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject equating Durham Police Department with Memphis PD, oppose targeting city employees, and invite the Police Chief before Council to address regional incidents.
side_b_arguments: Durham Police Department is not the Memphis Police Department, and policy disputes should be directed at elected officials on the ballot rather than W-2 city employees.
Bringing Durham's Police Chief before Council allows members to ask direct questions about local practices following regional tragedies such as the tasing death of Darryl Tyree Williams in Raleigh.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; DeDreana Freeman seconded Mark-Anthony Middleton's request to bring the Police Chief before Council during the upcoming budget/oversight cycle.

conflicts.issue: East Geer Street Residential Competition for Competitive 9% LIHTC Tax Credits
conflicts.summary: While all seven Council members backed the 90-unit East Geer Street affordable/workforce project, Jillian Johnson and Mark-Anthony Middleton initially expressed concern over whether pursuing competitive 9% tax credits would undermine DHA redevelopment plans.
conflicts.side_a_position: Avoid competing with Durham Housing Authority (DHA) for scarce 9% LIHTC credits unless DHA confirms it has no January 2023 application.
side_a_arguments: Long-standing city-DHA coordination seeks to protect 9% tax credits for public housing redevelopment such as Fayette Place.
conflicts.side_b_position: Zoning should not be conditioned on tax-credit choices, and the applicant committed 25% affordable units even if privately financed.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman viewed linking zoning approval to future 9% credit applications as off-putting, and Leah Bergman noted she checked with Community Development and was happy to build privately if DHA needed the credit.
conflicts.resolution: Jillian Johnson confirmed via text message with DHA CEO Anthony Scott that DHA had no 9% application ready for January 2023, and Council approved all three motions 7-0.

conflicts.issue: Procedural Continuance vs. Immediate Vote on Bull City Townhomes Rezoning (Item 19)
conflicts.summary: Although all five members ultimately voted against approving the Bull City Townhomes rezoning over unfinalized proffers, neighborhood engagement failures, and watershed/traffic concerns, members split over whether to grant applicant Mark Bullock another continuance until August.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue the public hearing to August to give the applicant another opportunity to formalize proffers and address neighborhood engagement.
side_a_arguments: Freeman cited Jordan Lake buffer concerns and unresolved community outreach while asking to continue to August.
Johnson supported townhome density in principle and said she was open to a continuance if proffers were solidified.
conflicts.side_b_position: Refuse a fourth continuance because the applicant had already had multiple meetings and did not commit to meaningful changes.
side_b_arguments: Middleton argued another continuance would set a bad precedent when the applicant indicated another meeting would not yield new outcomes.
Letting the applicant reapply later is cleaner than keeping neighbors in repeated hearing loops.
conflicts.resolution: Freeman's continuance motion died for lack of a second, and the Council voted 0-5 to deny the rezoning.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 24, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: ARPA Allocation Framework, 50% Funding Cap, and Black-Led Organization Focus
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over ground rules for the upcoming April 6 ARPA deliberation, specifically whether a circulated spreadsheet cutting County-function health proposals and capping initial awards at ~50% ($22M) of the $44M ARPA balance reflected Council consensus.
conflicts.side_a_position: Use the staff-vetted spreadsheet cutoff to release roughly half (~$22M) immediately for urgent community aid while reserving half for larger equity investments or county partnerships.
side_a_arguments: Avoids stalling urgent community funds and relies on staff scoring without re-reading 77 full RFPs.
Preserves ~$22M unencumbered for transformative equity projects or joint County health/wellness funding.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not pre-lock a 50% cap or exclude proposals prematurely without a broader strategic plan and explicit Black-led/Black-focused equity prioritization.
side_b_arguments: Freeman stated she had not agreed to a $22M cap and wanted a larger comprehensive strategy.
Council must explicitly confirm prioritization of Black-led and Black-focused proposals rather than assuming scoring suffices.
conflicts.resolution: Mayor O'Neal tasked Caballero and Williams with designing a structured April 6 deliberation and public comment framework bounded by staff cutoff tiers and explicit equity attention.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 10, 2022 (Livestream)
conflicts.issue: Boards and Commissions In-Person Return and Attendance Enforcement Policy
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over whether advisory and quasi-judicial boards and commissions (such as Housing Appeals Board and Board of Adjustment) should be directed to return in person with attendance enforcement restored, or remain remote until the Governor ends North Carolina's COVID-19 State of Emergency.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require business-critical boards and commissions to meet in person and restore attendance accountability now, accommodating immunocompromised members individually.
side_a_arguments: Freeman argued Housing Appeals Board and Board of Adjustment work is backing up because landlords and participants avoid virtual proceedings.
Williams advocated leading by example with masks, vaccines, and boosters to return boards to in-person work, though clarifying later he meant once the Governor's emergency order lifts.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep existing virtual meeting flexibility and suspended attendance penalties in place until the Governor lifts the State of Emergency.
side_b_arguments: Johnson warned toggling between in-person and virtual rules during future COVID spikes would confuse volunteers and strain staff.
City Attorney Kim Rehberg cautioned that City Hall lacks hybrid equipment outside Council Chambers and piecemeal board autonomy could create chaos.
conflicts.resolution: Council maintained the virtual/non-counted attendance status quo until the Governor lifts the emergency order.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 6, 2022 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Firefighter Living-Wage Hourly Calculation (56-Hour Week) & Mid-Year Pay Scope
conflicts.summary: Following firefighter testimony over step compression and sub-living hourly effective pay across 56-hour shifts, Jillian Johnson pressed administration for cost estimates to bring firefighters to the living wage on a 56-hour basis, whereas Wanda Page and JJ Scott advised against altering the ordinance's annual-salary framework mid-year.
conflicts.side_a_position: Obtain updated cost calculations to pay firefighters Durham's minimum livable wage on their actual 56-hour workweek and seriously weigh tax/funding options.
side_a_arguments: Basing firefighters' salaries on a 40-hour formula when they work 56 hours leaves them below Durham's hourly living wage despite city living-wage commitments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Advance the $4M sworn structure increase now under the existing annual-salary ordinance and examine compression and broader pay equity during the regular FY23 budget.
side_b_arguments: Moving entry firefighter recruits to ~$50,000 for 56-hour living-wage parity would trigger severe upward compression across pay grades and ripple across other city pay plans.
No general employees received merit increases over the last two years, so full structural compression must be weighed holistically in FY23.
conflicts.resolution: Item 26 stayed on track for the January 18 vote while City Manager Page committed to updating the May cost-calculation memo as an agenda addendum without recommending immediate structural overhaul.

conflicts.issue: Item 17 (Motion 1): Adopt Amended SCAD UDO Text Amendment (TC2200001) Excluding Staff-Unrecommended Sections, Topic 6, and PATH
conflicts.summary: Jillian Johnson moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the SCAD provisions recommended by planning staff while excluding Topic 3 (§6.10.2.A.1), Topic 4 (§4.6.6.C.1, §5.4.2.B.2.a), all of Topic 6, Topic 7 (§6.8.2.A.2.a, §6.8.3, §6.8.4), Topic 8 (§6.10.1.C.1, §6.10.1.D.1, §6.10.2.B.2), Topic 10 (§6.12.3.B.11), Topic 11 (§6.12.5.E), Topic 13 (§6.10.1.C.1.f, §6.10.1.D.1.f), and the Affordable Housing PATH proposal. The motion passed 4-3 by hand vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 17 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Amended SCAD UDO Text Amendment
conflicts.summary: Moved by Leonardo Williams and seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council adopted the statutory consistency statement for the amended SCAD ordinance by the same 4-3 hand vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Perry Farm Consolidated Annexation Ordinance and CSC Group LLC Utility Extension Agreement (Item 24, Motion 1)
conflicts.summary: Annexes Perry Farm into the City of Durham effective Dec. 31, 2023 and authorizes a utility extension agreement with CSC Group LLC.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Perry Farm Zoning Map Change to PDR 3.155 and Rural Residential Public/Civic (Item 24, Motion 2)
conflicts.summary: Transfers property from county Residential Rural (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B) to city Planned Development Residential 3.155 and Rural Residential with a textual development plan limiting uses to public and civic.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 21, 2023
conflicts.issue: Structure and Funding of Mid-Year City Employee Bonuses
conflicts.summary: Council members and staff disagreed over whether to pass the $6.5 million bonus ordinance immediately or delay for reworked tiers that shift more funds to lower earners without cutting part-time bonuses or destabilizing city reserves.
conflicts.side_a_position: Either pass the existing ordinance for immediate early-October payouts or avoid exceeding $6.5M without identified expenditure cuts.
side_a_arguments: Passing the current ordinance allows employees to see money in their first October paycheck.
Finding an extra $4.9M mid-year requires freezing positions or stopping contracts because the budget already assumes a $10M positive variance, and the city cannot jeopardize disaster reserves.
conflicts.side_b_position: Rework the $6.5M allocation (or identify Q2 savings) to increase bonuses for lower-earning workers without reducing part-time worker payouts.
side_b_arguments: The current distribution is unsatisfactory for the lowest-paid employees and higher-tier bonuses can be trimmed closer to the $300 already budgeted.
Part-time employees received only $500 previously and should not have their bonuses reduced.
conflicts.resolution: After a recess, at least six Council members supported deferring the vote and directing staff to bring back reworked bonus options.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 7, 2023
conflicts.issue: City Sanitation and Essential Worker Compensation Adjustments
conflicts.summary: Following protests from sanitation workers over wages and housing affordability, Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton expressed contrasting positions on mid-year pay adjustments versus staying within the adopted budget and compensation study.
conflicts.side_a_position: Stand with protesting workers and pursue immediate budget options to raise compensation.
side_a_arguments: Essential workers face severe inflation and cannot afford to live in Durham while doing vital city work.
Even under statutory balanced-budget rules, Council can identify ways within the numbers to support workers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Rely on the adopted 6% (4% + 2%) pay increase and ongoing compensation study rather than unsustainable mid-year promises.
side_b_arguments: Ad-hoc mid-year raises create recurring obligations that would require raising taxes or cutting services the next year.
The city already delivered a 6% raise and is conducting a compensation study to raise pay responsibly.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; compensation bonus options were subsequently brought back to the September 21 and October 5 work sessions.

conflicts.issue: Item 23 Motion 1: Adopt Zoning Map Amendment Z2200006 (RS-20 to PDR 7.203 and OI(D), 301 & 401 Infinity Rd)
conflicts.summary: The rezoning for 99 townhouses and 5,000 sq ft of office space failed on a 3-3 tie with Mayor Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman voting no after neighbor testimony on Infinity Road traffic, lack of STIP road funding, and unperformed geotechnical studies.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 17 Motion 1: Annex Fletcher Crossing (707 S. Mineral Springs Rd) and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with ODG 87 LLC
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 to annex the 9.47-acre Fletcher Crossing parcel effective September 30, 2023 and approve the utility extension agreement.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 17 Motion 2: Adopt Zoning Map Amendment for Fletcher Crossing (RS-20/RR F/J-B to PDR 8.347 F/J-B)
conflicts.summary: Council approved up to 80 townhouses at Fletcher Crossing 4-3 despite a 5-4 Planning Commission denial recommendation and objections over narrow roads, flooding, and lack of transit or affordable units.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Item 20 Motion 1: Annex 631 & 633 Clayton Road and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with Winmore 208 LLC
conflicts.summary: Council voted 4-3 to annex 631 & 633 Clayton Road effective September 30 and authorize the utility extension agreement.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Durham City Council Meeting March 23, 2023 10 a.m.
conflicts.issue: Hayti Historic Redress Funding Scale and Use of the $30 Million Projected Fund Balance Surplus
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over whether to commit up to $10 million for Hayti historic redress while safeguarding the City's ~$30 million reserve or pursue a larger multi-year/CIP commitment.
conflicts.side_a_position: Put real funding (up to $10 million) on the table for Hayti historic redress without draining the City's rainy-day fund balance.
side_a_arguments: Committing $10 million marks a historic first step that can be supplemented in future budget cycles, CIP updates, and ARPA allocations.
As a self-insured city, Durham cannot raid its entire ~$30 million reserve in one fell swoop without risking fiscal agility.
conflicts.side_b_position: Clarify how the $30 million surplus, ARPA, and CIP align and avoid capping Hayti investment at $10 million without a binding CIP roadmap.
side_b_arguments: If Hayti projects are not placed into the CIP and coordinated with NCDOT, larger transformative investments risk slipping past 2029.
Council should evaluate whether the $30 million surplus can better address department and community priorities alongside ARPA deadlines.
conflicts.resolution: Staff noted green-rated budget priorities totaled $15 million and agreed to return with options balancing ARPA, CIP, fund balance, and general fund sources.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Feb 9, 2023
conflicts.issue: Proposed 10-Cent Plastic Bag Fee Ordinance vs. Education-First Resolution
conflicts.summary: Following a presentation by Don't Waste Durham and university clinic researchers, council members divided over whether to advance an enforceable 10-cent plastic bag fee ordinance with a transition period or begin with a non-binding resolution and public education campaign.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support moving forward with a plastic bag fee ordinance paired with a clear timeline and bilingual public education campaign.
side_a_arguments: Pricing undesirable single-use items is a proven tool to drive both individual and collective behavior change.
An ordinance with an explicit transition timeline (such as 18 months) provides clarity while allowing thorough multilingual outreach.
Other jurisdictions worldwide—including countries with much lower average wealth—have successfully implemented plastic bag restrictions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support a robust public education campaign and resolution first, viewing a mandatory 10-cent fee ordinance as premature.
side_b_arguments: A 10-cent per-bag fee creates psychological and financial burdens on low-income residents who already pay more for healthy food.
Policing and enforcing local mandates proved challenging during the pandemic.
A robust education campaign coupled with a resolution can build public buy-in before considering an ordinance.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken at the work session; policy discussion left open for further council work.

conflicts.side_a_position: Implement the proposed 6%-8% base-pay increases (7% for public safety) while completing the pay study before adding unallocated funds, leaving retroactive raises open for consideration.
side_a_arguments: Higher taxes disproportionately burden lowest-income residents.
Adding unallocated money without a finalized plan is fiscally irresponsible.
The proposed budget already includes a 2% step plus 5% pay plan increase (7% total) added permanently to base pay for public safety staff.
conflicts.side_b_position: Explore reallocating $7 million to $8 million within the budget or raising taxes to protect employee morale and address public safety compensation sooner.
side_b_arguments: Public safety and city worker morale are suffering from salary compression and regional competition.
The city could examine finding $7M-$8M across the broader budget or consider a tax increase, though acknowledging four votes for a tax hike were unlikely.

conflicts.issue: Role of Public Housing vs. Mixed-Income Private-Market Partnerships
conflicts.summary: During the Durham Housing Authority deep-dive discussion, council members diverged on whether concentrated public housing is a failed model that must shift toward mixed-income communities or whether government-funded public housing must be championed as a guaranteed human right.
conflicts.side_a_position: Shift away from concentrated public housing toward structured mixed-income communities that integrate residents socioeconomically rather than isolating low-income households.
side_a_arguments: Concentrated public housing can trap residents in environments with maintenance failures and crime.
Mixed-income communities create better-run, welcoming environments that encourage upward mobility and integration into Durham.
conflicts.side_b_position: Government-funded public housing is 100% the solution and housing must be treated and funded as a guaranteed human right rather than left to a capitalist market.
side_b_arguments: Public housing only struggles when the federal government underfunds it, unlike systems in Western Europe where government investment keeps housing affordable.
Treating housing purely as a market commodity guarantees displacement and homelessness for residents who cannot pay market rates.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 21, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: In outgoing Mayor Elaine O'Neal's final work session on November 21, 2023 (with Jillian Johnson excused), Council heard three major presentations: the 2023 Third Quarter Crime Report (showing homicides up 9.4% to 45 and motor vehicle thefts up 156%, alongside an 80% homicide clearance rate and 24.7% police vacancy rate), the Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Initiative core team update on housing barriers for justice-involved individuals, and the FY 2023-24 First Quarter Financial Report. The session concluded with an explosive, nearly hour-long confrontation under Item 6 (City Council Procedures) over censure gaps, fraternization policy, the aborted March 2023 censure of Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and mutual accusations of dishonesty, bullying, and past physical altercation between DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton. Council unanimously settled the December 4 agenda (6-0) before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Carver Creek & Wheels Comments, and Citizen Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the meeting to order at 1:00 PM with Jillian Johnson excused. Mark-Anthony Middleton noted the County's guaranteed income documentary screening, speakers praised Carver Creek's anti-displacement preservation and urged ADA/roller-derby design attention at the former Wheels Skating Center, and solid waste worker speakers celebrated solidarity, while Dennis Garrett urged holiday youth crime prevention.

agenda_items.title: 2023 Third Quarter Crime Report Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Patrice Andrews reported overall Part 1 violent crime down 5.5% (612 per 100,000), with homicides up 9.4% to 45 (80% clearance rate) and rapes up 21.6% driven by prior-year reports, while robberies fell 21.3%. Property crime surged, led by a 156% jump in motor vehicle thefts (largely Hyundais and Kias) and 837 seized guns; ShotSpotter logged 1,125 alerts (26.3% with 911 calls), and sworn staffing stood at 77% (24.7% vacancy rate).

agenda_items.title: Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Initiative Core Team Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carmisha Wallace, Colin Davis, and community partner Dennis Garrett presented findings from nine months of Bloomberg Harvard coaching and interviews with justice-involved individuals, landlords, and service providers. They recommended a coordinated 'one-stop shop' entry system, peer support specialists, and landlord engagement, noting Bloomberg awarded 20 additional coaching hours that incoming Mayor Leonardo Williams committed to continuing.

agenda_items.title: FY 2023-2024 First Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Management Services Director Christina Reardon presented Q1 financial results, noting property tax revenues appeared 89% lower than Q1 FY23 only because tax bills mailed later, while occupancy tax rose nearly 40%, sales tax stood around $13M for two months, and inspections fund personnel remained under budget due to vacancies. DeDreana Freeman asked staff to highlight red-flagged CIP projects early to avoid re-bidding cost escalation.

agenda_items.title: Discussion of City Council Procedures, Censure Process, and Fraternization Gaps
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal presented a City Attorney-commissioned 23-page review identifying gaps in council rules regarding off-dais conduct, citizen censure petitions, fraternization, and lack of apologies/closure after Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's exoneration. Mark-Anthony Middleton countered that Rule 2.14 did not violate procedures, no apology was owed for a censure dropped at a private community meeting, and accused O'Neal and others of echoing activist talking points; heated exchanges followed between DeDreana Freeman, Middleton, and Holsey-Hyman.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations and Settling of December 4 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported a council tie on Item 1 (Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee) between re-advertising and nominating Hannah Bartlebaugh, leaving it for re-advertisement. Council unanimously approved placing Items 1-5 and 7-21 on Consent and Items 24-26 on Public Hearings before Mayor O'Neal closed her final work session with pointed parting remarks to Mark-Anthony Middleton.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for December 4, 2023 Regular City Council Meeting (Consent: 1-5, 7-21; Public Hearings: 24-26)
votes.notes: Jillian Johnson had an excused absence.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Mark-Anthony Middleton and seconded by Javiera Caballero, Council unanimously approved the agenda for the December 4 regular meeting among the six members present, omitting pulled Item 6 (City Council Procedures).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 21, 2023
disagreements.issue: City Council Procedures, Off-Dais Censure Rules, Fraternization Policy, and Handling of Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman Censure Effort
disagreements.summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman clashed sharply with Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton over procedural gaps in council ethics rules, the lack of formal apologies following Holsey-Hyman's exoneration, and allegations of workplace bullying and past physical assault on the dais.
disagreements.side_a_position: Council's rules of procedure contain serious governance gaps on off-dais conduct, citizen complaints, fraternization, and workplace harassment, and members owe closure and apologies to Dr. Holsey-Hyman.
side_a_arguments: Rule 2.14 focuses on dais conduct and lacks clear due-process steps for off-dais allegations, citizen censure requests, or fraternization between council members and senior staff.
After DA and SBI inquiries exonerated Dr. Holsey-Hyman, Council failed to formally close the matter or apologize for attempting to censure her.
DeDreana Freeman alleged ongoing workplace bullying and past physical confrontation by Mark-Anthony Middleton and called for an outside facilitator.
disagreements.side_b_position: No procedural rules were violated during the contemplated censure, citizen petitions do not trigger the Procedures Committee without a council majority, and no apology is owed.
side_b_arguments: Rule 2.14 does not preclude contemplating censure for off-dais conduct, and the resolution was dropped after a private meeting in the interest of healing the city.
The same investigative letter exonerated other council members of collusion, leaving nothing to apologize for.
Mark-Anthony Middleton flatly denied ever hitting DeDreana Freeman and argued any procedural overhaul should wait for the newly elected council.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote or procedural revision was adopted; the dispute remained unresolved at the close of outgoing Mayor Elaine O'Neal's final work session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov. 20, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: At the full November 20, 2023 Durham City Council meeting, Council honored late community leader Arnold Dennis and proclaimed the Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims before unanimously approving Consent Agenda Items 1-15 (6-0 with Mark-Anthony Middleton arriving at 7:45 PM). Under Item 16, Council rejected the state-enabled discretionary annexation of the Colvard Farms tract (0-5 by hand vote after an electronic voting malfunction) because city infrastructure standards had not governed its construction. Council then held a four-hour public hearing and intense deliberation on Item 17 (SCAD, TC2200001), ultimately passing a selective motion drafted on the dais by Jillian Johnson (4-3, with Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman opposed) that adopted staff-recommended provisions while stripping eight contested areas including the PATH proposal.

agenda_items.title: Tribute to Arnold Dennis and Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal paid tribute to the late Arnold Dennis—former Durham County Detention Center director, social worker, and community organizer with Just Passage—joined by his widow Betty Dennis and community members. Council also read a proclamation recognizing the Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims alongside advocate John Thomas.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda Items 1-15
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal read Consent Items 1 through 15—covering the Workers' Rights Commission appointment, Museum of Durham History technology/staff contract, ARPA COVID-19 small business impact model, Durham Symphony funding, Wheels public art, cloud connectivity, FY24 UPWP, NCDOT Austin Ave and Morreene Rd agreements, equity traffic calming, and water management expansion. Leonardo Williams moved approval, passing unanimously among the six present members.

agenda_items.title: Annexation Public Hearing: Colvard Farms Tract (S.L. 2014-47)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff explained that Session Law 2014-47 gave City Council sole discretion to annex Colvard Farms along Highway 751, separate from city acceptance of private infrastructure not built to city standards. After resident Brett Williams thanked Council for opposing forced taxes without infrastructure maintenance and roughly 20 neighbors registered opposition cards, Council rejected the annexation 0-5 by hand vote.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment Public Hearing & Vote: Simplifying Codes for Affordable Development (SCAD, TC2200001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a 6-0 procedural vote to extend public speaking time equally, Council heard hours of proponent and opponent testimony, closed the hearing, filed a November 3 letter from Habitat for Humanity's counsel, and recessed to review eight contested task force areas. Upon returning, Jillian Johnson moved—seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton—to adopt staff-recommended SCAD provisions while removing Topic 6, the PATH proposal, and specified clauses from Topics 3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 11, and 13; both the ordinance and consistency statement passed 4-3 at 11:45 PM.

votes.item_title: Item 16: Adopt Annexation Ordinance for Colvard Farms Tract (S.L. 2014-47)
votes.notes: Mayor O'Neal stated 'there is a no vote for annexation of Colvard Farms, 5' (with Mark-Anthony Middleton not yet arrived; one member present may not have raised a hand or 5 hands were counted, and no second motion was needed). Note: all six present members had indicated no intent to annex in the straw poll.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Leonardo Williams and seconded by DeDreana Freeman for procedural disposition, the annexation of Colvard Farms failed after an electronic clicker glitch prompted a hand vote in which zero members voted aye and Mayor O'Neal announced five no votes.

votes.item_title: Item 17 (Procedural): Extend Zoning Public Hearing Speaking Time Equally for SCAD Proponents and Opponents
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton arrived just as the vote concluded.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman and seconded by DeDreana Freeman, Council voted unanimously to extend speaking time equally for SCAD proponents and opponents beyond Rule 2.6.7(b)(1)'s 15-minute cap.

votes.item_title: Item 17 (Motion 1): Adopt Amended SCAD UDO Text Amendment (TC2200001) Excluding Staff-Unrecommended Sections, Topic 6, and PATH
votes.notes: Electronic voting system malfunctioned, so hand votes were recorded.
votes.discussion_detail: Jillian Johnson moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the SCAD provisions recommended by planning staff while excluding Topic 3 (§6.10.2.A.1), Topic 4 (§4.6.6.C.1, §5.4.2.B.2.a), all of Topic 6, Topic 7 (§6.8.2.A.2.a, §6.8.3, §6.8.4), Topic 8 (§6.10.1.C.1, §6.10.1.D.1, §6.10.2.B.2), Topic 10 (§6.12.3.B.11), Topic 11 (§6.12.5.E), Topic 13 (§6.10.1.C.1.f, §6.10.1.D.1.f), and the Affordable Housing PATH proposal. The motion passed 4-3 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 17 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Amended SCAD UDO Text Amendment
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Leonardo Williams and seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council adopted the statutory consistency statement for the amended SCAD ordinance by the same 4-3 hand vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Nov. 20, 2023
disagreements.issue: Passage of Modified SCAD UDO Text Amendment via Late-Night Dais Exclusion Motion
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 at 11:45 PM over whether to pass a selectively amended version of SCAD drafted orally on the dais from Attachment M or vote the private developer application down and allow staff to return with clean ordinance text.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve staff-recommended SCAD provisions tonight while carving out Topic 6, PATH, and disputed clauses for the UDO rewrite.
side_a_arguments: Passing uncontroversial staff-recommended reforms like detached row houses now avoids waiting years for the UDO rewrite.
Carving out specific UDO paragraph numbers recommended against by staff—plus Topic 6 and PATH—addresses major task force objections.
Council retains authority to monitor impacts and amend provisions later, as it did with Expanding Housing Choices.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject the private application as drafted or defer until staff returns with clear, finalized ordinance language for public review.
side_b_arguments: Reading out dozens of UDO section exclusions orally near midnight is confusing ('mumbly jumbly') and a disservice to residents and staff.
Voting SCAD down does not prevent staff from bringing back consensus items in clean ordinance form.
Major affordable housing advocates opposed PATH and task force discussions were incomplete.
disagreements.resolution: Both the selective SCAD ordinance motion and its consistency statement passed 4-3 by hand vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 9, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The brief November 9, 2023 Work Session—held two days after the municipal election with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman excused due to family illness—opened with council congratulations to newly elected and re-elected candidates and announcement of the November 20/21 Thanksgiving-week schedule. City Manager Wanda Page recognized the top three finishers in the 2023 Miles with the Mayor 2.5-mile race (Paul Wiebke, Stephanie Meiner, and Fire Chief Chris Iannuzzi), and Council unanimously placed all 15 consent items and two public hearings (Colvard Farms annexation and SCAD) onto the November 20 agenda with no pulled items. During Citizen Matters, Colvard Farms residents urged Council not to annex their county subdivision, and DeDreana Freeman pressed City Manager Page on restoring Spectrum cable broadcast access for Durham Television (DTV8), which Page estimated would take 60 days.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Election Remarks, and Miles with the Mayor Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the work session to order at 1:00 PM with six members present and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman excused due to her mother's illness and stepfather's hospice care. Council congratulated November 7 municipal election winners, and City Manager Wanda Page recognized Miles with the Mayor winners Chris Iannuzzi (3rd), Stephanie Meiner (2nd), and retiree Paul Wiebke (1st), approved by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Reading of Consent Items 1-15 and Public Hearings 16-17
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal read Consent Items 1 through 15—spanning the Workers' Rights Commission, Museum of Durham History, ARPA small business COVID impact study, Durham Symphony, Wheels public art, cloud connectivity, FY24 UPWP, NCDOT sidewalk/bike projects, equity neighborhood traffic calming, and water management expansion—plus Public Hearings 16 (Colvard Farms) and 17 (SCAD), with zero items pulled.

agenda_items.title: Neighborhood Gun Violence and Colvard Farms Annexation Opposition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Lora Burris raised concerns about violent crime and urged greater community unity. Multiple Colvard Farms speakers—including a resident addressing state legislative history, Vaidahi Desai, and Rafe Maser—spoke ahead of the November 20 public hearing to oppose forced annexation of their county homes.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Nov. 20 Agenda and DTV8 Broadcast Outage Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously adopted the November 20 City Council agenda (Consent Items 1-15; Public Hearings 16 and 17) on a motion by Leonardo Williams and Jillian Johnson. DeDreana Freeman asked when Durham Television (DTV8) would resume cable broadcasts for residents lacking internet; City Manager Page stated all agreements with Spectrum were executed with repairs expected in roughly 60 days, and Mayor O'Neal adjourned at 1:41 PM.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager Priority Item (2023 Miles with the Mayor Recognition)
votes.notes: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman had an excused absence.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Mark-Anthony Middleton and seconded by DeDreana Freeman, Council unanimously approved the City Manager's priority item recognizing winners of the October 21 Miles with the Mayor event.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for November 20, 2023 City Council Meeting (Consent: 1-15; Public Hearings: 16-17)
votes.notes: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman had an excused absence.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Leonardo Williams and seconded by Jillian Johnson, Council unanimously approved the November 20 meeting docket with Items 1-15 on Consent and Items 16-17 set for General Business public hearings.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 6, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council approved an excused absence for Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, passed the consent agenda unanimously, and heard post-vote public criticism regarding MWBE compliance on city and affordable housing contracts. Council reviewed draft RFP parameters for the 505 West Chapel Hill Street redevelopment, debating commercial square footage flexibility and whether to require preservation of the small existing building. In a 4-3 split vote, Council approved the Perry Farm consolidated annexation, utility extension agreement, and Planned Development Residential 3.155 rezoning over environmental, well-water, blasting, and transportation concerns raised by Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Council Members DeDreana Freeman and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman. Council also unanimously approved supplemental appointments to the Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence Request for Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman requested an excused absence for the November 9 meeting due to a family matter in New York. Council moved and voted immediately on the request by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Clerk Priority and Supplemental Updates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page reported additional information provided for Item 13 (505 West Chapel Hill Street), Item 17 (UNRBA consensus principles for the Falls Lake Nutrient Management Strategy), and Item 23 (Cortez Drive Townhouses comprehensive plan consistency attachment J). The City Clerk added supplemental Item 26 for Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee appointments.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval and Post-Vote Public Comment on Item 5 (MWBE Audit)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda unanimously after overcoming initial voting clicker issues. Mayor Elaine O'Neal then recognized Ms. Adams, who had intended to speak on Item 5 (Underutilized Business Compliance Performance Audit, Sept. 2023) and criticized General Services and Community Development for failing to meet MWBE participation commitments on affordable housing bond contracts and Item 13.

agenda_items.title: Redevelopment of 505 West Chapel Hill Street Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council discussed how to structure the 505 West Chapel Hill Street RFP to balance community housing priorities with developer feasibility. Key discussion points included dropping a hotel suggestion, undertaking a city-initiated rezoning if commercial space drops below 250,000 square feet, and whether to require or leave optional the preservation of the existing small building.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote recorded in digest

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Zoning Map Change: Perry Farm
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following extensive debate over Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B stream buffers and impervious limits, impaired nearby county wells, potential blasting, taxpayer transportation funding burdens, and the project's statutory non-contiguous annexation classification at filing, Council voted on three motions with Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton presiding. Annexation/utility extension and PDR 3.155 rezoning passed 4-3, while the consistency statement passed 6-1.

agenda_items.title: Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Under supplemental Item 26, Council considered the appointment of Tracy Gibson and Murphy Lu to at-large seats on the Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee with terms expiring June 30, 2024. The appointments were approved without dissent.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman (Nov. 9, 2023)
votes.notes: Voice vote with no opposition heard.
votes.discussion_detail: Holsey-Hyman requested an excused absence for a family matter in New York on November 9.

votes.item_title: Perry Farm Consolidated Annexation Ordinance and CSC Group LLC Utility Extension Agreement (Item 24, Motion 1)
votes.notes: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton held the gavel during the Item 24 motions.
votes.discussion_detail: Annexes Perry Farm into the City of Durham effective Dec. 31, 2023 and authorizes a utility extension agreement with CSC Group LLC.

votes.item_title: Perry Farm Zoning Map Change to PDR 3.155 and Rural Residential Public/Civic (Item 24, Motion 2)
votes.notes: Same 4-3 split as Motion 1.
votes.discussion_detail: Transfers property from county Residential Rural (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B) to city Planned Development Residential 3.155 and Rural Residential with a textual development plan limiting uses to public and civic.

votes.item_title: Perry Farm NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement (Item 24, Motion 3)
votes.notes: Council Member Freeman was the sole dissenter on consistency.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopts statutory comprehensive plan consistency statement under NCGS 160D-605.

votes.item_title: Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee Appointments (Item 26)
votes.notes: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton yielded the gavel back to Mayor O'Neal afterward.
votes.discussion_detail: Appoints Tracy Gibson and Murphy Lu to at-large seats on the Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee through June 30, 2024.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 6, 2023
disagreements.issue: Perry Farm Consolidated Annexation and PDR 3.155 Rezoning (Item 24)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 over annexing and rezoning the Perry Farm property in the Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation, utility extension, and PDR 3.155 rezoning with watershed protections.
side_a_arguments: The property already carries county Residential Rural zoning and is developable regardless of annexation.
Environmental proffers go beyond UDO minimums while maintaining the 24%/70% impervious limits and 100-foot/50-foot stream buffers.
Residents seeking pure natural heritage preservation would need to pursue nonprofit land acquisition.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexation and rezoning due to environmental, water, blasting, and infrastructure concerns.
side_b_arguments: Nearby county residential wells are impaired and county/city water availability remains unresolved.
Blasting impacts, natural heritage loss, and unfunded taxpayer transportation burdens need deeper scrutiny.
State law still classifies the annexation as non-contiguous based on its status at initial filing.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session (Oct. 19, 2023)
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Elaine O'Neal on an excused absence, Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over the October 19 work session. Council suspended the rules to adopt a resolution modifying the Durham–Chapel Hill annexation boundary (85 CVS 30108) to enable water and sewer service for a proposed 75-to-80-unit affordable housing project, and approved City Manager priority updates including removing previously acted-upon items and adding a Commerce Street Apartments affordable housing loan item. Council received an informational presentation on the Upper Neuse River Basin Association (UNRBA) Consensus Principles II for the revised Falls Lake Nutrient Management Strategy, reviewed the draft RFP for the 505 West Chapel Hill Street redevelopment, and discussed the timeline for a potential 2024 General Obligation infrastructure bond. Council concluded by settling the agenda for the November 6 regular meeting.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Attorney Priority Items (Incl. Item 6 Annexation Boundary)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted a memo on Oct. 5 carryover funding, removed Items 10 (Comprehensive Plan, approved Oct. 16) and 15 (Indian Monsoon lease, referred back), flagged Item 17 (UNRBA presentation), and added supplemental Item 25 (Commerce Street Apartments LLC affordable housing loan commitment). The City Attorney requested suspending the rules to vote on Item 6, modifying the Durham–Chapel Hill annexation boundary so a 75–80 unit affordable housing development (25% at 30% AMI, 75% at 60% AMI) could meet a May state deadline.

agenda_items.title: UNRBA Consensus Principles II for Revised Falls Lake Nutrient Management Strategy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Presenters explained that UNRBA Consensus Principles II align with Durham's goals and asked jurisdictions to adopt non-binding resolutions supporting the principles ahead of state Division of Water Resources and EPA rulemaking starting in 2024. The principles are intended to strengthen joint watershed negotiating power without locking the city into final rule text.

agenda_items.title: Redevelopment of 505 West Chapel Hill Street Draft RFP Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council and community advocates reviewed the first draft RFP for the city's last major publicly owned downtown parcel, discussing how to incentivize more than the 80-unit affordable housing minimum and deliver housing first. Members also weighed soft office market conditions against an existing development plan requiring 250,000–450,000 square feet of commercial space and a possible site test fit for the Museum of Durham History.

agenda_items.title: Discussion on a Potential Infrastructure Bond
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero led a discussion on pursuing a future infrastructure bond, with resident Trisha Smart urging funding for sidewalk gaps along state DOT roads in annexed areas. Finance Director Tim Flora outlined the six-month Local Government Commission and referendum timeline, advising that anchor projects should be identified during the upcoming budget and CIP process for a June resolution ahead of a November ballot.

agenda_items.title: Settling the Nov. 6, 2023 Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager presented the proposed consent and general business agendas for the November 6 meeting, keeping Item 13 (505 West Chapel Hill Street) on General Business for further council and public input alongside public hearings on Items 20–24. Council voted to settle the agenda.

votes.notes: Mayor Elaine O'Neal had an excused absence; Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's attendance was not shown in the truncated roll call.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspends work-session rules to permit formal voting on the annexation boundary resolution.

votes.notes: Mayor Elaine O'Neal was excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Approves boundary modification (already approved by Chapel Hill) as the first step before superior court review and a consolidated annexation for a 75–80 unit affordable housing development.

votes.notes: Mayor Elaine O'Neal was excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepts City Manager's agenda adjustments including removing Items 10 and 15 and adding supplemental Item 25 (Commerce Street Apartments LLC loan commitment).

meetings.title: Durham City Council Oct. 16, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: Council opened the October 16 meeting with ceremonial recognitions for Durham's arts and cultural sector, the NCCU women's tennis team, and Diligence Month, before approving the consent agenda unanimously after referring Item 12 (downtown trash compactor contract) back to staff and pulling Item 8 (Durham Comprehensive Plan) for discussion. Council Member DeDreana Freeman questioned Planning staff on the Southeast Future Growth Area, sewer-driven map additions in the Urban Growth Boundary, and Kemp Road boundaries prior to Item 17 (related UDO text amendments). In zoning public hearings, Council unanimously approved a Commercial General rezoning in Eno River District B (with a 6-0 consistency vote) and unanimously approved rezoning, consistency, and a utility extension agreement for 13.63 acres at 2610 South Miami Boulevard (PDR 19.824). Council also heard public comment on GoDurham Access bonuses, approved an excused absence for the October 19 work session, and announced three SCAD Task Force community forums.

agenda_items.title: Arts & Culture Report, NCCU Women's Tennis Recognition, and Diligence Month Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council received an economic impact presentation on Durham's nonprofit arts and cultural sector and heard from the Piedmont Laureate. Council also honored the NCCU Women's Tennis team and proclaimed Diligence Month.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval and Referral of Item 12
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager referred Item 12 (PINAM Construction Inc. downtown trash compactor contract at 315 Holland Street) back to General Services. Council Member DeDreana Freeman pulled Item 8 (Durham Comprehensive Plan), and Council unanimously approved the remaining consent items.

agenda_items.title: Durham Comprehensive Plan (2023) and Related UDO Text Amendments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff requested considering Item 17 (UDO text amendments) after Item 8 (Comprehensive Plan). Council Member Freeman questioned staff on the Southeast Future Growth Area, fire response exclusions around CIP Road, adding Farrington Mill and Pattison Road areas back into the Urban Growth Boundary based on private sewer solutions, and Kemp Road boundary lines before the digest middle truncation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Discussion recorded; vote section truncated in digest

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: O&I-GDP to Commercial General-TDP (Eno River District B)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following discussion in which the applicant agreed to prohibit an unspecified use in their textual development plan, Council closed the public hearing. Council approved the rezoning from Office & Institutional with a graphic development plan to Commercial General with a textual development plan in Eno River District B, followed by the consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change and Utility Extension: 2610 South Miami Boulevard
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented Chester Allen / East Wake Industrial LLC's request to rezone six parcels totaling 13.63 acres at 2610 South Miami Boulevard to Planned Development Residential 19.824 (recommended 8-0 by the Planning Commission) near the future Ellis Road commuter rail stop, including tree preservation and sediment buffers. Council unanimously adopted the rezoning ordinance, consistency statement, and utility extension agreement.

agenda_items.title: GoDurham Access Public Comment, Excused Absence, and SCAD Task Force Notice
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Marie Hill Facing spoke on including GoDurham Access workers in bonuses. Council granted an excused absence for the October 19 Thursday work session and read public notice of three SCAD Task Force special meetings scheduled for October 24, 25, and 27 at City Hall.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Unanimous voice vote for excused absence)

votes.item_title: UDO Rezoning: O&I-GDP (Eno River District B) to Commercial General-TDP (Eno River District B)
votes.notes: Clerk announced 'passes unanimously'; the companion consistency motion immediately afterward passed 6-0, indicating one member may have been temporarily away from the dais.
votes.discussion_detail: Rezones property from Office and Institutional with a graphic development plan to Commercial General with a textual development plan in Eno River District B.

votes.item_title: NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Eno River District B Commercial General Rezoning
votes.notes: Reported as 6-0; digest does not identify which single member was temporarily off the dais.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopts statutory consistency statement for the Eno River District B rezoning.

votes.item_title: 2610 South Miami Boulevard Rezoning to PDR 19.824 (Item 20, Motion 1)
votes.notes: Hand vote; full 7-member presence confirmed during Motion 3 count.
votes.discussion_detail: Rezones 13.63 acres from RS-20, CN, IL, and IL(D) to Planned Development Residential 19.824.

votes.item_title: 2610 South Miami Boulevard NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement (Item 20, Motion 2)
votes.notes: Unanimous hand vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopts consistency statement for 2610 South Miami Boulevard rezoning.

votes.item_title: Utility Extension Agreement with East Wake Industrial LLC (Item 20, Motion 3)
votes.notes: Unanimous hand vote after verifying all raised hands.
votes.discussion_detail: Authorizes the City Manager to enter into a utility extension agreement with East Wake Industrial LLC for the 2610 South Miami Boulevard project.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for October 19, 2023 Work Session
votes.notes: Voice vote with no opposition.
votes.discussion_detail: Excuses absence for the Thursday, October 19 work session (Mayor O'Neal was subsequently absent on Oct. 19).

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 5, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: At the October 5 work session, Council approved an excused absence for the November 21 work session, accepted City Manager priority changes (including a FY22-23 carryover budget/CIP amendment presentation and referring the Indian Monsoon lease back to General Services), and heard announcements on Week Without Driving and the upcoming SCAD Task Force community forums. The centerpiece of the meeting was the continued negotiation over mid-year city employee bonuses, where Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Council Members pressed to find additional savings toward a $5,000 bonus target for lower-paid employees while balancing adopted budget limits. After suspending the rules and recessing, Council voted unanimously to adopt Option 3 for employee bonuses with an explicit exemption excluding elected City Council members from receiving the $1,000 payout, and directed staff to identify potential departmental savings to support additional worker tiers. Council concluded by reviewing board nominations and settling the October 16 regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Week Without Driving, SCAD Task Force Dates, and Nov. 21 Excused Absence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton and Council Member Leonardo Williams highlighted Week Without Driving transit experiences, and Williams and Council Member DeDreana Freeman announced SCAD Task Force special meetings for October 24, 25, and 27 (noting Middleton was added). Council also approved an excused absence request for the November 21 Tuesday work session.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items (Carryover Funding & Indian Monsoon Lease Referral)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson presented Item 6 (FY22-23 to FY23-24 carryover funding and CIP/internal service fund budget amendments) and referred Item 13 (Candable Inc. DBA Indian Monsoon lease amendment at Morgan Rigsbee Parking Garage) back to General Services. Council voted to accept the priority items and briefly discussed whether work-session votes required suspending the rules.

agenda_items.title: Review of Oct. 16 Draft Agenda and Pulled Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal read items 5 through 20 into the record, including the Comprehensive Plan, Sprout Social contract, Piney Wood Park pickleball courts, Public Works Operations Center testing, Morgan Rigsbee leases, classification/compensation study contract, and zoning hearings. Items 6 and 12 (downtown trash compactor) were pulled for discussion.

agenda_items.title: Employee Retention Bonus Options and Council Member Exemption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal and Council debated funding sources for higher employee bonuses (including Participatory Budgeting, CIP adjustments, Community Safety expansion, and 3–5% departmental savings to find $3M beyond the $10M already targeted). After suspending the rules and recessing, Council unanimously adopted Option 3 while exempting elected Council members from receiving the bonus and directing staff to analyze further savings for three lower-earning tiers.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations Report and Settling Oct. 16 Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported board nominations (including Taylor Price to Environmental Affairs and Perna Desai to Discover Durham) and noted re-advertising a Participatory Budgeting vacancy after a duplicate nomination. Council unanimously settled the October 16 agenda with Item 12 on GBA, Items 17–20 as public hearings, and Item 13 referred back to staff.

votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepts Item 6 carryover presentation and referral of Item 13 back to General Services.

votes.item_title: Suspend the Rules to Vote on Employee Bonus Package at Work Session
votes.notes: Followed by a short recess before the main vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspends work-session rules so Council can take formal action on employee bonus Option 3.

votes.item_title: Adopt Employee Bonus Option 3 with Elected Official Exemption
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman and Jillian Johnson seconded simultaneously.
votes.discussion_detail: Approves Option 3 employee bonuses while exempting elected City Council members from receiving the bonus; staff directed to review options to bring three lower-earning groups up to $5,000.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 5, 2023
disagreements.issue: Scope of Mid-Year Employee Bonuses and Budget Savings Targets
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether Option 3 sufficiently addressed worker pay demands or whether staff should be pressed to cut an additional $3 million across city budgets to reach a $5,000 bonus goal for employees earning under $90,000.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt Option 3 today as a compromise while keeping pressure on staff to identify further savings for the $5,000 target.
side_a_arguments: The adopted budget already assumes $10 million in savings, requiring another $3 million in cuts (totaling $13 million) to reach $5,000.
Option 3 gets funds out quickly while providing higher tiers some relief beyond $500 and focusing more money on lower-paid workers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Push aggressively for departmental, CIP, Participatory Budgeting, or Community Safety reductions to fulfill the full $5,000 ask.
side_b_arguments: Department heads should evaluate 3–5% reductions, CIP slowdowns, or reallocating uncommitted funds to meet the original ask for employees under $90,000.
Option 3 is acceptable as an initial step only with a commitment to continue pursuing the remainder.
disagreements.resolution: Council unanimously adopted Option 3 with an exemption for elected Council members and directed staff to report back on options to cover the additional groupings up to $5,000.

meetings.title: Durham City Council - Oct. 2, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: Council began the October 2 meeting with Minority Enterprise Development (MED) Week proclamations and a ceremony awarding proclamations and Keys to the City to four historic Durham civic figures: Dr. E. Lavonia Allison, Judge Orlando F. Hudson Jr., former Mayor William V. Bell, and Rep. H.M. 'Mickey' Michaux Jr. Following a motion regarding Mayor Elaine O'Neal's upcoming excused absences and truncated middle agenda items, Council held a contested public hearing on the Smallwood Townhouses consolidated annexation and Planned Development Residential 7.405 rezoning next to a FedEx hub and All Saints United Methodist Church. Despite opposition from FedEx's counsel over 2–3 a.m. truck noise and headlights and concerns from Council Member DeDreana Freeman over the lack of a sound wall and unpaved cemetery access easement, Council approved annexation and rezoning 6-1 and passed the consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: MED Week Proclamation and Keys to the City Ceremony
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman read the Minority Enterprise Development Week proclamation presented to Deputy CFO Shayla Faucette. Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton then presented proclamations and Keys to the City to Dr. E. Lavonia Allison, Judge Orlando F. Hudson Jr., former Mayor William V. Bell, and Rep. H.M. 'Mickey' Michaux Jr.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal requested excused absences for October 19 and November 6 while handling other city business, noting Mayor Pro Tem Middleton would hold the gavel. A motion was made, though the vote completion was omitted in the transcript truncation.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Zoning Map Change: Smallwood Townhouses
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed the Smallwood Townhouses proposal (Holly Springs Associates LLC), featuring a shared stormwater facility with All Saints UMC and a 20-foot public access easement behind the cemetery. FedEx attorney Tina Powell warned of unbuffered 2–3 a.m. freight noise and lights and urged a sound wall, which the developer could not commit to; Council approved annexation and PDR 7.405 rezoning 6-1 (Freeman opposed) and consistency 7-0.

votes.notes: Council Member Freeman voted no.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council - Oct. 2, 2023
disagreements.issue: Smallwood Townhouses Compatibility Adjacent to FedEx Hub and Pedestrian Easement Paving
disagreements.summary: Council split 6-1 over approving residential townhouses immediately adjacent to an active FedEx freight facility without a sound wall or guaranteed paved path in the cemetery easement.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the Planning Commission-recommended project, shared stormwater upgrades, and cemetery easement.
side_a_arguments: The applicant worked out a shared stormwater facility with All Saints UMC and proffered a 20-foot public access easement per Planning Commission feedback.
It is not the Council's role to shield buyers or developers from obvious adjacent industrial uses visible on site, and late-stage requests like a sound wall were not raised at Planning Commission.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexation and rezoning due to overnight industrial noise/light impacts and uncommitted sidewalk construction.
side_b_arguments: Residential units will sit closer to the FedEx hub than existing neighborhoods, exposing residents to 2–3 a.m. truck noise and lights without a sound wall.
The applicant could not commit to paving or installing pervious surfacing within the 20-foot cemetery pedestrian easement due to uncalculated impervious limits.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and PDR 7.405 rezoning passed 6-1; consistency statement passed 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 21, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The September 21 work session opened with announcements on early voting, the groundbreaking of 132 affordable housing units on Greater Joy Baptist Church property, and District Attorney Satana Deberry's letter exonerating Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman. Council accepted City Manager priority items (Item 6 carryover funding and Item 9 cemetery ordinance updates) and reviewed the upcoming regular meeting agenda. The bulk of the session focused on an intense budget discussion over funding mid-year city employee bonuses—especially for sanitation and lower-wage workers—amid staff warnings that $4.9 million in additional payouts would require freezing positions or cutting contracts and that the proposed $6.5 million ordinance could not be split on the floor. After a recess, at least six Council members agreed to defer a vote and direct staff to rework the bonus tiers within the $6.5 million cap for the next meeting, before settling the remainder of the agenda unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Early Voting, Greater Joy Affordable Housing Groundbreaking, and DA Exoneration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton urged residents to vote early with ID and celebrated District Attorney Satana Deberry's letter exonerating Council Member Holsey-Hyman. Mayor O'Neal highlighted National Night Out and the 132-unit affordable housing groundbreaking at Greater Joy Baptist Church, and Holsey-Hyman thanked O'Neal and Council Member Freeman for supporting her throughout the investigation.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items and Consent Agenda Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously accepted City Manager priority items 6 (carryover funding presentation) and 9 (cemetery ordinance revisions presentation). The Mayor read administrative consent items 1–12 into the record, including board appointments, ARPA nonprofit support, NC Coalition to End Homelessness HMIS services, leases, and Solarize LMI.

agenda_items.title: Mid-Year Employee Bonus Proposal and Budget Capacity Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council and staff debated how to structure mid-year bonuses while preserving fiscal stability, with management explaining the FY23-24 budget already assumed a $10 million positive variance and finding another $4.9 million would require freezing positions or cutting contracts. After a recess, Council declined to force an up-or-down vote on the existing ordinance and instead reached consensus to have staff rework the $6.5 million allocation to better prioritize lower earners and protect part-time employees.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Deferred / Directed staff to rework options

agenda_items.title: Settling Consent Agenda and SCAD / Legislative Procedure Updates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously settled the agenda with Items 1–5 and 7–19 on consent, holding the reworked bonus item for the next session. Council Members Williams and Freeman reported finalizing academic facilitators for SCAD committee forums, and Mayor O'Neal asked Middleton to report on legislative procedures at the next work session.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager Priority Items (Items 6 and 9)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepts City Manager presentations on carryover funding (Item 6) and cemetery ordinance revisions (Item 9).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 21, 2023
disagreements.issue: Structure and Funding of Mid-Year City Employee Bonuses
disagreements.summary: Council members and staff disagreed over whether to pass the $6.5 million bonus ordinance immediately or delay for reworked tiers that shift more funds to lower earners without cutting part-time bonuses or destabilizing city reserves.
disagreements.side_a_position: Either pass the existing ordinance for immediate early-October payouts or avoid exceeding $6.5M without identified expenditure cuts.
side_a_arguments: Passing the current ordinance allows employees to see money in their first October paycheck.
Finding an extra $4.9M mid-year requires freezing positions or stopping contracts because the budget already assumes a $10M positive variance, and the city cannot jeopardize disaster reserves.
disagreements.side_b_position: Rework the $6.5M allocation (or identify Q2 savings) to increase bonuses for lower-earning workers without reducing part-time worker payouts.
side_b_arguments: The current distribution is unsatisfactory for the lowest-paid employees and higher-tier bonuses can be trimmed closer to the $300 already budgeted.
Part-time employees received only $500 previously and should not have their bonuses reduced.
disagreements.resolution: After a recess, at least six Council members supported deferring the vote and directing staff to bring back reworked bonus options.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting Sept. 18, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Elaine O'Neal traveling, Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over the September 18 regular meeting. Council issued ceremonial proclamations for the South Durham Little League State Champion All-Star Teams, Guatemalan Independence Day, and World Alzheimer's Awareness Day, and acknowledged city workers in the gallery by inviting them to the September 21 work session on employee pay. After referring Item 21 (260 South Miami Boulevard) back to Planning, Council unanimously (6-0) approved a rezoning from Office & Institutional to Commercial General in Eno River District B along with its consistency statement. Council then approved Item 24 (Shannon at Old Chapel Hill), a 3.08-acre mixed-use rezoning for 43 townhomes, 17 multifamily units, and 3,500 square feet of commercial space, by a 5-1 vote with Council Member Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman voting no on the rezoning and 6-0 on consistency.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations and Sanitation Worker Compensation Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council recognized the South Durham Little League All-Stars, Guatemalan Independence Day, Dementia Inclusive / World Alzheimer's Awareness Day, and workforce development graduates. Mayor Pro Tem Middleton noted gallery placard rules and invited city workers present to return on September 21 when the full Council would address compensation.

agenda_items.title: Referral of Item 21 (260 South Miami Blvd) and Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager referred Item 21 (260 South Miami Boulevard consolidated zoning map change) back to the City-County Planning Department. Mayor Pro Tem Middleton began reading the consent agenda into the record before the digest's middle truncation.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: O&I-GDP to Commercial General-TDP (Eno River District B)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council discussed use classification with Planning staff and the applicant agreed to voluntarily prohibit an unspecified use in its textual development plan. Council approved the rezoning and NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Shannon at Old Chapel Hill
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented Thomas & Hutton/Sutton's request to rezone 3.08 acres at 3641 Shannon Road and 3638 Old Chapel Hill Road to Residential Compact (D) and Commercial General (D) for up to 43 townhomes, 17 multifamily units, and 3,500 sq ft of commercial space (recommended 12-0 by Planning Commission). A resident raised traffic, transit, and pedestrian safety concerns; Council approved the rezoning 5-1 (Holsey-Hyman opposed) and the consistency statement 6-0.

votes.item_title: Rezoning: O&I-GDP (Eno River District B) to Commercial General-TDP (Eno River District B)
votes.notes: Mayor Elaine O'Neal was absent (traveling); companion consistency vote confirmed 6 members voting.
votes.discussion_detail: Rezones property from Office & Institutional (GDP) to Commercial General (TDP) in Eno River District B, with applicant proffering a use prohibition.

votes.notes: Mayor Elaine O'Neal absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopts statutory consistency statement for the Eno River District B Commercial General rezoning.

votes.notes: Mayor Elaine O'Neal absent.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Sept. 18, 2023
disagreements.issue: Shannon at Old Chapel Hill Mixed-Use Rezoning (Item 24)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 5-1 to approve the Shannon at Old Chapel Hill rezoning, with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman dissenting amid questions about affordable housing proffers and resident traffic/safety objections.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve mixed-use infill density within the Urban Growth Boundary.
side_a_arguments: The Planning Commission recommended approval 12-0 and the site is walkable to retail, dining, the post office, and the Southwest Durham Library.
The developer committed to affordable housing proffers and sidewalk construction linking to MLK.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the rezoning over traffic, pedestrian safety, transit gaps, and affordable housing proffer concerns.
side_b_arguments: Residents warned of severe congestion on a two-lane road, limited sidewalks and public transit, and whether a three-way stop is safe.
Holsey-Hyman specifically questioned the staff report and developer's affordable housing proffers before voting no.
disagreements.resolution: Rezoning passed 5-1; consistency statement passed 6-0.
