meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 7, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: Council opened the September 7 work session with Council Members Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson on excused absences and approved a City Manager priority title change for Item 22 (Lumley Road Multifamily consolidated annexation). During Citizens Matters, sanitation workers and residents protested city worker compensation and housing unaffordability amid stalled garbage collection, sparking a sharp exchange in which Mayor Elaine O'Neal pledged to find budget adjustments while Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton defended the adopted 6% pay increase and ongoing compensation study. Finance Director Tim Flora then presented the FY 2022–23 fourth-quarter financial report, showing an $11.5 million General Fund expenditure underspend and healthy reserves alongside a $527,000 Solid Waste overtime/temporary-worker overrun and a $1.3 million Parking Fund net loss. Council concluded by reviewing split committee nominations for Discover Durham and settling the September 18 regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Lumley Road Multifamily Priority Title Change and Draft Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Council Members Caballero and Johnson excused and Mayor Pro Tem Middleton arriving shortly after, Council approved retitling Item 22 from a zoning map change to a consolidated annexation for Lumley Road Multifamily. Mayor O'Neal read consent, presentation, and public hearing items into the record.

agenda_items.title: Sanitation and Essential Worker Pay Protest and Council Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sanitation workers and residents (including James Chavis and Ms. Johnson) demanded above-market compensation and cited rising living and housing costs as uncollected trash sat in the city. Mayor O'Neal sided with the workers and asserted that balanced-budget rules still allow finding solutions, whereas Mayor Pro Tem Middleton defended the 6% (4%+2%) pay raise and compensation study against unsustainable mid-year promises.

agenda_items.title: FY 2022-23 Fourth Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director Tim Flora reported that the General Fund finished $11.5M under budget ($5.4M personnel, $4.1M operating), with strong sales and property taxes offsetting a $1.9M decline in utility franchise taxes. Enterprise results showed Solid Waste with $527K in personnel overruns from overtime/temps, Parking with a $1.3M net loss from low downtown deck occupancy, Transit with a $4.9M surplus, Water/Sewer near breakeven ($150K net), and strong DPAC performance.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations (Discover Durham Split) and Settling Sept. 18 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported board nominations and noted a 3–2 split on Discover Durham Lodging Limited Services (two votes for Perna Desai vs. three votes to re-advertise). Council unanimously settled the September 18 regular meeting agenda with Items 1–18 on consent and Items 21–24 on GBA public hearings.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager Priority Item 22 Title Change (Consolidated Annexation: Lumley Road Multifamily)
votes.notes: Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson were excused; Mark-Anthony Middleton had not yet arrived.
votes.discussion_detail: Changes Item 22 title from Zoning Map Change to Consolidated Annexation, Lumley Road Multifamily.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 7, 2023
disagreements.issue: City Sanitation and Essential Worker Compensation Adjustments
disagreements.summary: Following protests from sanitation workers over wages and housing affordability, Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton expressed contrasting positions on mid-year pay adjustments versus staying within the adopted budget and compensation study.
disagreements.side_a_position: Stand with protesting workers and pursue immediate budget options to raise compensation.
side_a_arguments: Essential workers face severe inflation and cannot afford to live in Durham while doing vital city work.
Even under statutory balanced-budget rules, Council can identify ways within the numbers to support workers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Rely on the adopted 6% (4% + 2%) pay increase and ongoing compensation study rather than unsustainable mid-year promises.
side_b_arguments: Ad-hoc mid-year raises create recurring obligations that would require raising taxes or cutting services the next year.
The city already delivered a 6% raise and is conducting a compensation study to raise pay responsibly.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; compensation bonus options were subsequently brought back to the September 21 and October 5 work sessions.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Sept. 5, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: At the September 5, 2023 Durham City Council meeting (with Jillian Johnson excused), Council unanimously adopted 6-0 the Phased Development and Tree Preservation UDO text amendment (TC2200004), capping residential mass grading at 50 acres per phase and raising boundary buffers and tree preservation incentives. Council split 5-1 to approve the South Miami Boulevard annexation and rezoning (350 multifamily units with 10% affordable) over Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's opposition, and deadlocked 3-3 to defeat the 301 Infinity Road townhouse and office rezoning amid traffic, stormwater, and geotechnical concerns. Council also unanimously approved updated water and sewer connection, pump station review, and flow monitoring fees (6-0) while noting that SCAD engagement updates (Item 26) had been referred back to Planning.

agenda_items.title: National Recovery Month, Welcoming Week Proclamations, and City Worker Wage Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman presented the National Recovery Month proclamation with Michelle McKinney, and Javiera Caballero read the Welcoming Week proclamation while reflecting on the 50th anniversary of the Chilean coup. Council members also heard a representative for city workers and DeDreana Freeman expressed support for addressing the missed 2% pay increase in the next budget cycle.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Revisions and Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1-2, 4-16, 25)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted revised 10-year police personnel cost estimates on Item 22 and confirmed Item 26 (SCAD Engagement Plan Update) was referred back to the Planning Department. Council approved the Consent Agenda—including Merrick-Moore ARPA preservation, Bull City United and Project BUILD interlocal agreements, AOC domestic violence/gang caseload renewals, Legal Aid DEAR eviction diversion, Limited Obligation Bonds, Q2 crime report, water/stormwater contracts, and FAA grant 64—without pulling any items.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment: Phased Development and Tree Preservation (TC2200004)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner/Arborist Robin Schultz presented TC2200004 amending UDO Articles 7, 8, 9, and 13 to cap residential grading phases at 50 acres, require 20% to 30% tree preservation with affordable housing incentives, expand 0.6-opacity 30-foot buffers across tiers, and add 5- and 10-foot no-grading setbacks. Environmental advocates sought an even lower 20-to-25-acre cap and tighter variance controls while Morningstar Law attorney Keenan Conder argued phasing increases housing costs, but Council praised the measure as a balanced first step.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Zoning Map Change: 1102 & 1034 South Miami Boulevard (Z2200012)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Alexander Cahill and attorney Tom Johnson presented a 27-acre non-contiguous annexation and rezoning from RS-20 and Commercial Center to RS-M(D) for up to 350 apartments (at least 10% affordable), committing to 18% open space, 29% tree save, and US 70 right-of-way dedication. Residents Pam Williams, Donna Stanback, and Andrew Heffner opposed due to severe US 70 congestion, school overcrowding, and stream buffers, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and Leonardo Williams backed infill density to support transit and federal funding.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change & UEA: 301 & 401 Infinity Road (Z2200006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and applicants Jamie Schwedler and Jeremy Anderson presented an 18.1-acre rezoning from RS-20 to PDR 7.203 and OI(D) for up to 99 townhomes and a 5,000-square-foot office building, which had advanced 5-3 from the Planning Commission. Neighbors raised alarms over single-access traffic onto Infinity Road/Roxboro Street, removal of the road project from the STIP, Eno River runoff, and rock formations that stalled the adjacent Rocky Creek site, resulting in a 3-3 tie that defeated the rezoning.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Updates to Water/Sewer Connection, Pump Station Review, and Flow Monitoring Fees
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Don Greeley of Water Management presented fee schedule updates increasing water/sewer connection and pump station review fees and establishing a sewer flow monitoring fee to recover actual city costs. DeDreana Freeman asked about equity relief for disadvantaged households connecting to sewer, and Greeley noted state statutes mandate uniform fees across all customers.

agenda_items.title: Engagement Plan Update for SCAD UDO Text Amendments (TC2200001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Although Item 26 had been referred back to the City-County Planning Department, Mayor Elaine O'Neal introduced co-chairs DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams, who committed to sending written correspondence to public-hearing speakers and organizing community engagement on whether and how SCAD should move forward.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Referred back to Planning / No vote

votes.notes: Jillian Johnson absent (excused).
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the phased grading and tree preservation revisions effective October 1, 2023, framing the measure as an important first step on erosion control and tree canopy conservation to be further evaluated during the UDO rewrite.

votes.notes: Jillian Johnson absent (excused).
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the statutory consistency statement for the phased development and tree preservation text amendment.

votes.item_title: Item 22 Motion 1: Annex 1102 & 1034 South Miami Boulevard and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with BPC NC Miami Durham LLC
votes.notes: Jillian Johnson absent (excused).
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted 5-1 to approve the non-contiguous annexation effective September 30 and the utility extension agreement, with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman dissenting.

votes.item_title: Item 22 Motion 2: Adopt Zoning Map Amendment Z2200012 (RS-20/CC to RS-M(D), 1102 & 1034 South Miami Blvd)
votes.notes: Applicant required to submit updated development plan reflecting 18% UDO open space requirement prior to final approval.
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved rezoning the 27-acre site for up to 350 multifamily units (10% affordable) over Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's no vote.

votes.notes: Jillian Johnson absent (excused).

votes.item_title: Item 23 Motion 1: Adopt Zoning Map Amendment Z2200006 (RS-20 to PDR 7.203 and OI(D), 301 & 401 Infinity Rd)
votes.notes: Because Motion 1 (rezoning) failed on a tie, the utility extension agreement motion was not adopted separately and only the consistency statement proceeded.
votes.discussion_detail: The rezoning for 99 townhouses and 5,000 sq ft of office space failed on a 3-3 tie with Mayor Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman voting no after neighbor testimony on Infinity Road traffic, lack of STIP road funding, and unperformed geotechnical studies.

votes.notes: Jillian Johnson absent (excused).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Sept. 5, 2023
disagreements.issue: Infill Housing Density vs. Infrastructure Capacity and Geotechnical Risk at 301 & 401 Infinity Road
disagreements.summary: Council deadlocked 3-3 on rezoning 18.1 acres on Infinity Road for 99 townhomes and 5,000 sq ft of office, pitting proponents of infill density inside the proposed Urban Growth Boundary against opponents citing severe traffic delays, un-funded road upgrades, and Eno River rock/stormwater risks.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the infill townhouse and office rezoning as consistent with the draft Comprehensive Plan and necessary to grow inward inside an urban growth boundary.
side_a_arguments: Limiting outward sprawl via an Urban Growth Boundary requires accepting higher infill density within existing boundaries.
Withholding development until NCDOT funds every road project would stall municipal growth and reduce the city's priority for state SPOT 7 transportation intervention.
The applicant offered affordable housing and school fund contributions and committed to geotechnical borings prior to construction.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning due to unfunded road safety deficiencies on Infinity Road/Roxboro Street, lack of pre-zoning geotechnical testing, and neighborhood/environmental strain.
side_b_arguments: Transportation staff confirmed the Infinity/Roxboro project was dropped from the adopted STIP with no current funding.
Neighbors reported 5-to-10-minute delays exiting driveways and single-access bottlenecks, plus bedrock and runoff problems that stalled the adjacent Rocky Creek site.
No geotechnical study had been completed prior to the rezoning vote.
disagreements.resolution: Rezoning motion failed on a 3-3 tie.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Aug. 24, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: At the August 24, 2023 Work Session (with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman and Leonardo Williams excused), Council reviewed pulled items including the Merrick-Moore ARPA home preservation project, the AOC gang-reduction prosecutor renewal, and a $1M Hazen & Sawyer biosolids and methane-to-energy study. Staff delivered presentations on Q2 2023 crime trends, the Police Satisfaction Survey, city park soil lead testing, ARPA obligations ($48.1M obligated, $33.7M unobligated), and Bull City United's annual progress, and Council set the September 5 docket. At the end of the session, Mayor Elaine O'Neal's proposal to establish an ad hoc SCAD Community Engagement Task Force sparked a sharp rift, as Jillian Johnson and Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed bypassing standard application processes and duplicating Planning staff's analysis, leaving the formal task force without majority support.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences, Participatory Budgeting Update, and Manager/Clerk Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council excused Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman and Leonardo Williams (5-0), heard Jillian Johnson's announcement that Participatory Budgeting voting would run September through October, and approved City Manager and City Clerk priority items (5-0) including moving the infrastructure bond and plastic bag ordinance discussions to September.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Merrick-Moore Preservation, AOC Gang Reduction Prosecutor, and Water Biosolids Study
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Bonita Green and Chris Dreps spoke in support of Item 4's Merrick-Moore, Walltown, and Braggtown ARPA home repair, food, and senior tech project. On Item 8, Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned Community Safety Director Ryan Smith and ADA Michelle Cofield on whether the District Court gang-reduction prosecutor position targets gang/gun cases specifically or general understaffed caseloads, and on Item 14 Water Management Director Don Greeley confirmed the Hazen & Sawyer biosolids/methane study is proactive long-term planning.

agenda_items.title: 2023 Second Quarter Crime Report and ETC Police Satisfaction Survey
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Patrice Andrews presented Q2 crime figures showing overall Part 1 violent crime down 7% (with 23 homicides across 21 cases and an 82.6% year-to-date homicide clearance rate) alongside a 31% rise in reported forcible rapes driven partly by belated reports and an uptick in robberies targeting Hispanic victims. ETC Institute then presented the Police Satisfaction Survey results with representative demographic coverage.

agenda_items.title: City Park Soil Testing Update, ARPA Portfolio Update, and Bull City United Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Keith Chadwell delivered an oral update on soil testing at city parks, followed by a Finance/Budget team briefing on ARPA allocations totaling $48.1M obligated and $33.7M unobligated. Staff then presented the annual update on Bull City United's community violence interruption program.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Sept. 5 Agenda and Debate Over Proposed SCAD Engagement Task Force
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the September 5 meeting agenda (Consent Items 1-2, 4-16, 25; GBA Items 21-24). Mayor Elaine O'Neal then proposed a SCAD Community Engagement Task Force co-chaired by DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams, but Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned its statutory charge and Jillian Johnson opposed appointing pre-committed advocates outside normal application processes and departed, resulting in no majority for a formal task force while Freeman and Williams committed to direct outreach.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Agenda Set 5-0; SCAD Task Force rejected

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Aug. 24, 2023
disagreements.issue: Creation of an Ad Hoc SCAD Community Engagement Task Force
disagreements.summary: Council clashed over Mayor Elaine O'Neal's proposal to convene an ad hoc SCAD Community Engagement Task Force co-chaired by DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams using volunteers from the August 21 public hearing.
disagreements.side_a_position: Establish a balanced ad hoc task force of SCAD proponents and opponents co-chaired by Freeman and Williams to facilitate public dialogue and restore community trust.
side_a_arguments: Bringing opponents and proponents into the same room can counter misinformation and counterbalance perceived developer influence.
Having two council co-chairs representing differing perspectives would give the public a clear avenue to understand SCAD before a final vote.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject forming an ad hoc task force and rely on professional Planning staff's neutral analysis and standard UDO rewrite engagement.
side_b_arguments: Land use hearings are statutorily prescribed and it is unclear who the task force would report to or what work product it could produce when members already hold entrenched positions.
Past equity task forces used formal application and vetting processes rather than selecting self-selected speakers from one hearing.
Planning staff already provides an unbiased, neutral analysis of SCAD.
disagreements.resolution: Formal task force proposal dropped after lacking majority support (Jillian Johnson departed and Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed); DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams proceeded informally to contact hearing sign-ups.

meetings.title: Durham City Council August 21, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present on August 21, 2023, Council approved the Consent Agenda 7-0 (including participatory budgeting appointments, Low-Income Homeowners Relief ILA, Mist Lake solar contract, Edison Johnson Recreation Center renovation, and Woodcroft Parkway design) while pulling Item 16. The main business centered on Item 26, the Simplifying Codes for Affordable Development (SCAD) UDO text amendment (TC2200001), which opened with a recusal challenge raised by DeDreana Freeman against Javiera Caballero that Caballero rejected under NCGS 160D-109. Following public testimony from supporters and opponents and an applicant request, Council granted a 90-day continuance of the SCAD public hearing to November 20, 2023 by unanimous thumbs-up consensus, and subsequently passed Item 16 authorizing condemnation easements at 4000 Fayetteville Street 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1-15, 17-23)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman recounted touring Southeast Durham blasting damage with Preserve Rural Durham, Leonardo Williams praised Hillside and Southern high school bands, and Mayor O'Neal previewed the August 31 Comprehensive Plan hearing and secured a thumbs-up for a GoTriangle appointment. Council then adopted the Consent Agenda 7-0, excluding pulled Item 16 and noting Item 24 (water/sewer fees) was referred back to Water Management.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment: Simplifying Codes for Affordable Development (SCAD, TC2200001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant Planning Director Bo Dobrzynski summarized the privately initiated SCAD text amendment, six summer compromises with InterNeighborhood Council, and the Planning Commission's 6-6 denial vote. DeDreana Freeman questioned whether Javiera Caballero had to recuse due to emails alleging her husband's early involvement, which City Attorney Kim Rehberg and Caballero stated did not trigger NCGS 160D-109; after polarized testimony and an applicant continuance request, Council voted unanimously by thumbs-up to continue the hearing 90 days to November 20, 2023.

agenda_items.title: Condemnation Resolution for 4000 Fayetteville Street (ST-264 Road Improvement Project)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Earlier in the meeting (`00:21:44`), homeowner Jerry McLean urged Council to inspect his 4000 Fayetteville Street property and settle permitting and encroachment disputes before taking easements by eminent domain. Following the SCAD continuance, Council voted 6-1 to adopt the condemnation resolution for two easements, with DeDreana Freeman dissenting.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Grant 90-Day Continuance of SCAD UDO Text Amendment (TC2200001) Public Hearing to November 20, 2023
votes.notes: After the vote, resident Mimi Kessler objected to suspending further public comment that night; Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton raised a point of order supporting the Mayor's adherence to the continuance vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the applicant's formal request for a 90-day continuance to hold facilitated community dialogue, Council voted unanimously by thumbs-up consensus to continue the public hearing to November 20, 2023 and requested an engagement outline in two weeks.

votes.item_title: Item 16: Adopt Resolution Authorizing Condemnation of Portions of 4000 Fayetteville Street for ST-264 Road Improvement Project
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the condemnation resolution 6-1 after hearing property owner Jerry McLean's objections regarding prior encroachment and permit denials.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 21, 2023
disagreements.issue: SCAD (TC2200001) Recusal Challenge, Process Legitimacy, and Continuance Timing
disagreements.summary: Debate erupted over whether Javiera Caballero faced a conflict of interest requiring recusal under NCGS 160D-109 and whether delaying SCAD 90 days built public trust or rewarded obstruction ahead of municipal elections.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question potential conflicts of interest in SCAD's drafting and require structured 90-day community engagement with balanced task force oversight before any vote.
side_a_arguments: Emails cited by residents alleged a council member's spouse appeared on early SCAD planning documents, raising questions of inconsistent standards across council members.
Community trust in the planning process and application history had been damaged and required an objective, balanced engagement plan.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject unfounded recusal allegations under NCGS 160D-109, oppose tying land-use decisions to election calendars, and base the eventual SCAD vote on Planning staff's technical analysis.
side_b_arguments: City Attorney Kim Rehberg confirmed NCGS 160D-109 requires a direct, substantial, material financial benefit for recusal, and Javiera Caballero stated her husband had no SCAD involvement.
Tying zoning decisions to upcoming elections ('council shopping') sets a problematic precedent and delays addressing Durham's UDO rewrite and housing needs.
Many public criticisms relied on pre-packaged talking points or mischaracterizations rather than the staff analysis.
disagreements.resolution: Council unanimously granted the applicant's 90-day continuance request to November 20, 2023 while declining to force recusal.

meetings.title: City Council Subcommittee with Durham Association of Realtors - August 17, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: On August 17, 2023, the City Council Subcommittee with the Durham Association of Realtors—attended by Mayor Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and realtor/staff liaisons—held a brief informal Zoom check-in without a formal agenda. Participants reviewed the July 31 reopening of the City's Down Payment and Closing Cost Assistance Program (offering up to $80,000 through approved lenders) and discussed a realtor concern that the program's 20% combined-subsidy cap prevented buyers from stacking city aid with CPLP funds, unlike Raleigh's uncapped policy. Members agreed to follow up with Community Development and DHA Director Anthony Scott on applicant counts, removing the 20% cap, the ADU pilot program budget, and Homeownership Choice Voucher updates at the September 28 meeting.

agenda_items.title: Down Payment Assistance Program Reopening, 20% Subsidy Cap, DHA Homeownership Vouchers, and ADU Pilot

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session August 10, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: At the August 10, 2023 Work Session (with DeDreana Freeman and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman excused), Council approved excused absences 5-0 and gave unanimous consensus for future work-session discussions on the Don't Waste Durham plastic bag ordinance and a potential infrastructure bond. During Citizens Matters, residents raised safety concerns at W.D. Hill Recreation Center, lead in city parks, blasting permit rules, and fiercely debated the upcoming SCAD text amendment, while Jerry McLean opposed eminent domain at 4000 Fayetteville Street (Item 16). Planning staff presented the 2023 Durham Comprehensive Plan ahead of the August 31 joint hearing—highlighting the proposed 10.8-square-mile Urban Growth Boundary reduction, 143,000-unit capacity, Policy 165 edits, and six disputed map areas—before Council finalized board nominations and set the August 21 agenda 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences, Plastic Bag Ordinance & Infrastructure Bond Consensus, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 5-0 to excuse DeDreana Freeman and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman from the August 10 session and Elaine O'Neal from September 18. Javiera Caballero received unanimous thumbs-up consensus to schedule an updated Don't Waste Durham / Duke Law plastic bag ordinance presentation and a guided staff discussion on an infrastructure bond, followed by City Manager and Clerk agenda updates.

agenda_items.title: Citizens Matters (W.D. Hill Safety, Park Lead, Blasting, and SCAD) and 4000 Fayetteville St Condemnation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents addressed drug activity and safety at W.D. Hill Recreation Center (Ms. Bowie), lead contamination in parks (James Chavis), blasting permit revisions (Donna Stanback), and sharply differing views on SCAD (Robert Chapman supporting; James Chavis, Minister Rafiq Zaidi, Jackie Wagstaff, Donna Stanback, and Katie Ross urging delay or denial). On pulled Item 16, Jerry McLean objected to city condemnation of easements at 4000 Fayetteville Street and cited unresolved property-line and permit disputes.

agenda_items.title: Presentation: 2023 Durham Comprehensive Plan and Unresolved UGB/FGA Map Areas
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Kayla Seibel and Planning staff reviewed the draft 2023 Comprehensive Plan, noting the Planning Commission's June 13 unanimous approval with Policy 165 edits, a proposed 10.8-square-mile reduction in the Urban Growth Boundary (while retaining capacity for 143,000 units versus 60,000 projected by 2050), and six disputed areas (Stagville/Old Oxford Rd, Farrington Mill Rd/Sheffield Farms, Patterson Rd, Cheek/Redwood Rd, Hamlin Rd, and Southeast FGA). Javiera Caballero requested adding explicit UGB and housing-production review to the plan's biennial assessment policy, and Mark-Anthony Middleton cautioned that holding the UGB will require denser, taller infill development.

agenda_items.title: Board/Commission Nominations and Approval of August 21 Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported nominations for the Historic Preservation Commission, Environmental Affairs Board, Mayor's Council for Women, BPAC, CAC, and Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee (with Middleton and Williams shifting votes to resolve a split on Christopher Rhodes). Council then voted 5-0 to set the August 21 agenda with Consent Items 1-24 and GBA Public Hearing Item 26 (SCAD).

meetings.title: Durham City Council August 7, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: Returning from summer recess on August 7, 2023 with all seven members seated, Council unanimously approved the Consent Agenda (7-0), Item 10 stormwater web portal maintenance after James Chavis withdrew his pull (7-0), and four motions authorizing the Series 2023 Limited Obligation Bonds (7-0). Across five zoning and annexation public hearings, Council unanimously approved Brightleaf North (90 DHIC for-sale townhouses, 7-0), Fairhaven Walk (192 100%-affordable units plus a 6,000-square-foot daycare in Braggtown, 7-0), and 602 North Hoover Road light-industrial rezoning (7-0). However, Council split 4-3 on two Southeast Durham townhouse annexations—Fletcher Crossing (80 townhouses at 707 S. Mineral Springs Rd) and 631 & 633 Clayton Road (61 townhouses with 9 at <=80% AMI)—with Mayor Elaine O'Neal, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman voting no over traffic, missing development plan attachments, and infrastructure strain.

agenda_items.title: Compassion Month Proclamation, Sept. 7 Excused Absences, Consent Agenda, and Item 10
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal proclaimed August 2023 as Compassion Month, DeDreana Freeman flagged a request from the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People to delay SCAD, and Council excused Jillian Johnson and Javiera Caballero for September 7 (7-0). Council approved the Consent Agenda 7-0 (excluding Item 10), heard JFK Towers senior residents early, and later approved Item 10 (stormwater web portal contract) 7-0 after James Chavis withdrew his request to speak.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Limited Obligation Bonds Series 2023
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director Tim Floyd presented the required statutory public hearing for the Limited Obligation Bond Series 2023 sale (scheduled to close October 17) financing previously approved capital projects. With no public speakers, Council unanimously approved all four financing and LGC application motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Brightleaf North (548 & 2040 Copperleaf Pkwy and 2021 US 70 Hwy E)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Brooke Roper and attorney Neil Ghosh (with DHIC/Four Star) presented a 20.4-acre rezoning from CG(D) to CN(D) for up to 90 for-sale townhouses, noting a 300-foot NCDOT right-of-way reservation along US 70 eliminated the commercial parcel and that the developer proffered funds to DPS (for 42 students) and the affordable housing fund. A Brightleaf at the Park resident urged attention to traffic egress and Lick Creek, and Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Zoning Map Change: Fletcher Crossing (707 S. Mineral Springs Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and attorney Neil Ghosh presented ODG 87 LLC's 9.47-acre annexation and rezoning from RS-20/RR to PDR 8.347 for up to 80 townhouses (no affordable units, denied 5-4 by Planning Commission). Opponents Pam Williams and Donna Stanback cited narrow curvy roads, lack of transit, Mineral Springs traffic, Holder Road flooding, and school impacts, splitting Council 4-3 to approve annexation and rezoning (O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman voting no) while adopting the consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Fairhaven Walk (313 Old Oxford Rd & Dania Blane)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Brooke Roper, designer Pam Porter, and Commonwealth Development's Justin Mitchell presented an 8.19-acre rezoning to PDR 23.445 for 192 apartments (100% affordable, 30% at <=30% AMI) plus 6,000 sq ft of Head Start daycare space, a covered bus shelter, and off-site sidewalks developed with the Braggtown Community Association. Council members praised the project as a model of neighborhood collaboration and 2019 housing bond investment, passing both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: 602 North Hoover Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Brooke Roper and applicant Christian Santiago presented a 1.217-acre rezoning from RS-20 to Industrial Light with a textual development plan (IL(D)) consistent with the future land use map and banning adult establishments, bars, nightclubs, and internet sweepstakes cafes. Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Zoning Map Change: 631 & 633 Clayton Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and attorney Adam Stallings (for Winmore 208 LLC) presented a 7.706-acre annexation and rezoning from RS-20 to RS-M(D) across from Southern High School for up to 61 townhouses, including nine units restricted to <=80% AMI. Neighbor Tanisha Wiggins opposed townhomes next to long-time single-family homes, and DeDreana Freeman flagged that the site-plan exhibit was missing from Legistar due to a staff error; Council voted 4-3 to approve annexation and rezoning (O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman voting no) and 7-0 on consistency.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 7, 2023
disagreements.issue: Fletcher Crossing (Item 17) Southeast Durham Townhouse Density vs. Road and Stormwater Infrastructure
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 on annexing and rezoning 9.47 acres at 707 S. Mineral Springs Road for 80 townhouses, debating housing supply and diverse housing types against narrow road infrastructure, transit absence, and Planning Commission's 5-4 denial.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve Fletcher Crossing to add 80 missing-middle townhomes at 8.347 units per acre rather than 16 expensive single-family homes.
side_a_arguments: The draft Place Type map designates the area as Mixed Residential Neighborhood, which townhomes help diversify.
16 large-lot single-family homes by right would cost around $800,000 compared to mid-$300k/low-$400k townhomes.
The developer is dedicating 10 feet of right-of-way along Mineral Springs and Holder Roads and preserving rear tree cover and wetlands.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning due to inadequate road and transit infrastructure, neighborhood flooding, and lack of small-area planning or affordable housing.
side_b_arguments: Narrow 10-foot lanes, lack of streetlights or transit, and downstream Holder Road flooding show the infrastructure is not ready for cumulative density.
Without small-area planning or affordable housing proffers, piecemeal upzonings shift infrastructure burdens onto existing residents.
The Planning Commission recommended denial 5-4 and Council should respect differing neighborhood impacts across projects.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency statement passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 7, 2023
disagreements.issue: 631 & 633 Clayton Road (Item 20) Townhouse Rezoning and Missing Legistar Development Plan Exhibit
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on annexing and rezoning 7.7 acres across from Southern High School for 61 townhouses (with 9 at <=80% AMI) after adjacent homeowner opposition and discovery that the development plan map was missing from the public Legistar packet.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 61-townhome project with nine income-restricted units as an appropriate infill transition near Southern High School.
side_a_arguments: Planning Commission recommended approval 6-2 and the project proffers nine affordable units at 80% AMI plus enhanced erosion-control flocculents.
A 30-foot, 60%-opacity buffer separates townhomes from the neighboring Wiggins residence, and line-of-sight concerns alone do not justify denial.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose voting on the rezoning while the development plan building-envelope exhibit was omitted from the public Legistar file and adjacent long-time residents oppose.
side_b_arguments: Staff acknowledged an oversight left the development plan attachment out of Legistar, depriving residents and Council of exact building-envelope and sightline details.
Adjacent property owner Tanisha Wiggins testified the townhomes clash with long-established single-family homes on Clayton Road.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency statement passed 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session July 20, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: At the July 20, 2023 Work Session (with Jillian Johnson excused), Council approved priority updates from the City Manager, City Attorney (entering closed session for *Estate of Brooke Maynard v. City of Durham* and *Daryl Dowdy v. City of Durham*), and City Clerk (6-0). During Citizens Matters, residents spoke on HOA street-parking petitions, council ward residency rules, Pride Durham NC coordination, lead testing in parks, and severe maintenance failures—mold, broken elevators, and weekly water/AC shutoffs—at JFK Towers senior apartments. Mark-Anthony Middleton pulled Item 9 to confirm expanded staffing coverage under the police psychological services contract amendment, the Clerk resolved a tie on the Open Space and Trails Commission by re-advertising, and Council set the August 7 agenda 6-0 before adjourning to closed session.

agenda_items.title: Announcements, Manager/Attorney/Clerk Priority Items, and Closed Session Motion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman highlighted park lead testing as a priority, Mark-Anthony Middleton congratulated Christina Reardon on becoming permanent Budget Director, and Council welcomed youth from StrongHER TogetHER. Council approved 6-0 the Manager's technical corrections to Items 18-20, the Clerk's mayoral Historic Preservation appointment (Item 2), and the City Attorney's request for a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) on *Estate of Brooke Maynard v. City of Durham* and *Daryl Dowdy v. City of Durham*.

agenda_items.title: Citizens Matters: HOA Parking Petitions, Ward Residency, Pride Durham, JFK Towers, and Park Lead
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Gwen Silver requested reforms to residential street-parking petitions, Jacqueline Wagstaff sought legal clarity on council ward residency rules, and Pride Durham co-chair Jesse Huddleston asked for a city liaison ahead of September 23 Pride events. Sherman Henson and JFK Towers resident Johnetta Alston detailed uninhabitable senior-housing conditions (two inches of mold from AC leaks, failing elevators, blocked trash chutes, weekly water outages), while James Davis Jr./James Chavis demanded transparency on lead in parks and Mr. Roberson asked about the council investigation and worker pay.

agenda_items.title: Contract Amendment with FMRT Group LLC for Police Psychological Services
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned Assistant Police Chief David Anthony regarding the FMRT Group LLC psychological services amendment. Assistant Chief Anthony confirmed the expansion accommodates additional personnel entering covered units.

agenda_items.title: Board/Commission Nominations and Approval of August 7 Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced Glenda Ange, Courtney James, and Prince R. Rivers for the Durham Affordable Housing Implementation Committee and reported a 3-3 split on the Durham Open Space and Trails Commission, resolved when Javiera Caballero switched to support re-advertising (4 votes). Council then voted 6-0 to set the August 7 agenda (Consent Items 1, 3-15; GBA Public Hearings Items 16-21) and adjourned into closed session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting June 20, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The marathon June 20, 2023 Durham City Council meeting centered on a fierce 4-3 split over city employee pay and the $600 million FY 2023-24 budget. Mayor Elaine O'Neal's priority motion (moved by DeDreana Freeman) for an immediate ~$8 million / 2-cent tax increase to restore missed FY 2021 step raises failed 3-4, and Council then adopted the balanced budget with no tax increase 4-3 (O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman dissenting), funding a 6-8% pay increase, HEART expansion, Vision Zero, and Hayti initiatives while deferring structural pay adjustments to a comprehensive pay study. Council also approved 5-2 the Streets at Southpoint Mall #2 rezoning (O'Neal and Javiera Caballero dissenting over lacking on-site affordable units and binding community-benefit agreements), while unanimously passing 7-0 the RP Residential Studio Apartments (36 affordable units), $9.8 million in ARPA financing for Sankofa Landing (156 affordable units), and Downtown Durham Inc. contracts (6-0, Mark-Anthony Middleton recused).

agenda_items.title: Proclamations and Failed Motion for Immediate ~$8M / 2-Cent Tax Increase for Missed FY 2021 Step Raises
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After proclamations for the Mayor's Monarch Pledge, Cleft & Craniofacial Awareness Month, and hip-hop duo Little Brother, Mayor Elaine O'Neal recounted ride-alongs with Durham Fire and Police and invited a priority motion from DeDreana Freeman (seconded by Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman) to add ~$8 million via a 2-cent property tax increase to restore the missed FY 2021 step raise for all city staff. Mark-Anthony Middleton, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, and Leonardo Williams opposed raising taxes without a completed pay study or plan, defeating the motion 3-4.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption and Downtown Durham Inc. Agreements (Items 33 & 34)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the Consent Agenda 7-0 (including the UDO rewrite contract with Code Studio, Durham County EMS/HEART amendment, Replacement Tasers, Western Intake ARPA funding, and Hayti/housing grants; excluding pulled Items 22, 33, and 34, and referring Item 24 back). Council then approved Items 33 and 34 funding Downtown Durham Inc. 6-0 each, with Mark-Anthony Middleton recusing under state conflict-of-interest law due to his DDI board seat.

agenda_items.title: FY 2023-24 Budget, FY 2024-29 CIP, and FY 2024-26 Strategic Plan Ordinances
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following public comments from firefighters such as Kyle Hundings and Elsie Carvener citing step compression since 2016 and COVID freezes, Council sharply debated budget priorities. Middleton, Johnson, Caballero, and Williams argued the $600M budget delivers 6-8% raises without a regressive property tax hike on top of the county's 3-cent increase and responsibly awaits a pay study, while Freeman, Holsey-Hyman, and O'Neal voted no over the exclusion of missed step restoration.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: RP Residential Studio Apartments (2504 E. Hwy 54, Z2200059)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Alexander Cahill and Reinvestment Partners Executive Director Peter Skillern presented a 1.9-acre rezoning from OI(D) to RS-M(D) to convert an extended-stay hotel into 72 studio apartments, with 36 units restricted at 60% AMI and accepting housing choice vouchers. Opponents Frank Borden and Larry Booth raised fire-safety and 350-sq-ft occupancy concerns, which Skillern rebutted by citing building-code permitting and a two-person studio occupancy cap; Council approved both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Supplemental Item: Consolidated Zoning Map Change — Streets at Southpoint Mall #2
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Brookfield Properties (Neil Ghosh, Pat Anderson, Andre Banks, Jason Bonnet) sought rezoning to add up to 1,382 multifamily units, 300,000 sq ft of office, a 200-room hotel, and 100,000 sq ft of retail alongside a $1M Affordable Housing Loan Fund contribution, $23,000 to DPS, and GoTriangle/bikeway upgrades. Opponents (Larissa Cybel, Stella Adams, Jim Svara) demanded 20% on-site affordable units and binding local-hiring/MWBE targets, and Javiera Caballero sought a continuance for a development agreement, which the applicant declined; Council approved the UEA and rezoning 5-2 (O'Neal and Caballero voting no) and consistency 7-0.

agenda_items.title: ARPA $9.8M Financing for Sankofa Landing (156 Affordable Units) and Approval of May Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Braggtown residents Donna Frederick and Vanessa Mason-Evans praised LDG Multifamily Development's collaboration with the Braggtown Community Association on Sankofa Landing. Council unanimously approved all three motions committing up to $9,799,714 in ARPA funds for the 156 affordable rental units (7-0) and approved the May 15 and May 18 Council minutes (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Bull City Express Track Club $50,000 Junior Olympics Request (Omar Beasley)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Omar Beasley requested $50,000 to help send 65 youth athletes from Bull City Express to the Junior Olympics. While council members stressed the need for an established RFP or youth-emergency funding process rather than ad hoc end-of-meeting asks, Council gave an informal thumbs-up for City Manager Wanda Page to explore funding within existing budgetary authority.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informal thumbs-up direction to City Manager

votes.item_title: Mayor's Priority Item: Motion to Add ~$8 Million (~2-Cent Property Tax Increase) to Restore Missed FY 2021 Step Raise for City Employees
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Elaine O'Neal invited an out-of-sequence motion ahead of the budget vote to fund one missed FY 2021 step raise (~$8M via a 2-cent tax hike); the four-member majority voted no, opposing tax hikes prior to a completed pay study.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consent Agenda (Items 1-14, 16-21, 23, 25-32, 35-38, 41-43; Excluding Pulled Items 22, 33, 34; Item 24 Referred Back)
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously adopted the Consent Agenda excluding pulled Items 22, 33, and 34.

votes.item_title: Item 33: FY 2023-24 Agreement with Downtown Durham Inc. to Fund Economic Development Programs
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton statutorily recused.
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved the Downtown Durham Inc. economic development contract 6-0 with Mark-Anthony Middleton recused due to serving on DDI's board of directors.

votes.item_title: Item 34: Contract Amendment No. 2 with Downtown Durham Inc. for Downtown Durham Municipal Service District
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton statutorily recused.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting June 20, 2023
disagreements.issue: Immediate ~$8M / 2-Cent Tax Increase for Missed FY 2021 Employee Step Raises vs. Waiting for Pay Study in FY 2023-24 Budget
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on both Mayor Elaine O'Neal's priority raise motion and final adoption of the $600M FY 2023-24 budget over whether to immediately raise property taxes by 2 cents (~$8M) to restore a missed COVID-era step raise or complete a comprehensive pay study first.
disagreements.side_a_position: Immediately fund the missed FY 2021 step raise (~$8M / 2-cent tax hike) for firefighters, police, and all city employees in the FY 2023-24 budget.
side_a_arguments: Firefighters and city workers already waited through COVID freezes and 2016 study placement gaps, hurting retention and morale.
Withholding the step increase while prioritizing other spending places budget balancing on the backs of city staff.
A 2-cent tax increase is manageable and can be offset for low-income homeowners via the property tax grant program.
disagreements.side_b_position: Pass the balanced $600M budget with a 6-8% pay increase and no property tax hike now, and address structural step compression after a comprehensive pay study.
side_b_arguments: Adding an unvetted $8M obligation and 2-cent tax hike on top of the County's 3-cent increase after telling residents there was no tax hike is fiscally irresponsible and regressive during a housing crisis.
The proposed budget already includes a 6-8% pay increase alongside major investments in HEART, Vision Zero, sidewalks, and Hayti.
Major compensation adjustments require a pay study covering all employees—including 911 operators and non-step staff—rather than ad hoc floor amendments.
disagreements.resolution: Immediate raise motion failed 3-4; FY 2023-24 budget passed 4-3.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting June 20, 2023
disagreements.issue: Streets at Southpoint Mall #2 (Item 44) On-Site Affordable Housing and Binding Community Benefits Agreement
disagreements.summary: Council divided 5-2 on rezoning the Streets at Southpoint Mall for 1,382 market-rate apartments, office, retail, and hotel expansion, debating whether to approve with a $1M housing-fund proffer or continue the case for binding on-site affordable housing and local-hiring commitments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the Southpoint redevelopment with $1M to the Affordable Housing Loan Fund, $23,000 to DPS, and transit/bikeway upgrades to preserve Durham's top tax engine.
side_a_arguments: Southpoint generates $14M annually in city/county taxes with 71% of visitors coming from outside Durham, and delaying risks losing investment to Wake County.
Affordable housing partners testified that structured parking and non-QCT status make on-site LIHTC units financially unviable without scarce public subsidy.
Improved GoTriangle/GoDurham stops, park-and-ride spaces, and Triangle Bikeway easements deliver major transit benefits.
disagreements.side_b_position: Continue the hearing to negotiate a formal development agreement capturing on-site affordable units or land donation and enforceable local-hiring/MWBE commitments.
side_b_arguments: Brookfield built on-site affordable housing in DC, New York, and Jersey City, yet offered zero on-site units for Southpoint's 2,000 retail workers.
Promises on local hiring and supplier diversity cannot be enforced through zoning proffers and require a binding statutory development agreement.
disagreements.resolution: Applicant declined a further continuance; UEA and zoning motions passed 5-2 and consistency passed 7-0.

meetings.title: City Council Budget Work Session June 8, 2023 at 9:00 a.m.
meetings.executive_summary: The June 8, 2023 morning budget work session brought five seated council members together with City Manager Wanda Page and Interim Budget Director Christina Reardon ahead of the scheduled June 20 budget adoption. Council discussed potentially hiring an outside consultant out of the City Clerk's budget as a one-time project to update Council policies and procedures (last revised in 2017), as well as public safety and firefighter compensation ahead of a comprehensive pay study. Members debated whether to move forward with the proposed 7% public safety base-pay increase while awaiting the pay study and considering future retroactive adjustments, or whether to seek $7 million to $8 million in budget reallocations or a tax increase. Before adjourning at 9:37 a.m., Council approved a voice vote excusing the absences of DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Budget Work Session Opening
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the June 8, 2023 morning budget work session to order with five council members present (O'Neal, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, Jillian Johnson, and Leonardo Williams), noting expected absences for DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero. Interim Budget Director Christina Reardon and City Manager Wanda Page thanked budget staff for preparing data ahead of the June 20 budget adoption.

agenda_items.title: Council Policies and Procedures Consultant Budget Inquiry
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A council member proposed funding an outside consultant through the City Clerk's budget to help the Policies and Procedures Committee update council policies and procedures, which had not been overhauled since 2017. City Manager Wanda Page and staff explained that consulting contracts are budgeted as one-time, project-based costs determined by a defined scope of work rather than recurring line items, and noted that a white paper would be ready by the end of the summer for the Procedures Committee.

agenda_items.title: Public Safety and City Employee Compensation, Pay Study, and Tax Rate Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members and staff discussed firefighter and city worker retention, salary compression, and how to balance employee pay with impacts on lower-income residents. One perspective favored relying on the upcoming pay study before committing additional unallocated funds while keeping retroactive raises open as an option, whereas another voiced openness to a tax increase or reallocating $7 million to $8 million while acknowledging four council votes for a tax hike were unlikely. Staff clarified that unlike one-time bonuses, the proposed budget provides permanent base-pay increases of 6% to 8% for all employees, including 7% for public safety employees (a 2% step increase plus 5% pay plan implementation).

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences for Council Members Freeman and Caballero
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Before adjourning at 9:37 a.m., Mayor Elaine O'Neal noted upcoming work sessions later that afternoon at 1:00 p.m. and budget adoption scheduled for June 20, and entertained a motion to excuse the absences of DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero. The motion passed unanimously by voice vote of the five members present.

votes.item_title: Excuse Absences of Council Members DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero were absent and excused.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Elaine O'Neal entertained a motion to grant excused absences for DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero during the June 8 morning budget work session. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved without opposition by the five council members present.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Budget Work Session June 8, 2023 at 9:00 a.m.
disagreements.issue: Funding Immediate Additional Public Safety Raises vs. Relying on Proposed 7% Raise and Pay Study
disagreements.summary: Council members differed on whether to keep the proposed 7% public safety raise and wait for a comprehensive pay study before committing more money, or to seek $7M-$8M in immediate budget reallocations or a property tax increase.
disagreements.side_a_position: Implement the proposed 6%-8% base-pay increases (7% for public safety) while completing the pay study before adding unallocated funds, leaving retroactive raises open for consideration.
side_a_arguments: Higher taxes disproportionately burden lowest-income residents.
Adding unallocated money without a finalized plan is fiscally irresponsible.
The proposed budget already includes a 2% step plus 5% pay plan increase (7% total) added permanently to base pay for public safety staff.
disagreements.side_b_position: Explore reallocating $7 million to $8 million within the budget or raising taxes to protect employee morale and address public safety compensation sooner.
side_b_arguments: Public safety and city worker morale are suffering from salary compression and regional competition.
The city could examine finding $7M-$8M across the broader budget or consider a tax increase, though acknowledging four votes for a tax hike were unlikely.
disagreements.resolution: No formal budget amendment was offered; members asked staff to prioritize the pay study and consider retroactive payments if needed ahead of June 20 adoption.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session June 8, 2023 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the June 8, 2023 afternoon Work Session, six seated council members (with Mark-Anthony Middleton absent and excused) reviewed the docket for the June 20 regular meeting and discussed budget follow-up items and ATV traffic enforcement. Council unanimously approved an excused absence for Jillian Johnson's July 20 work session, City Manager Wanda Page's priority items (revising the Carver Creek Supportive Housing budget ordinance transfer and adding two Eckerd Youth Alternatives reentry contracts), and the June 20 agenda slate. During discussion of Item 16, staff noted that a $15,000 lawsuit settlement in October 2022 prompted the proposed city property trespass ordinance. At the end of the session, a last-minute request for roughly $40,000 to fund a seven-week Cornwallis summer camp sparked procedural objections over bypassing staff vetting protocols, though Council allowed the City Manager to evaluate the proposal.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements, July 20 Excused Absence, and ATV Traffic Enforcement Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman apologized for missing the morning budget session, Javiera Caballero and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman recognized graduates and Pride Month, and Leonardo Williams announced his keynote at the NC Fatherhood Conference and praised the Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association preserve. Council unanimously approved Jillian Johnson's excused absence request for the July 20 work session. Mayor Elaine O'Neal also led a discussion with the City Attorney and Police Chief regarding resident complaints about ATV riders and legal distinctions between moving and non-moving traffic enforcement.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items (Items 19, 42, and 43)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented priority revisions to Item 19 (Carver Creek Supportive Housing Acquisition Interlocal Cooperation Agreement), updating budget ordinance attachment 5 to reflect a general fund transfer to the dedicated housing fund and changing the ordinance number from 16093 to 16150. She also introduced supplemental Items 42 and 43 for PROWD and FY 2023-24 Training to Work reentry grant contracts with Eckerd Youth Alternatives Inc. Council approved the priority items unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Review of June 20 Agenda Items Including Trespass Ordinance, Censure/Recusal, Housing, and UDO Rewrite
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal read the full agenda covering board appointments, the External Auditor modification (Item 13), the May 2023 GoDurham Bus Safety Performance Audit (Item 14), the FY 2023-24 Budget and Strategic Plan (Item 15), the city property trespass standards ordinance (Item 16), council censure and recusal procedures (Item 17, pulled by O'Neal), Carver Creek (Item 19, pulled), the UDO comprehensive rewrite contract with Code Studio (Item 21), and multiple ARPA/housing grants (Items 18, 20, 22-25). During presentation of Item 16, staff explained the trespass ordinance allows manager-authorized re-entry when no alternative venue exists and stemmed from a $15,000 settlement in October 2022.

agenda_items.title: FY 2024 Budget Follow-Up: Recruit Academy Costs and Property Tax Rate Scenarios
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Ahead of placing the FY 2023-24 budget on the June 20 General Business Agenda, staff and council reviewed follow-up figures to be documented in an agenda memo. Staff reported total police/public safety academy recruit salary, benefits, and equipment costs at $64,393.67, a budgeted tax collection rate of 99.5%, and estimated that a two-cent property tax increase would add approximately $49 to $50 annually for a typical residential taxpayer while exempting nonprofits and churches.

agenda_items.title: Motion to Settle the June 20, 2023 Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved settling the agenda for the June 20 regular meeting with Consent Items 1-14, 16-38, and 41-43, General Business Agenda Item 15 (budget adoption), and GBA Public Hearing Item 40.

agenda_items.title: Last-Minute Funding Requests for Cornwallis Summer Camp and Sponsorship
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A council member requested informal council support for ~$40,000 to fund a seven-week science wraparound summer camp at Cornwallis to address DPR waitlists, alongside a second sponsorship request. While City Manager Wanda Page confirmed staff could vet the vendor and review end-of-year budget availability if directed by a majority, another member objected to bypassing established staff vetting via last-minute funding requests. Council agreed to let the manager review it while committing not to repeat the ad-hoc process, and discussed rotating council roles at awards presentations before adjourning at 4:24 p.m.

votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton was absent and previously excused.
votes.discussion_detail: Jillian Johnson requested an excused absence for the July 20, 2023 work session due to work travel out of the area. DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded the request, which passed unanimously by voice vote of the six members present.

votes.item_title: Approval of City Manager's Priority Items (Items 19, 42, and 43)
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton was absent and excused.
votes.discussion_detail: Following City Manager Wanda Page's presentation of priority updates to Item 19 (Carver Creek Supportive Housing Acquisition budget ordinance revision) and supplemental Items 42 and 43 (Eckerd Youth Alternatives Inc. reentry contracts), DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded approval, passing unanimously 6-0.

disagreements.issue: Protocol for Last-Minute Council Funding Requests (Cornwallis Summer Camp & Sponsorship)
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over the appropriateness of soliciting informal 'thumbs up' approval at the end of a work session for ~$40,000-$45,000 in unvetted summer camp and sponsorship requests.
disagreements.side_a_position: Provide informal council direction for the City Manager to fund a seven-week Cornwallis summer camp (~$40,000) before the fiscal year ends to help families on DPR waitlists.
side_a_arguments: DPR summer camps have long waitlists and community partners organized an immediate seven-week wraparound science option at Cornwallis.
The program would begin before the end of the current fiscal year if approved quickly.
disagreements.side_b_position: Require advance notice and standard staff vetting processes rather than approving ad-hoc last-minute funding requests from individual council members.
side_b_arguments: Council members received no advance information prior to the meeting.
Granting last-minute requests creates bad protocol and the appearance that council members can pull money out of thin air outside staff review.
disagreements.resolution: Council allowed the City Manager to evaluate the vendor and check end-of-year budget availability while agreeing not to handle future requests in this manner.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 5 2023 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the June 5, 2023 regular City Council meeting, all seven seated members convened for ceremonial proclamations, public hearings, and late-evening votes (with the middle portion of the meeting omitted from the transcript digest). Council issued five proclamations recognizing Juneteenth Weekend, NeighborWorks Week, LGBTQ Pride Month, Gun Violence Awareness Month, and Harmony Month. In recorded actions, Council corrected a technical clicker error on Item 37 for Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, continued the public hearing for Item 39 (The Streets at Southpoint Mall #2 rezoning) to June 20, 2023, unanimously approved a $500,000 economic development incentive grant (Item 40) for Eagle Landing Partners, LLC to restore the Scarborough House on Fayetteville Street into a boutique hotel, and unanimously approved the pulled 2023 First Quarter Crime Report (Item 22).

agenda_items.title: Five Ceremonial Proclamations (Juneteenth, NeighborWorks, LGBTQ Pride, Gun Violence Awareness, Harmony Month)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members presented five proclamations: Leonardo Williams read the Juneteenth Weekend Proclamation (June 16-19, 2023) to the Durham Juneteenth Collective/Village of Wisdom; DeDreana Freeman read the NeighborWorks Week Proclamation (June 3-10, 2023) honoring DCLT and DHIC; Jillian Johnson read the LGBTQ Pride Month Proclamation (June 2023) accepted by Natalie Watson of the LGBTQ Center of Durham; Mayor Elaine O'Neal read the Gun Violence Awareness Month Proclamation; and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman presented the Harmony Month Proclamation.

agenda_items.title: Vote Correction on Item 37 Motion 1 (Clicker Malfunction)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a break in the digest transcript, Mayor Elaine O'Neal announced a correction to an earlier vote on Item 37, Motion 1, noting that a voting clicker malfunction had incorrectly recorded Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's vote as 'no' when she intended to vote 'yes.'

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Zoning Map Change: The Streets at Southpoint Mall #2 (Continuance)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Brooke Roper presented an application by Laura Holloman (John R. McAdams Co.) to rezone seven parcels totaling 130.57 acres at Renaissance Parkway and Fayetteville Road from Commercial Center with a development plan and Residential Rural to Commercial Center with a development plan, noting the Planning Commission voted 10-3 to recommend denial on March 14, 2023. The applicant's representative requested a continuance to June 20, 2023 so two affordable housing developers could attend, which staff confirmed could be accommodated and Council approved without objection.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Economic Development Incentive Agreement: Eagle Landing Partners, LLC (Scarborough House)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chris Dickey (Office of Economic and Workforce Development) presented a $500,000 incentive agreement with Eagle Landing Partners, LLC to restore the 8,500 sq. ft. Scarborough House at 1406 Fayetteville Street into an 8-guest-room boutique hotel with a 5,000 sq. ft. conference/event space, providing NCCU hospitality training and revitalizing the Fayetteville Street commercial corridor. No public speakers came forward during the public hearing, and Council unanimously authorized the City Manager to execute the agreement.

agenda_items.title: 2023 First Quarter Crime Report (Pulled Consent Item)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council returned to pulled Consent Item 22 (2023 First Quarter Crime Report) to allow a remote public speaker (Mr. Cox) to address the council. Following public comment, Jillian Johnson moved and Leonardo Williams seconded approval, which passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Informal Polling on Pending Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Before adjourning at 11:35 p.m., a council member requested an informal 'thumbs up, thumbs down' poll on a resolution to be brought forward, receiving thumbs up from all members.

votes.item_title: Continue Public Hearing for Item 39 (Consolidated Zoning Map Change: The Streets at Southpoint Mall #2) to June 20, 2023
votes.notes: Planning Commission had previously recommended denial 10-3 on March 14, 2023.
votes.discussion_detail: After opening the public hearing on Item 39, the applicant requested a continuance until June 20, 2023 so two affordable housing developers could participate. Mayor Elaine O'Neal asked if any council member objected to continuing the hearing to June 20; seeing no objections, the continuance carried unanimously.

votes.item_title: Item 40: Authorize City Manager to Execute Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Eagle Landing Partners, LLC ($500,000 for Scarborough House)
votes.discussion_detail: Following the public hearing with no speakers in opposition or comment, Council voted unanimously 7-0 on a motion by Leonardo Williams and second by DeDreana Freeman to authorize up to $500,000 in economic development incentives for Eagle Landing Partners, LLC to renovate the Scarborough House at 1406 Fayetteville Street into a boutique hotel and event space.

votes.item_title: Item 22: 2023 First Quarter Crime Report (Pulled Consent Item)
votes.discussion_detail: Council took up pulled Consent Item 22 (2023 First Quarter Crime Report) after hearing remarks from virtual speaker Mr. Cox. Moved by Jillian Johnson and seconded by Leonardo Williams, the motion passed unanimously.

meetings.title: Budget Work Session Agenda May 25, 2023 at 9:00 am (Part 1)
meetings.executive_summary: In Part 1 of the May 25, 2023 City Council Budget Work Session (Day 2), Council received departmental FY 2024 budget presentations from Transportation and Community Safety without taking formal votes. Transportation Director Sean Egan highlighted the transition of 13 DCHC MPO positions to Triangle J Council of Governments, proposed additions of a Vision Zero Coordinator and Mobility Services Planner, raising starting GoDurham bus operator wages to $19.65/hour to address driver shortages and bus crowding, keeping GoDurham fare-free through June 2024, and leveraging over $30 million in federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law grants. Community Safety Director Ryan Smith began presenting the HEART department's proposed expansion from 20 to 47 FTEs, detailing over 5,200 first-response calls logged in its first year with a 95% clearance rate without police, fire, or EMS backup.

agenda_items.title: Opening of Day 2 FY 2024 Budget Work Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called Day 2 of the budget work session to order at 9:00 a.m. and turned proceedings over to Interim Budget Director Christina Reardon and City Manager Wanda Page to introduce the day's departmental budget briefings.

agenda_items.title: Transportation Department FY 2024 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan presented the department's FY 2024 budget covering ~80 city staff and >200 GoDurham and ACCESS transit workers, noting the transfer of 13 DCHC MPO positions to TJCOG and creation of a Vision Zero Coordinator and Mobility Services Planner. He highlighted starting GoDurham operator pay rising to $19.65/hour, keeping transit fare-free through June 2024 with $8M+ from Durham County transit sales tax, stabilizing parking without fee hikes, and securing >$30M in federal grants (including $10.8M for Durham Station). During Q&A, Egan discussed speeding up bus stop upgrades with GoTriangle despite NCDOT encroachment delays and awaiting a RAISE grant decision for the Holloway Street corridor.

agenda_items.title: Community Safety Department (HEART) FY 2024 Budget Presentation (Opening)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Safety Director Ryan Smith introduced his leadership team and reviewed the department's growth from 13 staff a year prior to 20 currently, proposing an expansion to 47 FTEs in FY 2024 (with 93% of the 27 new positions dedicated to direct first-response service). Smith reported that across Crisis Call Diversion, Community Response Teams, and Co-Response Teams, HEART logged over 5,200 responses, cleared roughly 95% of calls without police, fire, or EMS assistance, and set a 30-minute response time goal compared to the state's two-hour mobile crisis standard.

meetings.title: City Council Budget Work Session May 25, 2023 at 9:00 am (Part 3)
meetings.executive_summary: In Part 3 of the May 25, 2023 Budget Work Session, Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and staff presented the department's FY 2024 budget (35 FTEs) and the annual update on Forever Home, Durham. Staff detailed homelessness response metrics, shifting minor and substantial home repair intake and delivery to external vendors, launching the Down Payment Assistance program, continuing eviction diversion, and managing ~$44 million in FY 2024 Forever Home Durham contract funding. Council members questioned how pipeline rental unit counts are categorized and urged stronger security deposit support and landlord communication to help voucher holders secure housing. In closing, City Manager Wanda Page outlined next steps toward the June 5 public hearing and June 20 adoption, noting any recurring pay additions above the proposed 6%-8% raises and compensation study would require offsetting revenues or cuts.

agenda_items.title: Community Development Department FY 2024 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Director Reginald Johnson and leadership staff presented the Community Development Department's 35-FTE FY 2024 budget, reviewing system-wide homelessness metrics (targeting a 110-day median time homeless while serving higher-need populations). Key highlights included issuing RFPs for external vendors to handle both substantial home repairs (up to $50,000, 12-home goal) and minor repairs (under $9,500, 42-home goal), launching the city's Down Payment Assistance program, continuing eviction diversion, and advancing Commerce Street and Main Street apartment projects.

agenda_items.title: Forever Home, Durham Annual Update and FY 2024 Housing Budget
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff reported progress under the five-year Forever Home, Durham plan funded by the 2019 bond and federal entitlements: 162 rental units completed, 451 under contract, and 1,257 in pipeline (totaling 1,870 toward a 1,600-unit goal); 1,481+ homeless persons moved to permanent housing toward a 1,700 goal; and 1,818 of 3,000 low-income households stabilized. Council members pressed staff on whether pipeline units should be counted toward surpassing the 1,600-unit target and requested security deposit assistance and streamlined landlord communication for higher-barrier voucher holders.

agenda_items.title: Budget Next Steps, Public Safety Compensation Discussion, and Closing Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page explained that staff would compile a written follow-up memo for Council ahead of the June 5 required public hearing and June 20 adoption, emphasizing that any recurring salary additions would require recurring revenue or offsetting cuts. Council members discussed the proposed 6%-8% raises and comprehensive compensation study relative to an earlier $16 million / 4-cent tax estimate for immediate raises, and praised Interim Budget Director Christina Reardon and staff before adjourning at 1:05 p.m.

meetings.title: City Council Budget Work Session May 25, 2023 at 9:00 am (Part 2)
meetings.executive_summary: In Part 2 of the May 25, 2023 Budget Work Session, Council completed its review of the Community Safety Department (HEART) expansion and received the Durham Fire Department's FY 2024 budget presentation (with an intervening section omitted from the transcript digest). Community Safety Director Ryan Smith detailed how adding 27 FTEs—including four new Community Response Teams, three Co-Response Teams, two Crisis Call Diversion counselors, and five Care Navigators—would scale HEART citywide 12 hours a day, seven days a week, increasing eligible 911 call coverage from 28% to 69%. Council members praised HEART's national profile while asking about supportive housing barriers and whether unspent Community Safety and Wellness Task Force funds would remain available in fund balance. Later, the Fire Chief presented the Fire Department's budget (adding a fire inspector FTE and an engine at Station 7) and discussed firefighter morale, retention, and regional pay competition alongside the city's proposed 6%-8% raises and $400,000 pay study.

agenda_items.title: Community Safety Department (HEART) Citywide Expansion and Q&A
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Director Ryan Smith outlined HEART's proposed citywide expansion to 47 FTEs operating 12 hours/day, 7 days/week, enabling responses to ~11,000 additional resident-initiated 911 calls and increasing eligible call coverage from 28% to 69%, while continuing ~$1.7M in partner contracts and two paid NCCU social work internships. Council members praised HEART and asked about Care Navigation barriers in housing and mental health placement, RTI documentary screenings in June, and whether unspent Community Safety & Wellness Task Force funds (winding down in October) would remain accessible in fund balance.

agenda_items.title: Durham Fire Department FY 2024 Budget Presentation and Retention/Pay Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle segment, the Fire Chief presented the Fire Department's FY 2024 budget for 414 sworn personnel, including continuing education funding, one new fire inspector FTE (adding ~900 inspections toward 15,732 state-required inspections), and adding an engine at Station 7 so the existing quint can function as a ladder company. Addressing questions on firefighter morale and retention, the Chief noted regional pay competition had surpassed Durham's January raise; staff highlighted the proposed $400,000 citywide pay and classification market study starting in July alongside a 2% market adjustment and 4%-6% step/pay-plan increases (6%-8% total).
