meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 10, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the November 10, 2022 work session, Council suspended its rules by unanimous vote and voted 7-0 to authorize Mayor Elaine O'Neal to execute a $40 million HUD Choice Neighborhoods Implementation (CNI) Grant Agreement for Durham Housing Authority's 519 East Main and Liberty Street properties ahead of HUD's December 2 deadline. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton pulled two tree-maintenance contracts (Items 15 and 23, ArborMax Tree Service and NGE Services) to question UBE good-faith compliance, contractor capacity, and workforce diversity. Council also received a legal deep-dive presentation on affordable housing tools under North Carolina law—covering arms-length city land negotiations, voluntary rezoning proffers versus Fifth Amendment limits on mandatory inclusionary zoning, and statutory development agreements—before settling the November 21 regular meeting agenda (placing Ward Redistricting Item 8 on General Business).

agenda_items.title: Suspension of Rules and Approval of $40M HUD Choice Neighborhoods Implementation Grant
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After birthday acknowledgments for Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman and staff member Keisha Griffin and reading of the 36-item work session agenda, the City Manager requested suspending the rules to approve Item 13 ahead of HUD's December 2, 2022 deadline. Council unanimously suspended the rules and voted 7-0 to authorize the Mayor to execute the $40 million Choice Neighborhoods Implementation grant agreement with HUD for redeveloping DHA's 519 East Main and Liberty Street properties.

agenda_items.title: UBE Compliance and Workforce Diversity Review for ArborMax Tree Service and NGE Services
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton pulled Item 15 (ArborMax Tree Service LLC) and Item 23 (NGE Services Inc.) to question why a contractor deemed non-compliant on UBE good-faith efforts was recommended and to scrutinize workforce diversity and internal capacity. Urban Forestry Manager Alex Johnson participated remotely to respond before the middle portion of the digest was truncated.

agenda_items.title: Affordable Housing Deep Dive: Legal Authorities and Inclusionary Zoning Limits
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney's Office briefed Council on the legal boundaries distinguishing arms-length city land disposition negotiations, voluntary rezoning proffers and committed elements under charter authority, Fifth Amendment takings/nexus limits barring mandatory inclusionary zoning, and statutory development agreements or fee-grant allocations from the general fund. Council members probed whether expedited rezoning timelines (e.g., 6 months instead of 18 months) could be used to incentivize voluntary affordable housing proffers.

agenda_items.title: Setting the November 21, 2022 Regular City Council Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney clarified that staff made no recommendation between the two ward redistricting map options in Item 8, placing Item 8 on the General Business Agenda, while Middleton agreed to leave Item 23 on Consent pending requested follow-up info. Council unanimously settled the November 21 agenda (Consent Items 1–7, 9–12, 14–30; GBA Item 8; GBA Public Hearings Items 32–36) and adjourned at 4:11 PM.

votes.item_title: Suspend the Rules to Take Action on Item 13 (HUD Choice Neighborhoods Implementation Grant)
votes.notes: Leonardo Williams joined prior to 00:12:26; vote ruled unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended Council rules during the work session to act immediately on Item 13 ahead of HUD's December 2, 2022 submission deadline.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Execute $40M HUD Choice Neighborhoods Implementation (CNI) Grant Agreement
votes.notes: Confirmed as a 7-0 vote by the City Manager in the November 21, 2022 regular meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: Authorized the Mayor to execute the $40 million HUD Choice Neighborhoods Implementation Grant Agreement for the redevelopment of Durham Housing Authority's 519 East Main and Liberty Street apartment properties.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for the November 21, 2022 Regular City Council Meeting (Consent: 1–7, 9–12, 14–30; GBA: 8; Public Hearings: 32–36)
votes.notes: Voice vote ruled unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Settled the November 21, 2022 regular meeting agenda, placing Ward Redistricting (Item 8) on the General Business Agenda and Items 32–36 on GBA Public Hearings.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov. 7, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: The November 7, 2022 regular meeting opened with proclamations for Family Court Awareness Month, Thankfulness, and School/Law Counselor Awareness Month before Council passed the Consent Agenda 7-0—including Cedar Trace Apartments multifamily revenue bonds, green stormwater infrastructure, and a resolution supporting Duke graduate students' right to organize a labor union. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton recused himself on Item 14 (downtown social district ordinances and Downtown Durham Inc. management) due to serving on DDI's board, and Council passed the Section 38-21 amendment 6-0 with Middleton abstaining before the digest truncated earlier public hearings. When the digest resumed on Item 21 (Wilkinson Estates, 185 townhomes), Council split 5-2 on both annexation and PDR 3.850 rezoning—with Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voting no over inadequate community proffers while the 5-member majority approved them alongside a raised $24,000 DPS contribution—before unanimously approving Item 22 (Greater Love Worship Center) 7-0 and adjourning at 11:41 PM.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Election Turnout Remarks, and Meeting Flow
agenda_items.discussion_summary: All seven council members attended. Proclamations were read for Family Court Awareness Month (DeDreana Freeman), Thankfulness (Mayor Elaine O'Neal), and Counselor Awareness Month (Mark-Anthony Middleton), Leonardo Williams urged Election Day turnout, and O'Neal congratulated HR Director Win and noted ~30 public hearing speakers ahead.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval Including Cedar Trace Housing Bonds and Duke Grad Union Support
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After City Manager priority updates on Items 14, 18, 19, and 20, Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton read the Consent Agenda—including board appointments, the Participatory Budgeting audit, ARPA Green Stormwater Infrastructure, Cedar Trace Apartments multifamily housing revenue bonds, refuse truck purchases, and Item 23 supporting the right of Duke graduate students to organize a labor union—while pulling Item 14. Council approved the consent agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Social District Ordinance Amendments and Management Designee
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton recused himself due to his seat on the Downtown Durham Inc. (DDI) board and passed the gavel to Mayor O'Neal. Council voted 6-0 (with Middleton abstaining) on Motion 1 amending City Code Section 38-21 (alcoholic beverages), after which the transcript digest was truncated through subsequent social district motions and public hearing Items 18–20.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation: Wilkinson Estates (LTB Developers LLC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming during deliberation on Wilkinson Estates (185 townhomes at ~5.28 units/buildable acre after widened stream buffers, plus an updated text commitment raising the one-time contribution to Durham Public Schools from $5,000 to $24,000), Council debated growth and community benefits. DeDreana Freeman criticized insufficient developer proffers and vowed to vote no, Javiera Caballero cited stream-buffer protection and density balance, Leonardo Williams argued against halting approvals given revenue needs for neglected neighborhoods and schools, and the annexation and PDR 3.850 rezoning passed 5-2 with Mayor O'Neal and Freeman opposed, followed by a 7-0 consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Greater Love Worship Center
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Brooke Roper presented Pastor Robert Mason's request to rezone 1.27 acres from Office and Institutional (OI) to Industrial Light (IL) for associated warehousing, noting an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation and staff support for a future land use map change to Industrial. Pastor Mason spoke in favor, and Council approved both the rezoning ordinance and the NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement 7-0 before adjourning at 11:41 PM.

votes.item_title: Item 14: Social District — Amend City Code Section 38-21 (Alcoholic Beverages)
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton recused/abstained because he sits on the Downtown Durham Inc. (DDI) board. Motions 2 and 3 occurred after the digest truncation cutoff.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted an ordinance amending Section 38-21 (Alcoholic Beverages) to clarify social district allowances and special use permits for parks.

votes.item_title: Item 21: Consolidated Annexation (Wilkinson Estates) — Annexation Ordinance & UEA
votes.notes: Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voted no.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted an ordinance annexing Wilkinson Estates effective December 31, 2022, and authorizing the City Manager to enter into a utility extension agreement with LTB Developers LLC.

votes.item_title: Item 21: Consolidated Annexation (Wilkinson Estates) — UDO Amendment to PDR 3.850 F/J-B
votes.notes: Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voted no.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted an ordinance rezoning Wilkinson Estates from Rural Residential (RR) Falls/Jordan Watershed Protection Overlay B (F/J-B) county jurisdiction to Planned Development Residential 3.850 (PDR 3.850) F/J-B city jurisdiction, incorporating the updated $24,000 one-time contribution to Durham Public Schools.

votes.item_title: Item 21: Consolidated Annexation (Wilkinson Estates) — Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted the consistency statement required by NCGS 160D-605 for Wilkinson Estates.

votes.item_title: Item 22: Zoning Map Change (Greater Love Worship Center) — UDO Amendment to IL
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted an ordinance amending the UDO by taking 1.27 acres out of Office and Institutional (OI) and establishing Industrial Light (IL) for Greater Love Worship Center.

votes.item_title: Item 22: Zoning Map Change (Greater Love Worship Center) — Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted the consistency statement required by NCGS 160D-605 for Greater Love Worship Center.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Nov. 7, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Wilkinson Estates Annexation and PDR 3.850 Rezoning (Community Benefits, Infrastructure, and Growth Approvals)
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 on annexing and rezoning the 185-townhome Wilkinson Estates development, pitting members who viewed widened stream buffers, an increased $24,000 DPS proffer, and tax-revenue/housing supply as sufficient against members demanding stronger community benefits and infrastructure readiness before approving suburban growth.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the Wilkinson Estates annexation and PDR 3.850 rezoning with widened stream buffers and the increased $24,000 DPS proffer.
side_a_arguments: Widened stream buffers protect environmental features while keeping buildable density reasonable at roughly 5.28 units per acre.
Halting development approvals until roads and infrastructure are expanded is unrealistic and would starve the city budget of tax revenue needed for neglected neighborhoods and schools.
The applicant increased its one-time Durham Public Schools proffer from $5,000 to $24,000 prior to certificate of occupancy.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the annexation and rezoning until stronger community benefits and infrastructure protections are secured.
side_b_arguments: Current proffers and community benefits are inadequate, and sending inadequate proposals back can yield better outcomes for residents.
Continued residential approvals strain local schools and roads without commensurate infrastructure improvements.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and PDR 3.850 rezoning both passed 5-2; the NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement passed 7-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 20, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the October 20, 2022 work session with six members present and DeDreana Freeman on an excused absence, Council accepted the City Manager's priority items 6-0, suspended the rules 6-0, and voted 6-0 to approve Item 13 (an Accessibility for Parks grant application for C.R. Wood Park ahead of the October 31 deadline). Staff briefed Council on housekeeping amendments and designating Downtown Durham Inc. (DDI) to manage the downtown social district (Item 14), began presenting the FY2024–2026 Strategic Plan refresh (Item 15), and delivered the annual Sister Cities of Durham update (Item 17). Council also held an extended Affordable Housing Deep Dive (Item 16) examining AMI thresholds, homeownership versus rental disparities, and post-COVID home price escalation before voting 6-0 to settle the November 7 regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Priority Items Acceptance, and C.R. Wood Park Accessibility Grant Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Six members answered roll call (DeDreana Freeman had an excused absence). The City Manager introduced priority updates for Items 19 (5202 Leesville Rd) and 21 (Wilkinson Estates) and requested immediate action on Item 13 (Accessibility for Parks grant for C.R. Wood Park before the October 31 deadline); Council voted 6-0 to accept priority items, read Items 1–22 plus a supplemental resolution supporting Duke graduate students' unionization rights, suspended rules 6-0, and approved Item 13 by a 6-0 vote.

agenda_items.title: Social District Ordinance Housekeeping Amendments and DDI Management Designee
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented two housekeeping ordinance amendments aligning city property/parks and street/sidewalk rules with the newly adopted social district ordinance, along with a draft agreement designating Downtown Durham Inc. (DDI) to manage the district's boundaries, schedule, and communications.

agenda_items.title: FY2024–2026 Strategic Plan Refresh Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Strategy and Performance Manager Sherry Metcalf from Budget and Management Services began presenting the FY2024–2026 Strategic Plan refresh update; the remainder of her presentation was omitted in a truncated middle portion of the transcript digest.

agenda_items.title: Sister Cities of Durham Annual Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sister Cities representatives Bob and Brady reviewed educational, cultural, and medical exchange programs involving Durham Public Schools, Toyama (Japan), Durham Tech ESL, NCCU, Duke medical residents, and Sibiu. Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton and Council praised Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman's work as Council liaison.

agenda_items.title: Affordable Housing Deep Dive Presentation (AMI Tiers, Homeownership Gaps, and Market Trends)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff presented housing affordability data across AMI bands—noting LIHTC limits at 60% AMI, public housing averages in the teens percent AMI, weighted regional medians ($71,400 Durham vs. $80,294 Orange County), and stark homeownership drops below 80% AMI compounded by post-COVID price escalation and repair costs. Council members Elaine O'Neal, Javiera Caballero, and Leonardo Williams discussed why private developers do not build for the lowest income tiers without public subsidies and examined second-mortgage programs and school partnerships.

agenda_items.title: Clerk Report and Setting the November 7, 2022 Regular Council Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the City Clerk's report, the City Manager presented the November 7 agenda (Consent Items 1–12, 14, and 23; GBA Public Hearings Items 18–22). Council approved settling the agenda 6-0 and adjourned at 2:51 PM.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (Items 13, 19, and 21)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman had an excused absence; voice vote ruled unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted the City Manager's priority additions and memo updates for Items 13, 19, and 21.

votes.item_title: Suspend the Rules to Act on Item 13 (C.R. Wood Park Accessibility Grant)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman had an excused absence; voice vote ruled unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended Council rules during the work session to vote on Item 13 ahead of the October 31, 2022 grant deadline.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Approve Accessibility for Parks Grant Application for C.R. Wood Park
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman had an excused absence; voice vote ruled unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the Durham Parks and Recreation Accessibility for Parks grant application for C.R. Wood Park and authorized the Mayor to sign ahead of the October 31, 2022 deadline.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for the November 7, 2022 Regular City Council Meeting (Consent: 1–12, 14, 23; Public Hearings: 18–22)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman had an excused absence; voice vote ruled unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Settled the November 7, 2022 regular City Council agenda, placing Items 1–12, 14, and 23 on Consent and Items 18–22 on GBA Public Hearings.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Oct. 17, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Starting at 7:17 PM after a power outage in City Hall, Council opened with Hispanic Heritage Month and disability/lead-prevention proclamations alongside recognition of DHIC and Self-Help's Housing North Carolina Award for Willard Street Apartments. Operating with left-hand votes due to electronic clicker issues, Council unanimously adopted the Consent Agenda (7-0), the Downtown Social District ordinance (7-0) despite equity and policing concerns raised in Citizen Matters, 4214 Fayetteville Road rezoning (7-0), Water Street permanent closing (7-0), and South Alston Avenue multi-family rezoning (7-0). On contested sprawl and infrastructure hearings, Council narrowly passed Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2 (166 senior units) by 4-3 annexation/rezoning votes (7-0 consistency) and voted to refer the 666-unit Kemp Road Residential proposal back to staff after a unanimous Planning Commission denial over delayed Fire Station 19 CIP funding.

agenda_items.title: Hispanic Heritage Month, Willard Street Award, Disability Employment, Lead Prevention & Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero presented a Hispanic Heritage Month proclamation honoring the Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee, followed by Community Development Director Reginald Johnson, DHIC CEO Yolanda Winstead, and Self-Help EVP Tucker Bartlett accepting the 2022 Housing North Carolina Award for the 82-unit Willard Street Apartments (built on donated city land with $3.6M in city funds). Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman read the National Disability Employment Awareness Month proclamation and DeDreana Freeman presented Lead Poisoning Prevention Week to Lenora Smith of PEACH. Council members announced a Workers' Rights speak-out, a youth financial/crypto workshop defended by Leonardo Williams and Mayor Elaine O'Neal, local crisis-response study visits, and condolences for Raleigh shooting victims and Keith Wonderboy Johnson.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Items 1-18, 20-23, 25, 33)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal noted Item 19 was voted on October 6 and Mark-Anthony Middleton pulled Item 24 (Social District Ordinance) for separate consideration. Council approved all remaining consent items—including FY22 carryover budget amendments, Durham, The City of Books ARPA contract, bus procurement interlocal, Water Management and Equitable Community Engagement contracts, and NSP3 repayment—unanimously by raised-hand vote.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance to Create a Downtown Social District
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Mark-Anthony Middleton, City Attorney Kim Rehberg clarified that HB 890 gives cities flexible authority over district management agreements, and Parks and Recreation Director Wade Walcott confirmed no formal third-party designee contract was before Council yet. Resident Jackie Wagstaff opposed the ordinance as inequitable for non-downtown Black neighborhoods and worried about public drinking near Durham Central Park events; DeDreana Freeman and Jillian Johnson urged police non-enforcement clarity outside downtown, while Middleton and Leonardo Williams backed downtown business recovery. Council adopted the ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: 4214 Fayetteville Road (RS-20 to OI-D)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a routine public hearing on changing 4214 Fayetteville Road from Residential Suburban-20 to Office and Institutional with a Development Plan (OI-D). With no opposition debate, Council unanimously approved both the zoning map amendment and the NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement by 7-0 raised-hand votes.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2 (166 Units)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Epcon Communities proposed annexing rural acreage on Doc Nichols Road and rezoning from RR to PDR 2.242 for up to 166 age-targeted townhomes/courtyard homes, following an earlier Planning Commission flip from recommendation to denial and a prior 2021 council rejection. Neighbors cited blasting concerns, well-water turbidity, missing school/EMS/fire infrastructure, and rural-edge sprawl, while Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, and Leonardo Williams cited improved 33% tree preservation, no stream crossings, affordable housing proffers, and housing supply needs. The annexation and rezoning passed 4-3, and the consistency statement passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Permanent Closing of Water Street Right-of-Way
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Cole Renigar of the Planning Department and Chris Dreps of the Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association presented a request to permanently close Water Street—a 1930s paper street running through wetland and South Ellerbe Creek—to expand Pearl Mill Nature Preserve for a city-supported stream enhancement project while legally transferring an existing driveway sliver to 605 West Knox Street. Online neighbor John Bosch spoke in support, and Council approved closing the street and authorizing the City Manager to sign the plat 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: South Alston Avenue (O&I to PDR 15.371)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Andy Lester and developer Jared Edens of Edens Land Corp presented a 13-acre multi-family rezoning on South Alston Avenue next to a FedEx Ground distribution facility, committing 5% of units at 60% AMI and a $150,000 dedicated housing fund contribution. FedEx Ground representatives voiced concern over 24/7 truck noise and lighting conflicts with future residents; Edens added proffers for a 30-foot 0.8-opacity northern buffer and a decibel noise study with acoustic mitigation. Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: Kemp Road Residential (666 Units)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Sara Young reported that the 280-acre, 666-unit Kemp Road proposal received an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation of denial largely because Fire Station 19 lacked Capital Improvement Program funding to serve the area. Applicant attorney Nil Ghosh requested referring the case back to staff rather than withdrawing, proffering a condition prohibiting site-plan submittal until Fire Station 19 funding is identified in the CIP. After questioning the timeline gap before fire coverage, Council voted by raised hand to refer the item back to staff and concluded by approving a Thursday work-session excused absence 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Adopt Ordinance Creating a Downtown Social District
votes.discussion_detail: Following legal clarification from City Attorney Kim Rehberg and council discussion of police open-container enforcement equity, business recovery, and future designee agreements, Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Leonardo Williams seconded adopting the ordinance establishing a Downtown Social District, which passed unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 27 (Motion 1): Adopt Zoning Map Change for 4214 Fayetteville Road (RS-20 to OI-D)
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded rezoning 4214 Fayetteville Road from Residential Suburban-20 to Office and Institutional with a Development Plan (OI-D), passing unanimously 7-0 by raised hand.

votes.item_title: Item 27 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 4214 Fayetteville Road
votes.discussion_detail: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for the 4214 Fayetteville Road rezoning, passing 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 28 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement for Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2
votes.notes: Hand vote was 4-3 without individual member names read aloud. Floor remarks showed Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, and Leonardo Williams supporting while DeDreana Freeman voiced opposition/concern over blasting, wells, and infrastructure.
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the ordinance annexing Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2 effective December 31, 2022 and authorizing a utility extension agreement with Epcon Communities. Following a heated hearing over well water, blasting, and infrastructure capacity, the hand vote passed 4-3.

votes.item_title: Item 28 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2 (RR to PDR 2.242)
votes.notes: Hand vote was 4-3 without individual member names read aloud.
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Jillian Johnson seconded rezoning Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2 from Rural Residential (RR) Falls/Jordan County jurisdiction to Planned Development Residential 2.242 (PDR 2.242) City jurisdiction, passing 4-3 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 28 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Jillian Johnson seconded adopting the required statutory consistency statement for Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2, which passed unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 29 (Motion 1): Adopt Order Permanently Closing Water Street in Its Entirety
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded permanently closing Water Street right-of-way to facilitate the Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association's Pearl Mill Nature Preserve stream enhancement project and resolve a driveway encroachment at 605 West Knox Street, passing 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 29 (Motion 2): Authorize City Manager to Sign Plat Realigning Closed Water Street Land
votes.discussion_detail: Jillian Johnson moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded authorizing the City Manager to sign the realignment plat transferring city-shared closed right-of-way land equitably and conveying the curb cut and driveway to 605 West Knox Street, passing 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 30 (Motion 1): Adopt Zoning Map Change for South Alston Avenue (O&I to PDR 15.371)
votes.discussion_detail: After Edens Land Corp added a 30-foot 0.8-opacity northern buffer and decibel noise-study commitment to mitigate FedEx Ground truck noise, Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded rezoning 13 acres on South Alston Avenue to PDR 15.371 with 5% affordable units and a $150,000 housing fund proffer, passing 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 30 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for South Alston Avenue
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for South Alston Avenue, passing unanimously 7-0 by raised hand.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Refer Kemp Road Residential Annexation and Rezoning Application Back to Staff
votes.notes: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called for raised left hands in favor and announced the item goes back to staff without calling a numerical tally.
votes.discussion_detail: With Planning staff opposing referral and the Planning Commission having recommended denial 11-0 due to Fire Station 19 funding gaps, applicant attorney Nil Ghosh declined to withdraw and instead proffered prohibiting site-plan submittal until Fire Station 19 CIP funding is identified. DeDreana Freeman moved and Jillian Johnson seconded referring the item back to staff, passing by raised hands.

votes.item_title: Approve Excused Absence for Council Member for Upcoming Thursday Work Session
votes.discussion_detail: Under Other Matters, Mayor Elaine O'Neal requested an excused absence for the upcoming Thursday work session due to out-of-town work business. Moved by Javiera Caballero and seconded by Jillian Johnson, the excused absence passed unanimously 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Oct. 17, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Geographic Equity and Open-Container Enforcement in the Downtown Social District
disagreements.summary: While all seven Council members ultimately voted 7-0 for the Downtown Social District ordinance, speakers and council members clashed over downtown-focused privileges versus open-container policing risks in lower-income Black neighborhoods.
disagreements.side_a_position: Create the Downtown Social District to match peer NC cities and boost post-pandemic downtown restaurant and retail foot traffic.
side_a_arguments: Nearby cities already run social districts and downtown businesses need economic momentum.
Police Chief Patrice Andrews stated officers focus on violent crime and do not cite simple open containers absent disturbances, and ABC over-service laws still apply.
disagreements.side_b_position: Address geographic exclusivity outside downtown and protect Black residents and Central Park family events from disparate alcohol enforcement and over-policing.
side_b_arguments: Privileging downtown patrons to walk with alcohol while criminalizing open containers in East Durham or neighborhood corners perpetuates 'two Durhams'.
Public drinking zones could overlap with family programming in spaces like Durham Central Park unless boundaries and policing metrics are carefully tracked.
disagreements.resolution: Council passed the ordinance 7-0 while requesting continued oversight of future designee agreements and enforcement equity.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Oct. 17, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Courtyards at Doc Nichols #2 Rural Infrastructure, Blasting, and Housing Supply
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 over annexing and rezoning rural-edge land for 166 Epcon courtyard units amid neighbor testimony on well turbidity, dynamite blasting, and strained fire/EMS capacity.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the revised 166-unit community because housing supply, senior-accessible floor plans, 33% tree save, and affordable proffers outweigh sprawl concerns.
side_a_arguments: The applicant substantially improved the 2021 plan with 33% tree preservation, zero stream crossings, and senior-friendly ground-floor units.
Stopping new housing on the urban edge worsens displacement and rents inside the urban core.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose or pause outer-county annexations where cumulative blasting, well contamination, road congestion, and missing public infrastructure remain unresolved.
side_b_arguments: Neighbors near Doc Nichols and Olive Branch Roads reported sediment-laden well water, foundation concerns, and uninspected homes during blasting.
Rural roads and emergency services (EMS, schools, fire) lack an actionable capacity plan to absorb thousands of cumulative annexed units.
disagreements.resolution: The annexation and rezoning motions passed 4-3 by raised hand vote; the consistency statement passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Oct. 17, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Whether to Refer Kemp Road Residential (666 Units) Back to Staff Instead of Voting or Withdrawing
disagreements.summary: After Planning Commission recommended 11-0 denial because Fire Station 19 lacked CIP funding, Council debated whether referring Kemp Road back to staff with a site-plan hold condition would adequately prevent unserved homes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Accept the developer's proffered site-plan bar tied to Fire Station 19 CIP funding identification and refer the case back to staff.
side_a_arguments: Referring back preserves public engagement and gives staff a trackable, enforceable proffer barring site-plan submittal before CIP funding is identified.
Under city review rules, the application will still be administratively withdrawn if inactive after 90 days.
disagreements.side_b_position: Staff noted that even identifying funding in a multi-year CIP still leaves uncertainty and a multi-year gap before Fire Station 19 is actually built and operational.
side_b_arguments: Planning Director Sara Young preferred tying approval to actual station construction rather than just CIP funding identification, noting staff did not endorse referral without withdrawal.
disagreements.resolution: Council voted by raised hands to refer Item 31 back to staff rather than proceeding immediately with the public hearing.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 6, 2022 (audio corrected)
meetings.executive_summary: In the complete audio-corrected October 6, 2022 work session, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over priority items where Council suspended the rules (7-0) and approved the FY23 HUD Fair Housing Cooperative Agreement (7-0) to prevent grant drawdown delays. Council questioned staff on FY22 carryovers, the city's first ARPA subrecipient contract (Durham, The City of Books), MWBE bus procurement, and a $400K-$600K NSP3 grant repayment mismatch. Following packed business testimony backing Item 24 (Downtown Social District), Council debated equity, open-container policing, car-free streets, and legal contract prescriptions before placing it on GBA; heard a $1.77M, 15-month code/ADA assessment for reopening Wheels Skating Center; reviewed Participatory Budgeting Cycle 3's equity-mapped citywide shift; and heard DataWorks NC's 'Who Owns Durham' housing deep dive before settling the October 17 agenda.

agenda_items.title: Guaranteed Income Results, Duke Grad Union Support & Item 19 HUD Fair Housing Grant
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the work session to order at 1:07 PM (with Leonardo Williams arriving shortly after roll call). Mark-Anthony Middleton celebrated six-month results from Durham's guaranteed income pilot showing zero recidivism among justice-involved participants, Jillian Johnson gained thumbs-up consensus to introduce a resolution supporting Duke University graduate workers' unionization, and City Manager Wanda Page announced storm-response efforts and the passing of solid-waste employee Frankie Jones. Under Mark-Anthony Middleton's chairing, Council suspended the rules (7-0) and approved Item 19, the FY23 HUD Fair Housing Cooperative Agreement (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: Carryover Funds, First ARPA Contract, Bus Interlocal & NSP3 Grant Repayment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman questioned emergency watershed carryover grant delays (Item 9), MBE bus-procurement outreach (Item 12), and biosolids digester contract amendments (Item 14). On Item 11 (the city's first ARPA contract, Durham, The City of Books), Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson explained delays stemmed from staff turnover, U.S. Treasury April final rules, and rescoping recipients to 70% awards. On Item 33, Community Development Director Reginald Johnson explained Durham had to repay NSP3 funds because a 10-year-old Southside project included 22 market-rate homes alongside 26 LMI homes on reconfigured lots.

agenda_items.title: Presentation & Draft Ordinance to Create a Downtown Social District
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senator Mike Woodard, DDI's Nicole Thompson, Discover Durham's Susan Amey, and more than a dozen downtown business owners (Copa, Spaceway Brewing, Bull City Butler, Artisan Market, Durham Food Hall, Zen Succulent, Jess & Co, 360 Approach, Linx & Gray, Kingfisher, Sissy's Gallery, Dame's Chicken & Waffles, Glass Jug, Slush, Goorsha, Honeygirl Meadery) urged passage of a Downtown Social District to boost post-COVID foot traffic. After Wade Walcott's presentation, DeDreana Freeman and Jillian Johnson raised concerns over neighborhood equity and open-container policing disparities, Javiera Caballero advocated free transit and car-free streets, and Mark-Anthony Middleton and Woodard questioned Durham's unusually prescriptive third-party contract terms, prompting Item 24's placement on GBA.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Moved to Oct. 17 General Business Agenda

agenda_items.title: Former Wheels Skating Center Assessment and Probable Opinion of Cost
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents Gidean Bueno and Danielle Spratley urged rapid reinvestment in the former Wheels Skating Center as an accessible community space. General Services' Shauna Parker presented Ratio's assessment estimating $765,000 in required ADA/life-safety fixes ($284K ADA, $481K code/safety), $918,000 in maintenance including three aging HVAC units, and $85,000 in kitchen upgrades (~$1.77M total) on a compressed 15-month timeline. Council gave unanimous thumbs-up direction to advance the rink concurrently with aquatics master planning, start vendor RFQ outreach simultaneously, and subsidize low user fees.

agenda_items.title: Participatory Budgeting (PB) Durham Cycle 3 Restructuring Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget staff presented Cycle 3 reforms guided by an NCCU MPA evaluation, proposing to restore Cycle 1's physical capital infrastructure focus while replacing equal ward allocations with a citywide equity-weighted model prioritized via Neighborhood Compass demographic/eviction data and an extended fall-voting timeline. Council members explored ways to engage high school civics classes and asked Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar about legal hurdles to funding capital projects on private or nonprofit land.

agenda_items.title: DataWorks NC 'Who Owns Durham' Housing Presentation, Board Nominations & Agenda Settling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: John Killeen of DataWorks NC delivered a supplemental housing deep-dive tracing racial covenants, redlining, Hayti/Few Gardens displacement, 15% investor home purchases concentrated in Black neighborhoods, soaring COVID-era rents, concentrated evictions (88% in majority-POC census blocks), 11,000+ DHA/voucher waitlists, and why 60-80% regional AMI exceeds what Braggtown and Durham households actually earn. Council then received board nominations and settled the October 17 agenda.

votes.item_title: Suspend Council Rules to Vote on Item 19 (HUD Fair Housing Cooperative Agreement FY23)
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over the priority item and received a motion from Javiera Caballero and second from Leonardo Williams to suspend the rules for immediate action on Item 19 so HUD grant funds could be drawn down promptly; passed unanimously 7-0 by raised left hand.

votes.item_title: Item 19: Approve U.S. HUD Fair Housing Cooperative Agreement FY 2023
votes.discussion_detail: With rules suspended, Mayor Elaine O'Neal moved and Javiera Caballero seconded approving the FY 2023 HUD Fair Housing Cooperative Agreement, passing unanimously 7-0 by raised left hand.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 6, 2022 (audio corrected)
disagreements.issue: Downtown Social District Equity, Open-Container Policing, and Third-Party Contract Complexity
disagreements.summary: While Council generally favored supporting downtown recovery, members debated geographic equity outside downtown, potential disparate open-container enforcement, street closures, and whether Durham's proposed DDI designee contract was overly prescriptive.
disagreements.side_a_position: Move swiftly toward a Downtown Social District with light, streamlined designee agreements modeled on Greensboro to aid small businesses.
side_a_arguments: Downtown businesses are losing post-COVID weekday traffic and competing with Raleigh and Greensboro social districts.
DDI is a trusted city partner, and overly burdensome legal contracts conflict with HB 890's streamlined framework.
Social districts do not contradict equity work any more than balancing unarmed crisis response and ShotSpotter.
disagreements.side_b_position: Address inequities for non-downtown Black business corridors, guard against disparate open-container policing, and explore car-free/transit pairings.
side_b_arguments: Allowing alcohol downtown while people on neighborhood corners elsewhere face open-container enforcement risks creating 'two Durhams'.
City-funded signage and DDI staffing privilege downtown over business districts without paid staff.
Higher-frequency free transit and car-free streeteries should accompany expanded downtown alcohol consumption.
disagreements.resolution: Item 24 was moved to the October 17 General Business Agenda so the City Attorney could address questions regarding the designee contract.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Oct. 3, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, the October 3, 2022 regular Council meeting opened with proclamations honoring MED Week, The Chicken Hut (including the Key to the City to Toney Tapp), Domestic Violence Awareness Month, and Digital Inclusion Week, and unanimously adopted the Consent Agenda (7-0) plus the 812 North Mangum Street rezoning (7-0). On the contested 219-unit Windell at Crescent annexation and rezoning, DeDreana Freeman and Mayor Elaine O'Neal challenged the lack of on-site affordable units and transit access in a compact neighborhood after Light Rail cancellation, yet the project passed 5-2 ($200K affordable housing fund and $39K DPS proffers). Council also approved the four-lot 637 & 641 Conover Road annexation and RS-8 rezoning 6-1 (Freeman dissenting, consistency 7-0) and annexed/zoned one home at 216 Curlew Drive by clicker votes before closing with a tribute to a slain Bull City United worker.

agenda_items.title: MED Week, Chicken Hut Day & Key to City, Domestic Violence Month, Digital Inclusion Week
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mark-Anthony Middleton proclaimed Minority Enterprise Development (MED) Week with NCIMED's Kevin Price, Mayor Elaine O'Neal honored The Chicken Hut's Toney Tapp with a proclamation and Key to the City, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman marked Domestic Violence Awareness Month, and Javiera Caballero recognized Digital Inclusion Week with Durham's Digital Inclusion Coalition. Note Mayor O'Neal inadvertently said 'August 3rd' during opening remarks before proceeding with the October 3, 2022 agenda.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Items 1-6, 8)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal read the consent agenda noting Items 7 (Cultural Roadmap) and 15 (Historic Preservation) had already been voted at the September 22 work session and Items 10-13 were GBA Public Hearings. Council approved Consent Items 1-6 and 8 (including the Cultural Advisory Board, Planning Commission, RAC, and EAB appointments, August bid report, and Greater Triangle Commuter Rail/grant-related consent items) unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: 812 North Mangum Street (CG to CI-D)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Andy Lester and applicant representative Nil Ghosh presented a 0.344-acre rezoning from Commercial General to Commercial Infill with a Development Plan (CI-D) for an existing church/future civic use with Planning Commission 10-0 approval. Neighbor Mark Davis sought assurance of commercial/civic continuity, and Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: Windell at Crescent (219 Apartments)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff and attorney Nil Ghosh (representing Northwood Partners / Northview) presented an annexation and RS-20-to-RCD rezoning near I-40/Highway 54 for 219 apartments, replacing an earlier failed development agreement; the applicant proffered $200,000 for the affordable housing fund, $39,000 for Durham Public Schools, 15% tree preservation, and bus-stop pads. Neighbor Donna Stainback raised cumulative traffic and infrastructure concerns, while DeDreana Freeman pressed staff on why compact neighborhoods lacked transit after light-rail cancellation and lacked on-site affordable units, and Mark-Anthony Middleton praised placing market-rate density outside inner-city neighborhoods. Annexation and rezoning passed 5-2 (O'Neal and Freeman opposed), followed by an unannounced clicker-glitch consistency vote.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: 637 & 641 Conover Road (4 Lots)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Andy Lester and representative Jay Gellis III presented an annexation and RR-to-RS-8 rezoning on 0.926 acres to connect to city water/sewer and subdivide two lots into four single-family lots (Planning Commission 11-0). Neighbors Donna Stainback and Pam Williams sought clarification that RS-8 would yield only four single-family homes and renewed calls for cumulative eastern Durham traffic/EMS impact studies. Annexation and rezoning passed 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting no, and the consistency statement passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Initial Zoning: 216 Curlew Drive (Single-Family Home)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Roy and Beverly Lagarde sought non-contiguous annexation and city Rural Residential (RR) zoning on a 0.46-acre lot at 216 Curlew Drive to connect to utilities and build a single-family home for themselves and their adult child. Neighboring HOA president Ben Weinberger listened for details and neighbor Melanie Jones asked about an unopened right-of-way, which the Lagardes confirmed would not be used for their flag-lot driveway. Council approved annexation and initial RR zoning by unannounced electronic screen votes before adjourning at 8:52 PM with condolences for a slain Bull City United worker.

votes.item_title: Item 10 (Motion 1): Adopt Zoning Map Change for 812 North Mangum Street (CG to CI-D)
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Leonardo Williams seconded rezoning 812 North Mangum Street from Commercial General (CG) to Commercial Infill with Development Plan (CI-D), passing 7-0 by electronic vote.

votes.item_title: Item 10 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 812 North Mangum Street
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Leonardo Williams seconded adopting the consistency statement for 812 North Mangum Street, passing 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement for Windell at Crescent
votes.notes: ASR transcribed applicant entity as 'Norfolk Partners LLC' ('Northwood' / 'Northview' in discussion).
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded annexing Windell at Crescent effective December 31, 2022 and authorizing a utility extension agreement, passing 5-2 with Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for Windell at Crescent (RS-20 to RCD)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman seconded rezoning Windell at Crescent from RS-20 to Residential Compact with Development Plan (RCD) for 219 apartments, passing 5-2 with Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 11 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Windell at Crescent
votes.notes: Final numerical tally after Freeman's clicker clarification was not verbally stated aloud on the recording.
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded adopting the consistency statement for Windell at Crescent. After DeDreana Freeman reported her clicker failed to register her intended 'yes' vote correctly, Mayor O'Neal acknowledged the board display and proceeded to Item 12.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement for 637 & 641 Conover Road
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Leonardo Williams seconded annexing 637 and 641 Conover Road effective December 31, 2022 and entering a utility extension agreement with Nice Neighbors LLC, passing 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for 637 & 641 Conover Road (RR to RS-8)
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Leonardo Williams seconded rezoning 637 and 641 Conover Road from Rural Residential (RR) County jurisdiction to Residential Suburban-8 (RS-8) City jurisdiction to allow subdivision into four single-family lots, passing 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 637 & 641 Conover Road
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Leonardo Williams seconded adopting the consistency statement for 637 & 641 Conover Road, passing unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 13 (Motion 1): Adopt Non-Contiguous Annexation Ordinance and UEA for 216 Curlew Drive
votes.notes: Electronic voting tally was displayed visually in chambers without being read aloud in the audio transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting an ordinance annexing 216 Curlew Drive effective December 31, 2022 and authorizing a utility extension agreement with Roy and Beverly Lagarde for one single-family home; the electronic vote proceeded directly to Motion 2.

votes.item_title: Item 13 (Motion 2): Adopt Initial City Rural Residential (RR) Zoning Ordinance for 216 Curlew Drive
votes.notes: Electronic voting tally was displayed visually in chambers without being read aloud in the audio transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman seconded establishing initial City Rural Residential (RR) Falls/Jordan Watershed District B zoning for 216 Curlew Drive; electronic vote concluded without vocal dissent before moving to Other Matters.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Oct. 3, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Windell at Crescent: Compact Neighborhood Density Without On-Site Affordable Units or Transit
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 on annexing and rezoning Windell at Crescent for 219 apartments in a designated compact neighborhood without Light Rail transit or on-site income-restricted units.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 219-unit development with $200,000 affordable housing and $39,000 DPS proffers to add market-rate density outside gentrifying inner-city neighborhoods.
side_a_arguments: Adding walkable density on the periphery relieves displacement pressure on historic neighborhoods like Walltown.
State law restricts mandatory inclusionary zoning, making voluntary housing fund and school contributions practical levers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject annexing and granting compact-neighborhood density when Light Rail has disappeared and zero affordable units are provided on site.
side_b_arguments: City transit staff confirmed no transit line currently connects 15-501 and NC 54 through the area after Light Rail cancellation.
An earlier density-bonus/development-agreement framework had attempted to secure on-site affordability before being replaced by market-rate RCD.
disagreements.resolution: Both the annexation and RCD rezoning motions passed 5-2.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 22, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Jillian Johnson while Mayor Elaine O'Neal attended a White House delegation in Washington, D.C. (excused 4-0) and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton flew back (joining at 00:51:28), the September 22, 2022 work session moved rapidly through procedural and time-sensitive items. Council approved priority items and closed-session requests (5-0), suspended rules and approved both Item 7 (Cultural Roadmap Interlocal Agreement with Durham County, 5-0) and Item 15 (FY23 Historic Preservation Fund Grant Contract, 5-0), and heard Citizen Matters on traffic calming, Braggtown safety, Old West Durham bike/ped needs, and Monday-night decorum. On Item 9, GoTriangle and Durham County staff presented the Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Feasibility Study showing rising capital/Norfolk Southern capacity costs, earning informal consensus support for the County's federal RCEP grant letter (with DeDreana Freeman giving a sideways thumb to prioritize Route 9 local bus investments) before settling the October 3 agenda (6-0) and entering closed session on Oak Charter Academy litigation (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Mayor Excused Absence, Priority Items & Rule Suspensions (Items 7 and 15)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jillian Johnson presided with DeDreana Freeman, Javiera Caballero, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman present at roll call; Council approved Mayor Elaine O'Neal's excused absence (White House visit) 4-0, and Leonardo Williams joined for 5-0 approvals of the City Manager's and City Attorney's priority items. Council also suspended the rules (5-0 each) to pass Item 7 (Cultural Roadmap Interlocal Agreement with Durham County, 5-0) and Item 15 (FY23 Historic Preservation Fund Grant Contract, 5-0) immediately during the work session.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment on Vision Zero, Traffic Calming, Braggtown Safety, Bike/Ped Plan & Decorum
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Five residents addressed Council under Citizen Matters: Trisha Smarr advocated speed humps, raised crosswalks, and hiring a Vision Zero coordinator; Donna Frederick raised Braggtown intersection and pedestrian safety concerns; Fred Broadwell spoke on Old West Durham's bike/pedestrian study; and Jackie Wagstaff and Mary Molina criticized heated exchanges and council decorum during the previous Monday night's zoning hearings.

agenda_items.title: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Feasibility Study Presentation & RCEP Grant Support Letter
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GoTriangle's Chuck Lattuca and Katherine Eggleston alongside Durham County's Ellen Beckman presented updated Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Phase 2 feasibility findings, projecting 12,000-18,000 daily boardings by 2050 alongside steep cost escalation beyond earlier $1.8B-$2.1B estimates driven roughly in equal thirds by inflation, Norfolk Southern freight capacity infrastructure, and expanded engineering contingencies. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton joined at 00:51:28, council members probed Driver Street and Plum Street grade-crossing closure impacts and Wake County alignment, and Council gave informal thumbs-up support for a letter backing Durham County's federal RCEP grant application, with DeDreana Freeman offering a sideways thumb urging local bus investments like Route 9 not be sidelined.

agenda_items.title: Settle October 3 Agenda & Closed Session (Oak Charter Academy v. City of Durham)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With six members now present, Council settled the October 3 regular meeting agenda (noting Items 7 and 15 were already approved) by a 6-0 vote and then voted 6-0 to enter closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation regarding Oak Charter Academy v. City of Durham (21 CVS 2129).

votes.item_title: Item 7: Approve Durham County Interlocal Agreement for Cultural Roadmap Implementation
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded approving the interlocal agreement with Durham County for the Cultural Roadmap, passing unanimously 5-0.

disagreements.issue: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Costs, Neighborhood Grade Crossings, and Local Bus Prioritization

disagreements.side_a_position: Support sending the letter backing Durham County's federal RCEP grant application to study station-area connectivity and East Durham crossing issues.

Regional commuter rail could move 12,000-18,000 riders daily by 2050 if capital costs and Norfolk Southern negotiations can be managed.

side_b_arguments: Rising commuter rail capital estimates and potential Driver Street/Plum Street crossing closures risk diverting transit attention and funds away from residents relying daily on Route 9 local bus service.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Council gave informal consensus to send the County's RCEP grant support letter while noting local transit priorities.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Sept.19, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Held on Monday, September 19, 2022 (indexed under 2022-09-20) with all seven Council members present and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presiding over public hearings while Mayor Elaine O'Neal rested her voice, Council approved pay adjustments for its three direct-report officers (7-0), the Consent Agenda (7-0), and pulled Item 14 renewing Bull City United (7-0). On Item 27, Council approved the one-year $197,500 ShotSpotter gunshot-detection pilot 5-2 over dissents from Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson. In land-use public hearings, Council approved 1409 Doc Nichols Road (60 townhomes, 3 Habitat homes) 5-2 (O'Neal and Freeman opposed; consistency 7-0), narrowly passed 7926 Massey Chapel Road (28 townhomes, 1 Habitat unit) 4-3 (O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman opposed; consistency 5-2 after clicker corrections), approved five street closings 6-1 by hand vote (Freeman opposed), and unanimously backed the 182-unit Dearborn Drive affordable/VFW project and 44-unit Wabash Parcels townhomes 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations (Melissa Wade Day, Algonquin Tennis Club, Diaper Need, Dementia, Grace Month) & Charter Officer Raises
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council honored gospel broadcaster Melissa Wade, celebrated the centennial of the historic Algonquin Tennis Club with Dr. Eugene Victor Maffo, proclaimed Diaper Need Awareness Week and World Alzheimer's/Dementia Awareness Day, and read the Grace Month proclamation in honor of Chief Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson. Mark-Anthony Middleton also publicly reported and Council voted 7-0 to approve annual performance salary adjustments for City Manager Wanda Page ($255,000 to $265,200), City Attorney Kim Rehberg ($206,700 to $219,102), and City Clerk Diana Schreiber ($103,175 to $107,302).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval & Pulled Item 14 (Bull City United Contract Renewal)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the Consent Agenda (excluding pulled Item 14 and Item 27 on GBA) 7-0, including the $4.03M Water Management facility change order, Gang Reduction Strategy, Legal Aid DEAR renewal, and NICE intelligence center contract. Resident Dante Dunstan spoke strongly in favor of Item 14 (Bull City United), urging Council not to let one individual's misstep jeopardize funding for credible violence interrupters, and Council renewed Bull City United 7-0.

agenda_items.title: ShotSpotter Response Services Agreement ($197,500 One-Year Pilot)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Before the vote on the one-year ShotSpotter gunshot-detection contract, Javiera Caballero argued against investing $197,500 in technology she viewed as unproven elsewhere and likely to heighten police presence in Black and brown neighborhoods rather than funding root-cause prevention, while Jillian Johnson opposed the contract for similar civil-liberties and efficacy concerns. Mark-Anthony Middleton countered that Council should judge the vetted pilot based on Durham's own Wilson Center evaluation data rather than outside composites, and the contract passed 5-2.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: 1409 Doc Nichols Road (60 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Andy Lester and Jared Edens of Edens Land Corp presented a 60-townhome proposal (PDR 7.245) including a revised commitment to donate three completed townhouses (rather than building pads) to Habitat for Humanity, 100-year stormwater detention, double silt fencing, and DPS/housing donations, after a 5-5 Planning Commission tie. Neighbors and advocates clashed over blasting damage, well-water sediment, Highway 98/Doc Nichols traffic, and rural sprawl versus housing supply and 3 Habitat units, with Council passing annexation and rezoning 5-2 (O'Neal and Freeman opposed) and the consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: 7926 Massey Chapel Road (28 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Edens Land Corp proposed annexing 5.828 acres at 7926 Massey Chapel Road and rezoning from RR to PDR 4.928 for 28 townhouses, committing one completed Habitat for Humanity townhome, a Massey Chapel sidewalk to the American Tobacco Trail (subject to NCDOT approval), 100-year sediment ponds, and weekend construction limits following a 7-7 Planning Commission tie. Neighbors Pat Brocchino and Jeremy Tarr objected to three-story height, uphill lighting, traffic near Southpoint Mall, and speculative marketing; Council passed annexation and rezoning 4-3 (O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman opposed) and the consistency statement 5-2 after correcting clicker errors.

agenda_items.title: Permanent Street Closings: Greenmount Dr, Arborstone Way, Broadstone Ct, Flatstone Ct, Upland Meadows Ln
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Cole Renigar presented Steve Puckett's request (SC2200004) to permanently close five platted rights-of-way running parallel to East Ramseur Street and the North Carolina Railroad to recombine parcels into 18.78-acre and 13.63-acre lots for future development east of Chandler Road. With no public speakers and electronic clickers replaced by raised-hand voting for the remainder of the night, Council approved the street closings 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Dearborn Drive Multi-Family (182 Affordable Units & VFW/BCA Civic Space)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton disclosed his nonprofit owns nearby Braggtown land with no financial inducement, Andy Lester and attorney Nil Ghosh presented LDG Development's RU-5 to PDR 19.401 rezoning (Planning Commission 11-0) for 182 apartments averaging 60% AMI or below for 30 years plus 5,000 sq ft of deeded civic space for VFW Post operations and Braggtown Community Association offices. VFW Commander Larry Coleman, Vanessa Mason Evans, and Donna Frederick strongly praised the partnership and urged future city support to add 30% AMI units; Council praised the project unanimously and approved both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Wabash Parcels (44 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Dr. William Chambers, attorney Floyd McKissick III, engineer Landon Lovelace, and former State Senator/Council Member Floyd McKissick Jr. presented a 9.96-acre infill rezoning at 1500/1521 Wabash Street and 1214 Truman Street from RU-5 to PDR 5.170 for 44 owner-occupied townhomes targeted near $300,000 for NCCU/Durham Tech workers, with 32% tree save, Greenway easement along Third Fork Creek, and $25,000 housing fund proffer (Planning Commission 8-5). Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0 before adjourning at 11:08 PM.

votes.item_title: Approve Annual Salary Adjustments for City Manager, City Attorney, and City Clerk
votes.notes: Mover and seconder voices ('so move... second') were not named aloud by the chair.
votes.discussion_detail: Following Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton's closed-session evaluation report, Council voted 7-0 by electronic vote to approve fiscal year salary increases for City Manager Wanda Page ($255,000 to $265,200), City Attorney Kim Rehberg ($206,700 to $219,102), and City Clerk Diana Schreiber ($103,175 to $107,302).

votes.item_title: Approve Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 14 and GBA Item 27)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded approving the Consent Agenda excluding resident-pulled Item 14 and General Business Agenda Item 27, passing 7-0 by electronic vote.

votes.item_title: Item 14 (Pulled): Approve Bull City United Update and Contract Renewal
votes.discussion_detail: Following testimony from Dante Dunstan supporting Bull City United's community violence interruption efforts, DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded renewing the Bull City United contract, passing 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Approve ShotSpotter Response Services Agreement ($197,500 One-Year Pilot)
votes.discussion_detail: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman moved and Leonardo Williams seconded approving the one-year ShotSpotter gunshot-detection contract. After Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson stated their opposition and Mark-Anthony Middleton defended evaluating the local pilot, the electronic vote passed 5-2.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and UEA for 1409 Doc Nichols Road
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded annexing 1409 Doc Nichols Road and authorizing a utility extension agreement with Edens Land Corp, passing 5-2 with Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DeDreana Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for 1409 Doc Nichols Road (RR to PDR 7.245)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded rezoning 1409 Doc Nichols Road from Rural Residential (RR) to Planned Development Residential 7.245 (PDR 7.245) for up to 60 townhouses including three completed Habitat units, passing 5-2 with O'Neal and Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 1409 Doc Nichols Road
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for 1409 Doc Nichols Road; after correcting an initial 6-1 clicker display involving Mayor O'Neal, the Clerk reported 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and UEA for 7926 Massey Chapel Road
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded annexing 7926 Massey Chapel Road effective September 30, 2022 and entering a UEA with Edens Land Corp. After Mayor O'Neal corrected her malfunctioning clicker from 'not voting' to 'no', the vote was recorded 4-3 with O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for 7926 Massey Chapel Road (RR to PDR 4.928)
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded rezoning 7926 Massey Chapel Road from RR to PDR 4.928 for up to 28 townhouses with one completed Habitat unit, passing 4-3 with O'Neal, Freeman, and Holsey-Hyman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Motion 3): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for 7926 Massey Chapel Road
votes.notes: After this item, Mayor O'Neal requested hand votes for the remainder of the meeting due to persistent electronic clicker failures.
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the consistency statement for 7926 Massey Chapel Road. After clicker malfunctions initially displayed an invalid abstention for DeDreana Freeman (who confirmed voting no) and a false no for Mayor O'Neal (who confirmed pressing yes), the final count was recorded 5-2.

votes.item_title: Item 35: Adopt Order Permanently Closing Greenmount Dr, Arborstone Way, Broadstone Ct, Flatstone Ct, and Upland Meadows Ln
votes.notes: Mover's name was cut/inaudible in ASR ('councilman ...').
votes.discussion_detail: Switched to raised-hand voting after clicker failures and seconded by Javiera Caballero, Council approved closing five platted rights-of-way east of Chandler Road by a 6-1 vote with DeDreana Freeman dissenting.

votes.item_title: Item 36 (Motion 1): Adopt Zoning Map Change for Dearborn Drive Multi-Family (RU-5 to PDR 19.401)
votes.discussion_detail: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman moved and Leonardo Williams seconded rezoning three Braggtown parcels from RU-5 to PDR 19.401 for 182 affordable apartments (60% AMI average, 30 years) and 5,000 sq ft of VFW/BCA civic space, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 36 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Dearborn Drive Multi-Family
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for the Dearborn Drive project, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 37 (Motion 1): Adopt Zoning Map Change for Wabash Parcels (RU-5 to PDR 5.170)
votes.discussion_detail: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman moved and Jillian Johnson seconded rezoning 1500/1521 Wabash Street and 1214 Truman Street from RU-5 to PDR 5.170 for up to 44 townhomes with a $25,000 housing fund donation and Greenway easement, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

votes.item_title: Item 37 (Motion 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Wabash Parcels
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams moved and Jillian Johnson seconded (with Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman also seconding) adopting the statutory consistency statement for Wabash Parcels, passing unanimously 7-0 by hand vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Sept.19, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: ShotSpotter Gunshot-Detection One-Year Pilot Approval
disagreements.summary: Council voted 5-2 to launch the $197,500 one-year ShotSpotter acoustic gunshot-detection pilot after sharp disagreement over effectiveness, civil liberties, and police deployment in Black and brown neighborhoods.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the vetted one-year pilot to test whether acoustic gunfire detection speeds emergency medical response and evidence collection.
side_a_arguments: Independent evaluation by Duke's Wilson Center will measure real Durham data before any permanent renewal.
Faster alerts can locate shooting victims even when no 911 call is made.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose ShotSpotter and invest instead in proven root-cause violence prevention.
side_b_arguments: Other cities found high false-positive rates, minimal violence reduction, and heightened unnecessary police encounters in Black and brown neighborhoods.
$197,500 would yield greater safety returns in youth programs, mental health, and violence interruption.
disagreements.resolution: The ShotSpotter contract passed 5-2.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Sept.19, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: 1409 Doc Nichols Road Rural Annexation, Blasting/Well Water Impacts, and Housing Supply
disagreements.summary: Following a 5-5 Planning Commission tie, Council passed 1409 Doc Nichols Road 5-2 while splitting over neighbor reports of well turbidity, blasting, and Highway 98 traffic versus housing supply and three completed Habitat townhomes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the 60-townhome development given upgraded Habitat, stormwater, and erosion proffers and urgent regional housing demand.
side_a_arguments: Denying the rezoning leaves worse outcomes—either luxury single-family homes on well/septic or warehouses—while restricting supply drives downtown rents upward.
The developer added three completed Habitat townhomes, double silt fencing, and 100-year stormwater ponds.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexing County parcels lacking city water/sewer protections and infrastructure capacity for surrounding rural residents.
side_b_arguments: Existing County residents face well-water sediment and blasting fears without automatic city utility extensions or pre-blast inspections.
Cumulative eastern annexations outpace roads, schools, and emergency response planning.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 5-2; consistency passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Sept.19, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: 7926 Massey Chapel Road Townhomes Compatibility and Traffic Near Southpoint
disagreements.summary: Following a 7-7 Planning Commission tie, Council split 4-3 on approving 28 townhomes squeezed between rural homes and Southpoint retail.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve 28 transitional townhomes with one Habitat unit, sidewalk to the American Tobacco Trail, and 100-year stormwater controls rather than four million-dollar by-right houses.
side_a_arguments: Reducing density from 40 to 28 units and extending public water/sewer to neighbors with failing septic provides meaningful mitigation.
Townhomes near retail and the American Tobacco Trail are far more attainable than $1M single-family estates.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject the rezoning due to neighborhood traffic congestion, flood-zone/stormwater concerns, height transition, and unverified sidewalk feasibility.
side_b_arguments: Southpoint weekend traffic already congests Massey Chapel Road, and no traffic study was required below 150 peak trips.
Neighbors disputed site elevation/light-pole spillover and questioned NCDOT approval for sidewalks.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and rezoning passed 4-3; consistency passed 5-2 after correcting clicker errors.

meetings.title: City Council Retreat- September 9, 2022 [Livestream]
meetings.executive_summary: At this five-hour facilitated City Council Housing Retreat held at Durham's new Water Management/Public Works facility with all seven Council members present, facilitators guided Council through a 'Wall of Wonder' retrospective spanning the 1980s through 2022 and future visions toward 2040. Members reflected on Durham's historical housing milestones—urban renewal, Hayti, the $95M housing bond, dedicated penny taxes, Eviction Diversion, Expanding Housing Choices, and the 2020-2021 pandemic—while surfacing sharp philosophical disagreements over market-rate supply versus public-interest housing subsidies, public housing stereotypes, growth's environmental impacts, and institutional trust. No formal votes were taken during the workshop; Council closed by calling for concrete data-driven follow-ups from DataWorks NC, community equity benchmarks, and clearer affordability definitions.

agenda_items.title: Retreat Opening, Personal Housing Stories & 1980s-2022 'Wall of Wonder' Timeline
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Facilitators opened the retreat at the new Public Works/Water Management/Fleet complex with each Council member sharing an image or personal story about home and stability—ranging from Mayor Elaine O'Neal's childhood home built on Morehead Avenue by her factory-worker father to Leonardo Williams's post-eviction search and DeDreana Freeman's loss of her sister. City staff and Council then mapped Durham's housing trajectory from the 1980s through 2022, highlighting Hayti/Southside redevelopment, the penny tax and $95M affordable housing bond, Expanding Housing Choices, Eviction Diversion, and pandemic dislocation.

agenda_items.title: Debate Over Market Supply, Affordable Housing Priorities, Environmental Stewardship & 2040 Vision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reviewing the Wall of Wonder and envisioning 2040, Council engaged in candid, occasionally tense exchanges over market-rate development versus targeted low-income subsidies, gentrification, public-housing stereotypes, water/tree stewardship, and how Council votes are framed publicly. Leonardo Williams urged building for high-income arrivals to shield historic neighborhoods while arguing public housing was meant to be transitional; Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman defended housing as a human right and pushed back against stereotyping low-wage, senior, and disabled residents; and Mark-Anthony Middleton pressed for concrete tax/bond policy tools and civility. Mayor O'Neal closed by outlining upcoming educational sessions including DataWorks NC.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Retreat- September 9, 2022 [Livestream]
disagreements.issue: Market-Rate Housing Supply, Public Housing Responsibility, and Environmental Trade-Offs
disagreements.summary: During the five-hour housing retreat, Council divided sharply on whether building market-rate housing prevents displacement, how public housing and low-wage workers are framed, and whether pro-growth annexations compromise water and environmental stewardship.
disagreements.side_a_position: Build supply across all price tiers to absorb high-wealth newcomers, rely on concrete bonds/taxes for subsidies, and view public housing as transitional.
side_a_arguments: Leonardo Williams argued Durham must create higher-end supply so $189,000+ earners do not bid away downtown Black neighborhoods, adding that public housing was meant to be transitional and some people walk off $19/hour jobs.

Mark-Anthony Middleton contended government action only materializes through budgets, bonds ($95M), and dedicated taxes, and pushed back against framing pro-growth votes as 'harm' or 'poisoning water'.
disagreements.side_b_position: Treat housing as a human right, prioritize deep subsidies for low-wage, senior, and disabled residents, and center environmental stewardship in growth decisions.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson and Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman pushed back against stigmatizing public housing residents, noting many are elderly, disabled on fixed Social Security, or working multiple low-wage jobs.
DeDreana Freeman and Mayor Elaine O'Neal emphasized protecting tree canopy, water quality, and longtime residents rather than letting private developers dictate Durham's growth pattern.
disagreements.resolution: No formal votes were taken; Council agreed to continue housing deep-dive sessions including a data presentation from DataWorks NC.
