meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session May 5, 2022 at 1 p.m. (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: In the livestream recording of the May 5, 2022 Durham City Council Work Session, Council unanimously approved (6-0) both the City Manager's and City Attorney's priority items before voting 5-1 to suspend the rules for immediate action on two affordable housing development loan commitments (Items 6 and 7). Over the lone dissent of Council Member DeDreana Freeman, Council voted 5-1 to authorize up to $1.5 million in affordable housing bond funds as a conditional binding permanent financing commitment for the rehabilitation of 177 rental units at JFK Towers (4900 Old Farm Road). Later in the session, staff presented the FY 2022–29 stormwater rate model and $21.5 million FY 2023 CIP budget, the Clerk presented board and commission nominations, and Council unanimously voted (6-0) to settle the upcoming meeting agenda and enter closed session on Darryl Howard v. City of Durham.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and City Manager / City Attorney Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following reminders on primary early voting (Caballero) and recognition of Durham's Innovate Durham award (Williams), City Manager Wanda Page presented six priority items including rule suspensions for JFK Towers (Item 6) and Cedar Terrace Apartments (Item 7). Council unanimously approved the Manager's priority items (6-0) and the City Attorney's request for an end-of-meeting closed session (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Rule Suspension and Item 6: JFK Towers Affordable Housing Bond Loan Commitment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 5-1 to suspend the rules to act immediately on Items 6 (JFK Towers) and 7 (Cedar Terrace Apartments) so developers could meet permanent financing lock and May 15 tax credit deadlines. Council Member Jillian Johnson then moved, seconded by Council Member Leonardo Williams, to authorize up to $1.5 million in affordable housing bond funds to rehabilitate 177 affordable rental units at JFK Towers (4900 Old Farm Road), passing 5-1 with Council Member DeDreana Freeman voting in opposition.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Item 22: FY 2023 Stormwater Rates and CIP Rate Model Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented the FY22–FY29 stormwater rate model, noting upcoming Jordan Lake and Falls Lake rule rewrites and explaining that operating reserves are projected to move from $24.4 million in FY 2022 to $8.9 million in FY 2023 due to $21.5 million in FY 2023 CIP spending, nearly half for the South Ellerbe Creek restoration project. Staff also compared Durham's residential and commercial stormwater rates against peers and reviewed rate history since 2010.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Nominations, Agenda Settling, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Clerk read board nominations for BPAC (Cesar Castro), the Historic Preservation Commission (Rakim U. Chambers), and the Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee (Italo Medelius). Council unanimously voted 6-0 to settle the regular agenda (returning Item 8 to administration for one cycle) and voted 6-0 to enter closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) regarding Darryl Howard v. City of Durham.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items (Items 5, 6, 7, 12, 20, and 22)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted City Manager Wanda Page's priority schedule including rule-suspension requests for Items 6 and 7 and presentations on Items 5, 12, 20, and 22.

votes.item_title: Approve City Attorney's Priority Item (Closed Session Request)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted City Attorney's request to schedule a closed session at the conclusion of regular business.

votes.item_title: Suspend the Rules to Vote on Items 6 (JFK Towers) and 7 (Cedar Terrace Apartments)
votes.notes: Voice vote recorded by presiding chair as passing with one unnamed member in opposition (5-1).
votes.discussion_detail: Motion to suspend Council rules to take immediate action on two affordable housing development loan commitments during the work session.

votes.item_title: Item 6: JFK Towers NC TCLP Conditional Permanent Financing Commitment (Up to $1.5M)
votes.notes: Council Member DeDreana Freeman was explicitly named as the sole opposition vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Authorized the City Manager to issue JFK Towers NC TCLP (or approved affiliate) a conditional binding permanent financing commitment up to $1.5 million in affordable housing bond funds to rehabilitate 177 affordable rental units at 4900 Old Farm Road.

votes.item_title: Settle Regular Meeting Agenda (Return Item 8; Consent 1–3, 5, 9–19; GBA 20; Public Hearings 21–22)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Settled agenda with Item 8 returned to administration for an additional cycle due to technology issues and additional questions.

votes.item_title: Enter Closed Session Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) (Darryl Howard v. City of Durham)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Closed session for attorney-client consultation concerning handling or settlement of Darryl Howard v. City of Durham, 1:17-cv-477 (Middle District of North Carolina).

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council May 3, 2022 at 6 p.m. Council Vacancy Public Comment (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: On May 3, 2022, the Durham City Council held a special public comment meeting with all six seated members present to hear community input on the four finalists for the vacant At-Large Council seat: Nate Baker, Shaniqua Nicole Diggs, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and Henry McCoy Jr. Mayor Elaine O'Neal opened the meeting and turned presiding duties over to Legislative Committee Co-Chair Jillian Johnson, who allotted 30 minutes of speaking time per candidate in alphabetical order. In the portions captured by the digest, speakers supporting Nate Baker highlighted his Planning Commission service, Braggtown advocacy, and mastery of the Unified Development Ordinance and Comprehensive Plan on affordable housing and growth, while supporters of Dr. Henry McCoy Jr. emphasized his national inclusive economic development work, Helius entrepreneurship initiatives, and cross-community bridge building. No formal votes were taken, and Mayor O'Neal adjourned the session at 7:59 p.m.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Presiding Handoff, Ground Rules, and Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal welcomed residents in chambers and online to the Council vacancy public comment session for the four finalists and invited Legislative Committee Co-Chair Jillian Johnson to preside. Johnson outlined the format granting 30 minutes per finalist's supporters in alphabetical order (Nate Baker, Shaniqua Nicole Diggs, Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and Henry McCoy Jr.), and the Clerk confirmed all six seated Council members were present.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of At-Large Finalist Nate Baker
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Virtual and in-person supporters—beginning with Braggtown resident Celeste Ritchie and environmental/planning advocates—urged Council to appoint Nate Baker. Speakers emphasized his urban planning expertise, grassroots work encouraging proactive developer engagement in Braggtown, and command of Durham's Unified Development Ordinance and Comprehensive Plan in addressing affordable housing and intense development pressures.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of At-Large Finalist Dr. Henry McCoy Jr. and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Supporters of Dr. Henry McCoy Jr.—including a Harvard adjunct professor whose inclusive economic development guide co-developed with McCoy was adopted by the Biden administration's OMB, Matt Kopac, and local partners—highlighted McCoy's entrepreneurship training via Helius and his ability to unify Black, Latino, and business communities. Council Member Johnson thanked all applicants and residents before Mayor O'Neal adjourned the special meeting at 7:59 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 2, 2022 at 7 p.m. (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 2, 2022 Durham City Council regular meeting, all six seated members attended as Mayor Elaine O'Neal, Council Member Jillian Johnson, and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presented ceremonial proclamations for National Drinking Water Week, Internal Audit Week, and Children's Mental Health Awareness Week. Following a spirited discussion on an agenda item captured only at its outcome in the truncated digest, Council passed that motion 4-2 over 'No' votes from Mayor O'Neal and Council Member DeDreana Freeman. Council then held a public hearing with no speakers on Item 18—the Limited Obligation Bonds (LOBs), Series 2022 interim capital financing not to exceed $132 million—and adopted all five authorizing resolutions and motions unanimously (6-0). At adjournment at 9:44 p.m., members reacted to the leaked U.S. Supreme Court draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade and urged residents to register to vote.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance, Roll Call, and Ceremonial Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the meeting to order with a moment of silent meditation, Council Member DeDreana Freeman led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all six seated members answered roll call. O'Neal presented a National Drinking Water Week proclamation to Williams Water Treatment Plant Assistant Superintendent Robert Fullwood—recognizing Durham's third consecutive NC best-tasting water award and student poster contest winners—while Jillian Johnson and Mark-Anthony Middleton handled Internal Audit Week and Children's Mental Health Awareness Week proclamations.

agenda_items.title: Contested Agenda Item (Preceding Item 18; Subject Truncated in Digest)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following what Mayor O'Neal characterized as a 'spirited discussion,' Council voted on the agenda item immediately preceding Item 18. The motion passed 4-2, with Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Council Member DeDreana Freeman voting No; the item title and preceding debate occurred within the truncated middle section of the transcript digest.

agenda_items.title: Item 18: Limited Obligation Bonds (LOBs), Series 2022 Public Hearing and Financing Resolutions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director Tim Flora presented the Series 2022 Limited Obligation Bond interim financing—structured as a two-year interest-only bank placement line of credit not to exceed $132 million for previously adopted capital projects, with LGC filing scheduled for May 3, an approving resolution on June 6, and closing on June 16. After opening and closing the statutory public hearing with no speakers, Council unanimously adopted all five required resolutions and authorizations by 6-0 votes.

agenda_items.title: Closing Voter Registration Appeal and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Before adjourning at 9:44 p.m., members referenced breaking news of the Supreme Court draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade and urged residents to register to vote.

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council May 2, 2022 at 3 p.m. Council Vacancy Interviews (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal convened a special Durham City Council meeting on May 2, 2022, with all six seated members present (Elaine O'Neal, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, and Leonardo Williams), and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton facilitated questioning as Procedures Committee chair for the four finalists seeking the at-large seat vacated by Charlie Reece. Council interviewed urban planner Nate Baker, North Carolina Central University public administration professor Dr. Nicole Diggs, social work educator and DSS Board Vice Chair Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman, and former North Carolina Assistant Secretary of Commerce Dr. Henry McCoy Jr. Questioning focused on Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) reform and small-area planning, affordable housing strategies, support for the Community Safety Department and unarmed crisis response versus traditional policing, economic equity and small-business growth, local voting engagement, and potential conflict-of-interest optics regarding Dr. McCoy's uncompensated advisory work with Hayti Reborn on Durham Housing Authority matters. No formal motions or votes were taken during the interview session, which concluded with Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton announcing a May 3 public comment hearing at 6:00 p.m. and a Council appointment vote scheduled for the Thursday work session.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Finalist Introductions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the special meeting to order at 3:00 p.m. and directed the City Clerk to call the roll, confirming all six seated members (Elaine O'Neal, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, and Leonardo Williams) were present. Mayor O'Neal introduced the finalists present for the at-large seat vacated by Charlie Reece before Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton assumed facilitation on behalf of the Procedures Committee.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Vacancy Finalist Interview: Nate Baker
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Urban planner and four-year Durham Planning Commission member Nate Baker identified gun violence, traffic fatalities caused by car-dependent design, and rapid growth/displacement as Durham's top challenges. He advocated a comprehensive rewrite of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), proactive small-area and corridor planning linked to Engaged Durham, and continued investment in the Community Safety Department while stating he did not favor defunding the police. During follow-up questioning, Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman challenged his suggestion that Durham lacked small-area planning, citing the Ninth Street Compact Design District.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Vacancy Finalist Interview: Dr. Nicole Diggs
agenda_items.discussion_summary: NCCU assistant professor of public administration Dr. Nicole Diggs emphasized housing affordability, rental and down-payment assistance, pacing development with 80%, 60%, and 30% AMI set-asides, workforce alignment for incoming tech jobs, and unarmed alternatives to policing. DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned her local voting history, and Dr. Diggs explained she had remained registered in Virginia until recently voting in North Carolina the prior Thursday. Jillian Johnson also asked Dr. Diggs to clarify she was not formally declaring a future candidacy during the broadcast to avoid triggering campaign committee filing deadlines.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Vacancy Finalist Interview: Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Social work professor and Durham County DSS Board Vice Chair Dr. Monique Holsey-Hyman outlined her background in intensive case management, family preservation, and grassroots social services. She prioritized community safety, youth programming, expanded reentry support before release, developer 'pay-to-play' housing affordability expectations alongside financial literacy rather than temporary subsidies alone, ShotSpotter technology, and a proposed 'community safety intensive case management mobile crisis unit' pairing social workers, medical/mental health staff, and peer support.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Vacancy Finalist Interview: Dr. Henry McCoy Jr.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Former NC Assistant Secretary of Commerce and faculty member Dr. Henry McCoy Jr. centered his remarks on 'equity by design,' leveraging public land, inclusionary zoning, impact-investor partnerships to connect residents to economic growth without displacement, and expanding unarmed crisis and traffic response. Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman pressed Dr. McCoy on potential conflict-of-interest optics regarding his advocacy for the Hayti Reborn proposal before the Durham Housing Authority (DHA); Dr. McCoy stated on the record that he held no equity stake, was not a paid consultant, and had no financial interest in the project.

agenda_items.title: Procedures Housekeeping and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton thanked all four finalists and announced that public comment on the vacancy finalists would be held on May 3, 2022 at 6:00 p.m., followed by a Council appointment vote at the Thursday work session. He yielded back to Mayor Elaine O'Neal, who adjourned the special meeting at 03:02:08 ahead of the 7:00 p.m. regular meeting.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session April 21, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the April 21, 2022 Durham City Council Work Session, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton had an excused absence while Council Member Leonardo Williams arrived shortly after the priority-item vote. Council unanimously approved (4-0 among members present at the time) City Manager Wanda Page's priority presentations on the Upper Neuse River Basin Association (UNRBA) FY 2023 budget and the Forever Home, Durham FY 2022 update, and welcomed new Assistant City Attorney Carlos Hernandez. Later, Council members discussed aligning Community Development, Workforce and Economic Development, open space planning, and community engagement prior to budget adoption, with Mayor O'Neal challenging colleagues to submit specific budget asks across federal, state, and city levels. During board nominations, Council resolved a 3-3 deadlock over re-advertising versus appointing Haley Thompson after staff confirmed the seat had already been re-advertised twice, and unanimously voted 5-0 to settle the May 2 regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the work session to order with Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton excused and Council Member Leonardo Williams in transit. Council Member Jillian Johnson highlighted the April 22 primary voter registration deadline, DeDreana Freeman welcomed USDA Deputy Secretary Dr. Jewel Bronaugh to Duke's food policy discussions, Javiera Caballero announced the May 18 ARPA special meeting, and Mayor O'Neal praised Lincoln Community Health Center and her small-business tour.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items (UNRBA Budget and Forever Home, Durham Update) and Staff Introduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested 20-minute priority presentations for Agenda Item 12 (UNRBA FY 2023 budget) and supplemental Agenda Item 19 (Forever Home, Durham FY 2022 update), which passed 4-0 by voice vote right before Council Member Leonardo Williams took his seat. City Attorney Rehberg then introduced new Assistant City Attorney Carlos Hernandez, who joined the office on April 4.

agenda_items.title: Interdepartmental Community Development, Open Space, and Budget Priorities Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: During budget-season discussion, Council members questioned whether Community Development had open-space planning capacity and urged stronger coordination among grants, federal funds, affordable housing bond investments, Workforce and Economic Development, and community partners rather than defaulting to consultants and RFPs. Mayor O'Neal challenged Council to bring concrete lists of federal, state, and city-level asks—including Leonardo Williams's call for a centralized resource hub—to the next work session.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Tie-Breaking and May 2 Agenda Settling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After resolving one nomination in favor of Ebony, Council faced a 3-3 split between appointing Haley Thompson and re-advertising; once the Clerk confirmed with staff that the vacancy had already been re-advertised twice, members shifted votes to appoint Thompson. Council then unanimously voted 5-0 to settle the May 2, 2022 regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 1–13 and GBA Public Hearings 15–18) and adjourned at 3:39 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council April 18, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal delivered her first State of the City address, highlighting gun violence intervention efforts including the reconvened Durham Crime Cabinet, the Community Safety Department's HEART crisis response pilot, police pay raises and recruiting bonuses, affordable housing investments, and nearly $20 million in federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law transit and trail grants. The Council granted Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton an excused absence and passed the Consent Agenda unanimously 5-0, including early general obligation bond refunding. Following public hearings, the Council unanimously approved 5-0 the Cedar Trace Apartments zoning map change for a 200-unit 4% LIHTC affordable housing community despite a pending RFP award appeal on an associated development loan item. The Council also unanimously adopted 5-0 the FY 2022-2023 HUD Annual Action Plan and four corresponding grant project ordinances totaling over $4.2 million across CDBG, HOME, ESG, and HOPWA.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Invocation, and Excused Absence for Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal opened the meeting and acknowledged five seated members present, noting Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton was traveling by air. Council Member Leonardo Williams moved and Council Member Javiera Caballero seconded an excused absence for Middleton.

agenda_items.title: Mayor Elaine O'Neal's First State of the City Address
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal reviewed her first four months in office alongside 29 city departments and thanked community violence interrupters, Ceasefire organizers, and Love & Respect for addressing gun violence after six recent deaths. She highlighted reconvening the Durham Crime Cabinet with Board of County Commissioners Chair Brenda Howerton, launching the 911 Training Academy with Durham Tech, standing up the HEART program, police compensation and $10,000 signing bonuses, $2.88 million in Small Business Opportunity Loan funds, $6.5 million in DERA eviction relief, youth employment applications, and $19.8 million in federal grants including a $9 million RAISE grant for the downtown rail trail and $10.8 million for bus facility renovations. She also urged the Council to purchase property to build workforce housing for teachers, firefighters, police, and city staff, and called on residents to log five hours of community service.

agenda_items.title: Fair Housing Month Proclamation and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero read a Fair Housing Month proclamation accepted by Sharon Sunkel of the Durham Regional Association of Realtors, emphasizing housing equity and historic discrimination under the 1968 Fair Housing Act. Council Member Caballero thanked colleagues for excusing her absences after contracting COVID-19 abroad and noted upcoming ARPA meeting scheduling, while Council Member Leonardo Williams shared transit observations from Miami and London and asked that an unspecified Hayti Reborn-related matter be sent to the City Attorney to ensure council process transparency.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 3, 4, 7-10, 12-17, and 20)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page confirmed there were no priority items and no items pulled from Consent. Council Member Leonardo Williams highlighted Item 12 for early general obligation bond refunding savings, and Council Member DeDreana Freeman moved approval.

agenda_items.title: Cedar Trace Apartments Zoning Map Change and Consistency Statement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a zoning map change across five parcels totaling 16.88 acres along Carver Street and Miami Boulevard from RS-8 (Falls/Jordan protected watershed) to RSM(D), alongside a Future Land Use Map change to Medium Density Residential for a 200-unit 4% LIHTC community serving households at or below 80% AMI (averaging 60% AMI). Applicant representative Toby Coleman (with Taft Mills Group) and supporters Matt Lowder and CJ Tyree spoke in favor; Planning Commission had recommended approval 11-0. Council Member DeDreana Freeman asked about the related Cedar Trace and JFK Towers development loan items referred back at the work session, and City Manager Wanda Page confirmed an RFP award appeal was pending.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (2 votes: rezoning ordinance and consistency statement)

agenda_items.title: FY 2022-2023 HUD Annual Action Plan and CDBG, HOME, ESG, and HOPWA Grant Ordinances
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented the draft FY 2022-2023 Annual Action Plan allocating federal HUD formula grants: $2,100,000 in CDBG, $1,100,000 in HOME, $174,000 in Emergency Solutions Grants (ESG), and $858,000 in HOPWA funding. Resident Bonita Green urged targeting home repair and roof assistance to seniors in historically redlined neighborhoods to counter displacement pressures, and Council Member DeDreana Freeman endorsed coordinating anti-gentrification home repair efforts through the city housing task force.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous among five present members.
votes.discussion_detail: Middleton was noted as traveling by airplane.

votes.item_title: Item 18: Cedar Trace Apartments Zoning Map Change Ordinance
votes.notes: Council Member Jillian Johnson registered her affirmative vote verbally because her electronic clicker battery died.
votes.discussion_detail: Rezones 16.88 acres across 5 parcels from RS-8 F/J-B to RSM(D) and updates the FLUM for 200 LIHTC affordable units.

votes.notes: Roll call taken verbally due to Johnson's malfunctioning remote.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopts statutory consistency and reasonableness statement for Cedar Trace zoning map change.

meetings.title: Joint City Council - DHA Board Meeting April 11, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council and the Durham Housing Authority (DHA) Board of Commissioners held a virtual special joint informational meeting to review Forever Home Durham investments, DHA's operational stabilization, and HUD Troubled Agency Recovery Agreement obligations. Community Development Director Reginald Johnson detailed $160 million in city affordable housing commitments including $59 million in bond funds for the first four Downtown Durham Neighborhood Plan (DDNP) phases and $4.5 million for non-DDNP repairs at McDougald Terrace, Laurel Oaks, and Morreene Road. DHA CEO Anthony Scott reported progress cutting work-order backlogs from 1,600 to under 13 and reducing Fresh Start eviction risks, while explaining HUD mandates requiring 95% occupancy, a REAC score of 60 or higher by June 30, 2023, and repositioning McDougald Terrace out of public housing within two years. No formal votes were taken, though Council members and public residents raised sharp questions about McDougald Terrace preservation, right-to-return protections under RAD conversions, and holding regular quarterly joint meetings.

agenda_items.title: Opening Remarks and Joint Council-DHA Board Introductions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal and DHA Board Chair Dan Hudgins opened the 1:00 PM virtual joint session with introductions from seated City Council members (O'Neal, Middleton, Caballero, Freeman, with Johnson joining during the meeting and Williams absent out of town) and DHA Commissioners (Hudgins, Vice Chair Mimi Webb Bledsoe, Christine Westfall, Bo Glenn, Terrell Armstrong, Pebbles Lucas, and Angela Holmes). Participants emphasized strengthening formal communication between the City and DHA after past tensions and crises.

agenda_items.title: City of Durham Affordable Housing and Forever Home Durham Partnership Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented the City's $160 million Forever Home Durham capital framework combining the $95 million affordable housing bond, dedicated two-cent housing tax funds, and HUD grants. He highlighted $59 million in bond funds committed to the first four DDNP redevelopment phases, $4.5 million for urgent non-DDNP repairs across McDougald Terrace, Laurel Oaks, and Morreene Road, $2.7 million in operations and relocation support, and homelessness coordination delivering 225 Housing Choice Vouchers and 68 Emergency Housing Vouchers.

agenda_items.title: DHA CEO Anthony Scott Comprehensive Operations, HUD Recovery Agreement, and DDNP Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DHA CEO Anthony Scott reported serving over 4,000 families (9,200+ residents) amid 33% staff vacancies and 35% turnover, while cutting >30-day work-order backlogs from 1,600 to fewer than 13 through a centralized call line. He reviewed DHA's February 2022 HUD Recovery Agreement resulting from its 2018 PHAS score of 59, requiring 95% occupancy and a REAC score >=60 by June 30, 2023 (or third-party management) plus a repositioning plan for McDougald Terrace due February 2023 given a preliminary $53 million 20-year capital need. Scott and staff also updated redevelopment at JJ Henderson, The Joyce (80 senior units), Liberty Street/East Main phases (Elizabeth Street and Commerce Street), Phase II RFP planning for DHA headquarters, Fayette Place, and Forest Hill Heights, Fresh Start rent-arrears relief, and ConnectHome Wi-Fi, while taking tough questions from residents Jacqueline Wagstaff and Mr. Robertson about McDougald Terrace and Lincoln Apartments.

agenda_items.title: Joint Policy Discussion, Public Chat Q&A, and Quarterly Meeting Cadence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton pressed Scott to clarify for residents what HUD's phrase 'repositioning out of public housing inventory' means under RAD and Section 18 (preserving subsidies and right-to-return guarantees) and asked how work orders are closed out. Council members addressed public chat inquiries from Raquel Williams-Jones and Sonia Laurie regarding Jobs Plus outreach, Section 3 contracting, and RAD resident council organizing rights, and Council and DHA Board leaders agreed to pursue quarterly joint meetings.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session April 7, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Operating with four members present (O'Neal, Middleton, Freeman, and Johnson) due to excused travel and illness absences for Williams and Caballero, the City Council granted Caballero an excused absence 4-0 and approved priority adjustments from the City Manager and City Clerk 4-0, including referring back the Cedar Trace and JFK Towers development loan awards pending an RFP appeal. Under a 4-0 suspension of the rules, the Council unanimously adopted a resolution authorizing a Western Intake Partnership ARPA regionalization feasibility grant application ahead of an April 13 deadline. During pulled-item review, Council Member DeDreana Freeman pressed City Manager Wanda Page for greater transparency and equity guardrails in housing RFP protest reviews after speakers from Geer Street Residential challenged their rejected bid, while Council Member Jillian Johnson strongly endorsed pursuing legislative authority for civilian crash investigators. The Council settled the April 18 agenda 4-0 and informally agreed to move at-large vacancy finalist cuts to April 21 so absent colleagues could participate.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Excused Absence for Javiera Caballero, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal convened the work session with four members present, noting Council Member Leonardo Williams was already excused and granting an excused absence to Council Member Javiera Caballero who was ill. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton and Council Member Jillian Johnson congratulated Bethesda Elementary fourth-grader Frank Dumas on advancing to the Scripps National Spelling Bee.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Clerk Priority Items and Item 11 (Western Intake Partnership ARPA Grant)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested adding and suspending rules to act immediately on Item 11 (Western Intake Partnership ARPA merger/regionalization feasibility grant facing an April 13 deadline), referring back Items 5 (Cedar Trace loan) and 6 (JFK Towers loan) to Community Development, and adding a presentation for Item 20 (Small Business Recovery Fund amendment). City Clerk Diana Schreiber introduced assistant clerk Ashley Adams, referred back Item 1 (Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee) for re-advertising, and moved Item 2 (At-large vacancy selection) to Other Matters. Following 4-0 approvals of both priority lists, the Council suspended rules 4-0 and adopted Item 11.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-0 (4 votes: Manager priority, Clerk priority, rule suspension, Item 11 adoption)

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: Civilian Crash Investigators (Item 4) and Affordable Housing RFP Protests (Items 5-9)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton pulled Item 4 (2022 Legislative Short Session Agenda) to examine the request for General Assembly authority to hire civilian traffic crash investigators, with Deputy Police Chief Ryan Smith and Chief of Staff Karmisha Wallace answering operational questions and Council Member Jillian Johnson strongly backing the reform. Community speakers Leah Bergman and Tiffany Elder pulled Items 7, 8, and 9 (Lofts at Southside Phases 3 & 4) to protest Community Development's RFP scoring and lack of debrief transparency regarding Geer Street Residential's rejected application under Items 5 and 6. Council Member DeDreana Freeman pressed City Manager Wanda Page for clearer scoring accountability and equitable processes for nonprofit/local developers, whereas Middleton cautioned against council members adjudicating staff procurement bids mid-appeal.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (Items 3-4, 7-10, 12-17 kept on Consent; 5-6 referred back)

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Durham Small Business Recovery Fund First Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD Director Andre Pettigrew and Carolina Small Business Development Fund CEO Kevin Dick presented amendments to rebrand the fund as the Durham Small Business Opportunity Fund, permit refinancing high-interest predatory fintech debt, raise the eligible business revenue cap from $2 million to $5 million, and partner with traditional banks on joint lending. Council members asked about repayment terms, outreach to Black-owned and Hispanic-owned firms, and tracking capital deployment.

agenda_items.title: Set April 18 Council Agenda and Adjust At-Large Vacancy Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Council voted 4-0 to set the April 18, 2022 meeting agenda with Consent Items 3, 4, 7-10, and 12-17 and Public Hearings 18 and 19. Under Other Matters, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton proposed shifting the initial cut of at-large vacancy applicants from April 7 to the April 21 work session because Caballero and Williams were absent, noting he would submit his ballot electronically prior to his own April 21 excused absence. Members signaled informal consensus via thumbs-up and congratulated Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson on her Senate confirmation to the U.S. Supreme Court.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-0 (Agenda settled); Informal consensus on vacancy schedule

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Council Member Javiera Caballero
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous among four members present.
votes.discussion_detail: Caballero was ill; Leonardo Williams had previously been granted an excused absence on April 4.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager Priority Items (Add Item 11 Rule Suspension, Refer Back Items 5 & 6, Add Item 20 Presentation)
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Adds expedited handling of Western Intake Partnership ARPA grant resolution and removes Cedar Trace/JFK Towers loans from cycle pending RFP appeal.

votes.item_title: Approve City Clerk Priority Items (Refer Back Item 1, Move Vacancy Selection to Other Matters)
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Refers back Mayor's Hispanic/Latino Committee nomination to re-advertise and defers vacancy cut to Other Matters.

votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspension needed to meet April 13 regional grant submission deadline.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Adopt Western Intake Partnership ARPA Regionalization Feasibility Grant Resolution
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Authorizes joint regional water intake merger/regionalization feasibility study ARPA grant application.

votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Sets Consent Items 3, 4, 7-10, 12-17 and GBA Public Hearings 18 and 19.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 7, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Affordable Housing RFP Scoring Transparency and Council Oversight Role (Items 5-9)
disagreements.summary: Following public complaints from Geer Street Residential representatives over rejected development loan applications and lack of RFP scoring feedback, Council Member DeDreana Freeman pushed City Manager Wanda Page for clearer scoring transparency and equity guardrails for local/community developers, whereas Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton cautioned against council intervention in staff procurement appeals.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require stronger RFP scoring transparency and equity guardrails so local/nonprofit housing developers understand and trust award outcomes.
side_a_arguments: Unexplained RFP rejections breed distrust among local community housing developers.
Council must ensure scoring rubrics include clear equity guardrails before projects advance.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain strict staff insulation in procurement scoring while formal protest appeals proceed through administrative channels.
side_b_arguments: Referring Items 5 and 6 back to Community Development protects the integrity of the pending appeal.
Council members should avoid adjudicating technical RFP scoring during live procurement disputes.
disagreements.resolution: Items 5 and 6 remained referred back pending administrative appeal resolution, while Items 7-9 stayed on Consent.

meetings.title: Durham City Council April 4, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: The City Council excused travel-related absences for Council Members Javiera Caballero (April 4), Mark-Anthony Middleton (April 18 and 21), and Leonardo Williams (April 7), and voted 5-0 to postpone its April 6 ARPA special meeting so Caballero could participate. After spirited policy debate over the 2014 lease putting Major League Baseball stadium upgrade obligations on taxpayers, the Council voted 5-0 to approve an amended FY 2021-22 CIP and Skanska design-build contract doubling the Durham Bulls Athletic Park upgrade budget toward $10 million. On the Bull City Townhomes rezoning for up to 147 townhomes at 1343 Ellis Road and 1326 Clinton Road, Council divided over whether to grant applicant Mark Bullock a fourth continuance until August; Freeman's continuance motion died for lack of a second, and the Council rejected the rezoning 0-5 before adopting the denial consistency statement 5-0 and approving a pulled VPN performance audit 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences and Postponement of April 6 ARPA Special Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Council Member Javiera Caballero unexpectedly delayed abroad, the Council voted 5-0 to excuse her absence and 5-0 to postpone the scheduled April 6 ARPA work session. Members also voted 5-0 to approve excused absences for Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton (April 18 and 21) and Council Member Leonardo Williams (April 7), and noted delaying the April 7 at-large vacancy finalist selection to April 21.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations for National Public Safety Telecommunicators Week and National Community Development Week
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Leonardo Williams read a proclamation honoring April 10-16 as National Public Safety Telecommunicators Week, accepted by Durham Emergency Communications Center master specialist Ileana O'Sullivan. Council Member DeDreana Freeman then presented the National Community Development Week proclamation (April 11-15) to Community Development Director Reginald Johnson.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 2, 4-12, and 14-16; Item 3 Pulled)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After confirming supplemental attachments for Items 13 and 16 and noting citizen Helen Calloway pulled Item 3 (VPN Access and Digital Technology Audit), the Council approved the remainder of the Consent Agenda 5-0.

agenda_items.title: FY 2021-22 CIP Amendment and Skanska Design-Build Contract for Durham Bulls Athletic Park Upgrades
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated amending the CIP and Skanska USA contract to accommodate roughly $10 million in Major League Baseball Player Development License facility upgrades at Durham Bulls Athletic Park, nearly double the original $5.2 million projection. Council Member Jillian Johnson criticized the 2014 lease expiring in 2033 for placing 100% of mandatory upgrade costs on the city while granting the Bulls naming rights, while Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton, Williams, Freeman, and Mayor O'Neal defended the investment by citing the Bulls' estimated $33.3 million direct economic impact and civic value.

agenda_items.title: Bull City Townhomes Zoning Map Change (1343 Ellis Road and 1326 Clinton Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Returning from a February 7 continuance, applicant Mark Bullock and engineer Cliff Cradle sought to rezone 12.25 acres from Rural Residential to RSM(D) for up to 147 townhomes (following a 0-13 Planning Commission recommendation against). Neighbors and opponents including Thomas Linds, Kellen Arney-Johnson, Gabriel Carrillo, Phillip Lawson, Steve DeVries, and Charles Hansen raised traffic, watershed/creek runoff, and community-engagement objections, while supporters including Steve Raj and Albert Baptist urged housing supply and backing a Black local developer. Freeman moved to continue the hearing to August after reopening it, which died without a second; Council then voted 0-5 against rezoning and 5-0 for the denial consistency statement.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Rezoning Failed 0-5; Denial Consistency Statement Passed 5-0

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item: VPN Access and Digital Technology Performance Audit (February 2022)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal called Helen Calloway regarding pulled Item 3, the February 2022 VPN Access and Digital Technology Performance Audit; Calloway was not in the queue to speak. Council voted 5-0 on roll call to accept the audit.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council April 4, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Procedural Continuance vs. Immediate Vote on Bull City Townhomes Rezoning (Item 19)
disagreements.summary: Although all five members ultimately voted against approving the Bull City Townhomes rezoning over unfinalized proffers, neighborhood engagement failures, and watershed/traffic concerns, members split over whether to grant applicant Mark Bullock another continuance until August.
disagreements.side_a_position: Continue the public hearing to August to give the applicant another opportunity to formalize proffers and address neighborhood engagement.
side_a_arguments: Freeman cited Jordan Lake buffer concerns and unresolved community outreach while asking to continue to August.
Johnson supported townhome density in principle and said she was open to a continuance if proffers were solidified.
disagreements.side_b_position: Refuse a fourth continuance because the applicant had already had multiple meetings and did not commit to meaningful changes.
side_b_arguments: Middleton argued another continuance would set a bad precedent when the applicant indicated another meeting would not yield new outcomes.
Letting the applicant reapply later is cleaner than keeping neighbors in repeated hearing loops.
disagreements.resolution: Freeman's continuance motion died for lack of a second, and the Council voted 0-5 to deny the rezoning.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 24, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: The City Council approved priority additions from the City Manager and City Clerk 6-0 and heard intense debate over doubling Durham Bulls Athletic Park upgrade costs to $10.2 million, with Council Member Jillian Johnson pressing staff for a net economic-impact and debt-service accounting and moving Item 13 off Consent onto the General Business Agenda. Resident Stella Adams pulled Items 4 and 5 to criticize transit matching funds ahead of Route 9 improvements and urge explicit racial equity wording in FY 2022-23 budget guidelines. Council received major updates on Durham Safe Routes to School, the 2019 Trail Implementation Program's nine priority trails, and the Small Business Work Plan, Built to Last, and YouthWorks, where Leonardo Williams and DeDreana Freeman pressed for an overarching macroeconomic strategic plan rather than piecemeal pilots. Finally, Council members clashed over assumptions in a circulated 77-proposal ARPA spreadsheet regarding a 50% funding cap and County-function deferrals before settling the April 4 agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: All six members answered roll call and shared announcements covering YouthWorks corporate sponsor needs, Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton's Tree of Peace planting with Israeli Consul General Anat Sultan-Dadon, at-large vacancy deadlines, and sickle cell advocacy. Council voted 6-0 to add Manager Priority Item 20 (Small Business/Built to Last/YouthWorks presentation) and 6-0 to accept Clerk Priority items on vacancy processing.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (2 votes: Manager priority and Clerk priority)

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items Review (Budget Guidelines, Transit Bus Repowering, Eno River Force Main, Durham Bulls Upgrades, and Solid Waste Study)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Stella Adams challenged Item 4 over perceived use of county transit dollars before Route 9 expansion (which Transportation Director Sean Egan clarified uses city 3.75-cent property tax funds for fleet state-of-good-repair) and asked for explicit racial equity language in Item 5's budget guidelines. Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton pulled Item 9 (bus repowering lifecycle), Item 10 (local HUB contractor representation on Eno River Force Main), and Item 13 (DBAP MLB upgrades rising from $5.22M to $10.2M), sparking sharp debate after Johnson called the stadium a 'money suck' and demanded full fiscal impact data. Council Member Freeman pulled Item 16 to request adding an air quality baseline study at the Waste Disposal Center.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (Item 13 moved to GBA)

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Update on the Durham Safe Routes to School Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation planner Dale McKeel and Bike Durham Executive Director John Thomas reviewed NCDOT-funded walk/bike-to-school events engaging over 5,000 students at 13 elementary schools (targeting 20 schools in May) and in-school bike safety courses prioritizing free/reduced-lunch campuses. Council members praised the co-op bike distribution program and urged mapping bicycle repair stations and improving safe pedestrian/bike infrastructure around schools.

agenda_items.title: Presentation: 2019 Trail Implementation Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Parks and Recreation planner Lindsey Smart presented the 2019 Trail Implementation Program assessing Durham's 31 miles of trails compared with 245 miles Triangle-wide, Trail Action Group lessons learned on permitting, right-of-way, and watershed constraints, and nine DOST-endorsed priority trail corridors. Smart outlined a diversified funding strategy matching three competitive trails to NCDOT SPOT funds while steering two toward city CIP funds and four toward CIP and private development partnerships.

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Shared Economic Prosperity — Durham Small Business Work Plan, Built to Last, and YouthWorks Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD staff Adria Graham-Scott and Andre Pettigrew, joined by Built to Last Board Chair Stella Adams, reviewed YouthWorks streamlining after 375 summer participants and ~760 current applicants, the $1 million SBA Community Navigator E3 grant with Forward Cities, the SEED Legacy Business pilot, Small Business Recovery Fund loans ($860,000 disbursed across 39 loans), and Built to Last's 501(c)(3) launch and feasibility study. Council members Williams and Freeman criticized the lack of a macro economic strategic plan and convention/corridor revenue drivers, while Middleton and Johnson debated departmental capacity for an added $75,000 employee-ownership contract.

agenda_items.title: Boards/Commissions Report, At-Large Vacancy Vetting, and ARPA Framework Deliberation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Clerk Diana Schreiber reported Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee nominees and five at-large Council applicants so far (Brenda Hill Pollard, Markey Brown, Shalia Ann Huggins, Dr. Monique Holsey, and Tim Allran), with council consenting to let clerk vetting finish slightly after March 28 if needed. Council Member Javiera Caballero sought clarity ahead of April 6 on a circulated 77-proposal ARPA spreadsheet assuming a 50% (~$22M) cap and County deferrals, prompting debate before Mayor O'Neal tasked Caballero and Williams with structuring the April 6 session.

agenda_items.title: Set April 4, 2022 City Council Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page confirmed Item 13 (DBAP upgrades) would be placed on the General Business Agenda per Council Member Jillian Johnson's request, with Consent Items 1-12 and 14-16 and GBA Public Hearing Item 19. Council approved settling the agenda 6-0.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager Priority Item (Add Supplemental Item 20 Presentation)
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous among all six seated members.
votes.discussion_detail: Adds supplemental Shared Economic Prosperity presentation to the work session.

votes.item_title: Accept City Clerk Priority Items (Vacancy Processing Discussion)
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Adds clerk update on processing at-large vacancy applications for April 7.

votes.item_title: Set Agenda for April 4, 2022 City Council Meeting
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous.
votes.discussion_detail: Sets Consent Items 1-12 and 14-16, GBA Item 13 (DBAP upgrades), and GBA Public Hearing Item 19 (Bull City Townhomes).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 24, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Durham Bulls Athletic Park $10.2 Million MLB Upgrades and Public Accountability (Item 13)
disagreements.summary: Council members split over doubling city funding toward $10.2 million in MLB-mandated Durham Bulls stadium renovations, with Jillian Johnson questioning whether the city should invest further public dollars in a 'money suck' private franchise without full net fiscal-impact accounting, while Middleton, Freeman, and O'Neal argued keeping the Bulls is vital to Durham's brand, downtown economy, and contracts.
disagreements.side_a_position: Withhold automatic Consent approval and require full fiscal-impact, debt-service, and lease-consequence reporting before committing $10M+.
side_a_arguments: Taxpayers already cover substantial debt and maintenance costs while MLB imposes unfunded renovation mandates.
Residents deserve a clear financial ledger comparing stadium costs against direct city revenues before spending another $10 million.
disagreements.side_b_position: Move forward unconditionally to satisfy MLB standards and keep the Durham Bulls franchise in Durham.
side_b_arguments: Losing the franchise would damage Durham's civic identity and downtown hospitality economy, as occurred in Richmond.
Delaying the Skanska bid jeopardizes construction before the 2023-2025 compliance deadlines.
disagreements.resolution: Item 13 was moved to the April 4 General Business Agenda at Johnson's request while staff committed to compiling economic-impact and lease briefs.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 24, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: ARPA Allocation Framework, 50% Funding Cap, and Black-Led Organization Focus
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over ground rules for the upcoming April 6 ARPA deliberation, specifically whether a circulated spreadsheet cutting County-function health proposals and capping initial awards at ~50% ($22M) of the $44M ARPA balance reflected Council consensus.
disagreements.side_a_position: Use the staff-vetted spreadsheet cutoff to release roughly half (~$22M) immediately for urgent community aid while reserving half for larger equity investments or county partnerships.
side_a_arguments: Avoids stalling urgent community funds and relies on staff scoring without re-reading 77 full RFPs.
Preserves ~$22M unencumbered for transformative equity projects or joint County health/wellness funding.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not pre-lock a 50% cap or exclude proposals prematurely without a broader strategic plan and explicit Black-led/Black-focused equity prioritization.
side_b_arguments: Freeman stated she had not agreed to a $22M cap and wanted a larger comprehensive strategy.
Council must explicitly confirm prioritization of Black-led and Black-focused proposals rather than assuming scoring suffices.
disagreements.resolution: Mayor O'Neal tasked Caballero and Williams with designing a structured April 6 deliberation and public comment framework bounded by staff cutoff tiers and explicit equity attention.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting March 21, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With all six seated members present, the City Council passed the Consent Agenda unanimously 6-0, including Durham City-County Appearance Commission appointments, the 2021 ASOC report, a Gang Reduction Strategy interlocal agreement, and Braggtown sidewalk funding. During a well-attended FY 2022-23 Budget and FY 2023-28 CIP public hearing, residents urged equity-based CIP investments, eviction diversion, DOST open space staffing, and rejection of the ShotSpotter pilot, while Council Members Leonardo Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton voiced strong defense of evaluating a guarded ShotSpotter trial. Following an extensive rezoning hearing on the 134-acre Carver Street Assemblage (up to 821 homes including 198 affordable units), Council Member Freeman raised Cub Creek infrastructure concerns with NCDOT, and Council unanimously approved 6-0 annexation, utility extension, PDR zoning, and consistency statements. The Council concluded by conducting a quasi-judicial hearing and unanimously voting 6-0 to grant TROSA a Major Special Use Permit and Major Site Plan expanding its James Street residential capacity from 275 to 450.

agenda_items.title: March for Meals Proclamation, NLC Announcements, and Consent Agenda (Items 1-7)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero presented a March for Meals proclamation to Meals on Wheels Durham Executive Director Jason Peace, and council members recapped National League of Cities advocacy in Washington, D.C. With no pulls, Council unanimously passed Consent Items 1-7 by a 6-0 vote.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing on FY 2022-23 Budget and FY 2023-28 Capital Improvement Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director John Allore opened the initial FY 2022-23 Budget and FY 2023-28 CIP hearing (comment remaining open until June 21). Speakers Stella Adams (equity CIP scoring for Braggtown, Walltown, Southside, and NE Central Durham), Hibo and DOST Chair Laura Stroud (open space implementer FTE and $100k fund), Larissa Sybel ($6M eviction diversion and local vouchers), Angela Vick Lewis (hotel-to-home/shelters), and Bike Durham's John Tallmadge and Austin Harper (fare-free transit and capital delivery) outlined budget priorities, while Danette Wilkins and Brittany Price urged rejecting ShotSpotter. In response, Council Members Williams and Middleton strongly defended testing a guarded ShotSpotter gunshot-detection pilot, while Freeman endorsed equity CIP funding, DOST staffing, and homelessness support.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (Public hearing remains open)

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Rezoning: Carver Street Assemblage (KLA Development Co.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Alexander Cahill presented a consolidated voluntary annexation and rezoning for ~134 acres along Carver Street and Old Oxford Road from RS-20 and RU-5 to PDR 7.000 F/J-B for up to 821 residences (single-family, townhomes, and apartments including 198 4% LIHTC units) with 22% tree save, 150-foot stream buffers, and $2 million in infrastructure commitments. Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and Braggtown Community Association leaders including Vanessa Mason-Evans spoke in support, while Cub Creek Road residents (represented by Matthew Council and neighbors including Rebecca Painter, Lalit Yadav, and Onofrio Castiglia) objected to unpaved state-maintained Cub Creek conditions and well-water impacts rather than housing affordability. Assistant Transportation Director Bill Judge explained southern Cub Creek lies outside annexation limits, and Council approved annexation, rezoning, and consistency statements 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (3 votes: annexation/utility agreement, zoning map change, consistency statement)

agenda_items.title: Quasi-Judicial Hearing: TROSA Main Campus Expansion (1820 James Street)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council conducted a sworn quasi-judicial hearing on TROSA's Major Special Use Permit and Major Site Plan requests to consolidate operations from North Street onto its 13.2-acre James Street campus, increasing residential capacity from 275 to 450 residents and adding ~55,000 square feet including a new dormitory. Planner Robin Schultz, applicant counsel Patrick Byker, former Mayors Bill Bell and Nick Tennyson, Tuscaloosa-Lakewood Neighborhood Association President Grant Gardner, and expert witnesses entered Exhibits A-E into the record without opposition. Council approved both the Major SUP and Major Site Plan 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (2 votes: Major SUP and Major Site Plan)

votes.item_title: Item 11a: Carver Street Assemblage Annexation Ordinance & Utility Extension Agreement (KLA Development)
votes.notes: Unanimous electronic vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Approves voluntary annexation and water/sewer utility extension agreement for the ~134-acre assemblage.

votes.item_title: Item 11b: Carver Street Assemblage Zoning Map Change Ordinance (to PDR 7.000 F/J-B)
votes.notes: Middleton disclosed an organizational UDI landholding in the vicinity that did not constitute a statutory conflict.
votes.discussion_detail: Rezones seven annexed parcels plus 937 Old Oxford Road to PDR 7.000 for up to 821 homes including 198 income-restricted units.

votes.item_title: Item 11c: Carver Street Assemblage NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Unanimous electronic vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopts statutory consistency and reasonableness statement for Carver Street Assemblage.

votes.item_title: Item 12a: TROSA Main Campus Expansion Major Special Use Permit
votes.notes: Quasi-judicial approval based on sworn evidence.
votes.discussion_detail: Approves Major SUP allowing residential capacity increase from 275 to 450 residents at 1820 James Street.

votes.item_title: Item 12b: TROSA Main Campus Expansion Major Site Plan
votes.notes: Quasi-judicial approval unanimous 6-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Approves Major Site Plan for ~55,000 sq ft campus expansion including a new dormitory.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 10, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: The six seated Council members approved City Manager priority updates 6-0 and engaged in pointed scrutiny during presentations on the Greater Triangle Commuter Rail (GTCR) Study and the Durham County Transit Plan update. Council Member Leonardo Williams, Mayor Elaine O'Neal, and Council Member Javiera Caballero pressed GoTriangle CEO Chuck Lattuca for an itemized breakdown of the $157 million spent on the canceled light rail project, clearer accounting on the $9 million commuter rail study, and direct City Council voting governance rather than relying on an advisory August support letter. Council also received public comment on recovery housing, reviewed pulled consent items on Appearance Commission gender diversity and Moss+Ross outreach, and established a vacancy timeline opening at-large applications March 11-25 ahead of May 2 interviews and a May 3 final vote. On boards and commissions rules, members split over returning to in-person mandatory attendance immediately versus retaining the remote status quo until the Governor lifts the State of Emergency before settling the March 21 agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items, Board Attendance Bylaw Referral, and Citizen Matters (Divine Trust Ministries)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested technical updates to Consent Item 5 (Gang Reduction Strategy ILA attachments) and Item 9 (Transit Plan slide 7), which Council approved 6-0 on roll call. City Clerk Diana Schreiber raised reverting boards and commissions to pre-COVID attendance rules (deferred to Other Matters), and resident Andrew McDonald of Divine Trust Ministries appealed for recovery housing support.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: Appearance Commission (Item 1) and Moss+Ross Communications Contract (Item 4)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Jillian Johnson pulled Item 1 to recommend re-advertising a vacant Appearance Commission seat to improve gender balance after two male nominees advanced, gaining informal thumbs-up consensus. Council Members Leonardo Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton discussed Item 4 with staff, focusing on print/mail reach and expanding NCCU/university community engagement under the Moss+Ross contract amendment.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Informal consensus to re-advertise 1 seat

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail (GTCR) Feasibility Study Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GoTriangle President and CEO Chuck Lattuca, STV consultant Mariah Ellington, and GoTriangle staff briefed Council on Phase 2 commuter rail alternatives—comparing low-level Concept 2 (+$15M estimated capital) and high-level Concept D (+$35M), operating speeds, and 18-mile vs 43-mile service horizons—noting Durham would only be asked for a non-binding support letter around August. Council Members Williams, Freeman, Caballero, and Mayor O'Neal challenged GoTriangle's lack of project cost breakdowns, Durham's lack of a direct seat on the transit plan voting structure despite generating ~80% of transit activity, and unresolved questions over the $157 million spent on the canceled Durham-Orange Light Rail project.

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Durham County Transit Plan Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham County Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and DCHC MPO Transportation Planning Manager Aaron Cain outlined financial updates to the 20-year Durham County Transit Plan, noting rising GoTriangle (7.4%) and GoDurham (20.5%) operator/fuel cost pressures, a $10 million revenue reserve, a $1.95 billion commuter rail capital placeholder, and an unresolved funding gap depending on whether non-federal local share settles at 20% ($388M) or 33% ($649M). Council members discussed revising the 2013 interlocal governance agreement, securing federal infrastructure grants, and organizing public education ahead of May public release.

agenda_items.title: At-Large Council Vacancy Schedule, Board Remote Attendance Policy, and Set March 21 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton clarified that North Carolina statute does not strictly enforce a 60-day penalty clock on filling Charlie Reece's seat and won consensus for a timeline opening applications March 11-25, distributing packets March 28, picking finalists April 7, conducting interviews May 2 at 4:00 PM, and holding public comment and voting May 3 at 6:00 PM. Council then debated whether to enforce pre-COVID in-person board attendance rules immediately before opting to retain the virtual status quo until the Governor lifts the emergency order, and voted 6-0 to settle the March 21 agenda.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager Priority Items (Updated Attachments on Item 5 and Item 9)
votes.notes: Roll call unanimous 6-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Revises attachments on Gang Reduction Strategy ILA and Durham County Transit Plan update.

votes.item_title: Set Agenda for March 21, 2022 City Council Meeting
votes.notes: Roll call unanimous 6-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Sets Consent Items 1-7 and GBA Public Hearings 10-12 for the March 21 regular meeting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 10, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: Boards and Commissions In-Person Return and Attendance Enforcement Policy
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over whether advisory and quasi-judicial boards and commissions (such as Housing Appeals Board and Board of Adjustment) should be directed to return in person with attendance enforcement restored, or remain remote until the Governor ends North Carolina's COVID-19 State of Emergency.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require business-critical boards and commissions to meet in person and restore attendance accountability now, accommodating immunocompromised members individually.
side_a_arguments: Freeman argued Housing Appeals Board and Board of Adjustment work is backing up because landlords and participants avoid virtual proceedings.
Williams advocated leading by example with masks, vaccines, and boosters to return boards to in-person work, though clarifying later he meant once the Governor's emergency order lifts.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep existing virtual meeting flexibility and suspended attendance penalties in place until the Governor lifts the State of Emergency.
side_b_arguments: Johnson warned toggling between in-person and virtual rules during future COVID spikes would confuse volunteers and strain staff.
City Attorney Kim Rehberg cautioned that City Hall lacks hybrid equipment outside Council Chambers and piecemeal board autonomy could create chaos.
disagreements.resolution: Council maintained the virtual/non-counted attendance status quo until the Governor lifts the emergency order.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting March 7, 2022 (Livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: In an emotional session honoring outgoing At-Large Council Member Charlie Reece with a proclamation declaring Charlie Reece Day, the Council voted 7-0 to accept Reece's resignation effective during the meeting and later previewed the Charter vacancy-filling process via the Procedures Committee. Following Reece's departure, the remaining six members passed Consent Items 6-0 after pulling Item 6, then split 5-1 on Item 6—a $39,000 GoTriangle cost-sharing interlocal agreement for Gregson Street bridge waterline work—as Council Member DeDreana Freeman cast the sole dissent citing GoTriangle's lack of transparency on commuter rail. The Council then held two public hearings and voted unanimously 6-0 on both rezonings and consistency statements: approving Ellis Road PDR Rezoning 2 (up to 519 apartments after applicant counsel Patrick Byker proffered $50,000 each to DPS and the Affordable Housing Fund) and U Tower at 3007 Petty Road (up to 208 apartments).

agenda_items.title: Proclamations for Senator Jeanne Hopkins Lucas Day and Charlie Reece Day, Announcements, and Resignation Acceptance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal presented a proclamation declaring March 24, 2022 Senator Jeanne Hopkins Lucas Day, accepted by Lucas's sister Bernadette Hopkins David Yarmo, followed by Council Member Jillian Johnson reading a farewell proclamation honoring outgoing At-Large Member Charlie Reece and heartfelt tributes from colleagues and senior staff. Under Clerk priority items, Council voted 7-0 to accept Reece's resignation effective immediately, and Reece stepped down from the dais.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-5, 7-12, and 18; Item 6 Pulled)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Earlier in the meeting Tara Romano of Pro-Choice North Carolina spoke in favor of Consent Item 3 (Declaration of Fundamental Reproductive Freedoms). With Item 6 pulled by resident Jacqueline Wagstaff, the six remaining members approved Consent Items 1-5, 7-12, and 18 by a 6-0 vote.

agenda_items.title: GoTriangle Interlocal Agreement for Gregson Street ('Can Opener Bridge') Waterline Adjustments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan explained the $39,000 GoTriangle cost-share ILA covering half of $78,000 in preliminary waterline engineering tied to commuter rail coordination near Gregson Street. Speaker Jacqueline Wagstaff opposed approving any GoTriangle funds citing distrust over the canceled light rail project, and Council Member DeDreana Freeman announced she would vote no over GoTriangle's lack of financial transparency, while Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton defended moving the engineering study forward. Council approved the agreement 5-1.

agenda_items.title: Ellis Road PDR Rezoning 2 (~30 Acres, CG(D) to PDR 18.220)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a rezoning across five parcels totaling ~30 acres along Ellis Road to allow up to 519 multi-family units at PDR 18.220 (recommended 10-1 by the Planning Commission). In response to Council Member Jillian Johnson's request for community benefit commitments, applicant attorney Patrick Byker verbally proffered $50,000 to Durham Public Schools and $50,000 to the city's Affordable Housing Fund alongside transportation trip-reduction commitments. Council approved both the zoning map change and consistency statement 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (2 votes: rezoning ordinance and consistency statement)

agenda_items.title: U Tower Zoning Map Change (3007 Petty Road, OI(D) to OI)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented case Z200045 rezoning ~1.5 acres at 3007 Petty Road near University Tower from Office and Institutional with a development plan to OI, enabling an infill development of up to 208 apartments (recommended 10-1 by the Planning Commission). Applicant representatives responded to brief council questions without public opposition, and Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 6-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-0 (2 votes: rezoning ordinance and consistency statement)

votes.item_title: Accept Resignation of At-Large Council Member Charlie Reece
votes.notes: Electronic voting board recorded 7-0 prior to Reece's departure.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepts Reece's formal letter of resignation effective immediately; Reece stepped down from the dais immediately afterward.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting March 7, 2022 (Livestream)
disagreements.issue: GoTriangle Financial Transparency and Cost-Sharing for Gregson Street Waterline Adjustments (Item 6)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 5-1 on approving a $39,000 GoTriangle cost-share interlocal agreement for waterline engineering near the Gregson Street railroad bridge ahead of Greater Triangle Commuter Rail briefings.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the $39,000 cost-share agreement so city waterline planning stays coordinated with bridge/rail engineering.

disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose signing new GoTriangle cost-sharing agreements until the agency demonstrates accountability and transparency.

disagreements.resolution: Interlocal agreement passed 5-1 with Freeman voting No.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat Day Four (March 4, 2022)
meetings.executive_summary: On the fourth and final day of its virtual FY 2022-23 Budget Retreat (with Council Member Javiera Caballero on excused absence), the City Council reviewed Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) competitive grant tracking, Transit Fund sustainability, and draft FY 2022-23 Budget Development Guidelines without taking formal votes. Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson and Trenay Snyder detailed Durham's pursuit of 16 direct local BIL programs after winning a $9 million RAISE rail-trail grant, while Transportation Director Sean Egan warned that $42 million in federal COVID transit relief ends in FY 2024 leaving a $6-$7 million structural Transit Fund gap in FY 2025-26 even as operator wages rise and fare-free transit continues. Budget Director John Allore presented draft budget guidelines keeping the General Fund rate at 30.95 cents while flagging room for 1-3% market salary adjustments, prompting pointed questions from Jillian Johnson and Mark-Anthony Middleton about lowering the fund-balance floor from 16.7% to 12% and relying on $4 million in fund balance for annual street resurfacing. The retreat closed with warm farewell reflections for outgoing Council Member Charlie Reece prior to his March 7 resignation.

agenda_items.title: Welcome and Opening Retreat Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director John Allore and City Manager Wanda Page opened Day Four of the FY 2022-23 Budget Retreat with six Council members present (O'Neal, Middleton, Johnson, Reece, Freeman, and Williams; Caballero excused absent).

agenda_items.title: Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) Competitive Grant Readiness and Tracking
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson and Grant Administrator Trenay Snyder reported Durham's eligibility for ~155 of 380 BIL programs and 16 of 25 direct municipal programs, highlighting a $9 million RAISE award for the downtown rail trail and pending applications for $20 million (Holloway Street corridor) and $10.8 million (bus maintenance facility renovations). Staff confirmed a WSP grant-writing retainer, CMO tracking dashboard, and discussions with local universities without needing additional FY 2023 operating funds.

agenda_items.title: Transit Fund Overview, Fare-Free Operations, and Operator Recruitment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan reported that $42 million in federal CARES, CRRSA, and ARPA relief sustains Durham's Transit Fund through FY 2024 but leaves a $6-$7 million structural deficit starting FY 2025-26. He reviewed extending fare-free transit beyond June 30, 2022—citing ~$175,000 in annual farebox collection savings and reduced operator assaults—alongside GoDurham ($17.70/hr) and GoDurham Access ($15 to $17.50/hr) driver wage boosts, full retirement of 2003/2005 DATA buses, electric bus deliveries, and bus security partitions. Council members questioned Village Transit Hub safety, ADA paratransit improvements, and post-FY 2024 fiscal cliffs.

agenda_items.title: Draft FY 2022-23 Budget Development Guidelines and Compensation Scenarios
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director John Allore presented draft FY 2022-23 guidelines maintaining current tax allocations (30.95 cents General Fund, 11.50 cents Debt Service, 5.59 cents Solid Waste, 3.38 cents Dedicated Housing, 3.75 cents Transit, plus BID and Half-Penny for Parks) while outlining pay scenarios including 4.8% pay-for-performance/4% step raises, 5% police/fire step increases, up to 3% market structure adjustments ($779k-$2.4M), up to 10% health insurance increases, and 12.1% LGERS retirement contributions. He also flagged up to 4.1% water/sewer and $0.94/month stormwater rate adjustments. Council Members Jillian Johnson and Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned lowering the unassigned fund-balance floor from 16.7% to 12% and treating $4 million in fund-balance transfers as de facto recurring street-resurfacing revenue.

agenda_items.title: Closing Reflections and Farewell to Council Member Charlie Reece
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page, Mayor Elaine O'Neal, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Council Members Williams, Johnson, and Freeman offered warm closing tributes to Charlie Reece at his final budget retreat, and Reece delivered farewell remarks on fiscal stewardship before adjournment.
