meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat Day Three (March 3, 2022)
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council convened its third FY 2022-23 Budget Retreat session, receiving presentations on employee pay and benefits (including rising turnover and a July 2022 livable wage adjustment to $17.60/hr), a Language Access Plan implementation update from coordinator Michelle Gomez, six Council budget requests totaling roughly $1.9M plus $40k-$108k recurring items, and pandemic recovery scenarios for the Parking Enterprise Fund. Council reached informal consensus to advance budget requests for Council interns ($26,500) and boards/commissions ($4,000), support adding a Durham Open Space and Trails (DOST) FTE ($108,000), defer a $75,000 employee-ownership technical support pilot to the March 24 work session, and await staff's tiered language-incentive proposal. Members split informally 4-3 in favor of bringing forward a $197,000 one-year ShotSpotter acoustic gunshot detection pilot (with a 3-month free trial option) into the proposed budget for deeper review, while remaining divided over whether to set aside $1.5M specifically for urban DOST land acquisition. No formal roll-call votes were held during this retreat session.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Welcome & Finance Director Introduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Management Services Director John Allore and Mayor Elaine O'Neal opened Day Three of the FY23 budget retreat with six members present and Javiera Caballero initially excused (joining later at 01:50:53). City Manager Wanda Page emphasized balancing market salary adjustments with FY23 fiscal constraints and introduced newly hired Finance Director Tim Flora.

agenda_items.title: FY23 Employee Pay & Benefits Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim HR Director JJ Scott reviewed Durham's four pay plans, rising post-pandemic turnover and retirements, restoration of pay-for-performance/merit steps, market adjustments for general and open pay ranges beyond recent sworn public safety raises, and raising the minimum livable wage to $17.60/hr in July 2022. City Manager Page explained why staff presented a range of market adjustment options for Council budget guidelines while monitoring peer cities like Raleigh.

agenda_items.title: Language Access Plan Implementation Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Communications Director Beverly Thompson introduced Language Access Coordinator Michelle Gomez, who detailed Phase 1 implementation of Durham's 2019 Language Access Plan, including Title VI compliance (with Spanish meeting the 5%/1,000 safe-harbor threshold and growing Arabic and Korean speakers), LanguageLine Solutions expansion for on-demand telephonic/video and ASL interpretation, translated web pages, Bull City Today videos, and staff webinars.

agenda_items.title: FY23 City Council Budget Requests Deliberation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: John Allore and Assistant Budget Director Christina Riordan presented staff analyses on six Council requests: language incentive pay increases ($40,000), a DOST FTE ($108,000) and $1.5M open-space land acquisition fund, Boards and Commissions funding ($4,000), Council Interns ($26,500), an OEWD employee-ownership 2-year pilot ($75,000), and a ShotSpotter gunshot detection pilot ($197,000 first year, roughly $700k-$1M four-year commitment). Council agreed to advance the interns, boards/commissions, and DOST FTE, defer OEWD employee-ownership to March 24, let staff finalize tiered language-incentive pay, and divided over ShotSpotter and the $1.5M DOST acquisition reserve.

agenda_items.title: Parking Enterprise Fund Overview & Recovery Scenarios
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan presented COVID-19 revenue losses in the Parking Enterprise Fund and compared Scenario A (peer-aligned rates around $2.25/hr on-street and $2.00/hr off-street with continued negative fund balance for five years) against Scenario B (higher rate recovery). Council discussed special-event flat rates ($7 after 7 PM), discounted low-wage downtown worker parking passes, and potential General Fund interfund support versus ARPA reimbursement constraints.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat Day Three (March 3, 2022)
disagreements.issue: ShotSpotter Acoustic Gunshot Detection Pilot ($197,000 Year 1)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 informally over Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton's request to fund a ShotSpotter acoustic gunshot detection pilot in the FY23 budget, with a narrow majority supporting advancing the $197,000 proposal (and exploring a 3-month free trial) to the proposed budget while three members opposed the technology altogether.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance the $197,000 one-year ShotSpotter pilot (potentially utilizing the vendor's 3-month free trial) into budget review as an urgent evidence-gathering and response tool against gun violence.
side_a_arguments: Gun violence requires deploying every viable investigative and emergency response tool, and 80% of residents surveyed felt less safe.

Advancing the item in the budget process (or testing a no-cost 3-month trial) lets Chief Patrice Andrews and DPD present detailed performance metrics and contract guardrails before a final FY23 budget vote.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject funding ShotSpotter and invest instead in evidence-based violence interruption, unarmed crisis response, and community-led safety strategies.
side_b_arguments: Independent evaluations, including Chicago's Inspector General report, show acoustic detection rarely produces evidence or reduces gun violence while driving unproductive police deployments.
Public funds should prioritize proven behavioral health responders, community violence interrupters, and root-cause investments rather than proprietary surveillance contracts.
disagreements.resolution: With an informal 4-3 majority favoring further evaluation, the proposal was kept alive for consideration during the City Manager's FY23 proposed budget review rather than eliminated at the retreat.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat Day Three (March 3, 2022)
disagreements.issue: DOST $1.5M Dedicated Open Space Land Acquisition Fund
disagreements.summary: While Council broadly backed hiring an Open Space and Trails FTE ($108,000), members disagreed on whether to immediately allocate $1.5M into a dedicated land acquisition fund.
disagreements.side_a_position: Seed a dedicated $1.5M land acquisition pot (preferably from fund balance as a one-time startup) alongside the new FTE so urban-core open space parcels do not compete with general real estate acquisitions.
side_a_arguments: A dedicated pool mirrors peer municipalities like Raleigh and empowers the new staffer to move rapidly on urban-core green space before parcels are lost to private development.
Using one-time fund balance avoids locking in recurring General Fund commitments before transaction cadence is known.
disagreements.side_b_position: Fund the Open Space FTE first and evaluate existing Real Estate / General Services acquisition channels before tying up $1.5M in an unused reserve.
side_b_arguments: Council must already review individual real estate purchases and can fund acquisitions through existing mechanisms without holding idle non-interest-bearing cash.
General Services and Real Estate input on the 44 candidate parcels should precede choosing an arbitrary dollar figure.
disagreements.resolution: Council signaled consensus for the DOST FTE while leaving the $1.5M land acquisition reserve without full consensus for staff and General Services follow-up.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Feb, 24, 2022 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its February 24, 2022 work session (streamed/archived with metadata date February 25, 2022, with Javiera Caballero excused absent), Durham City Council unanimously approved priority items from the City Manager (updating the Police Satisfaction Survey attachment and adding the appointment of Finance Officer Tim Flora) and the City Attorney (scheduling closed-session attorney-client consultation on City of Durham v. Vickers Land Co. LLC and Darryl Howard v. City of Durham). Resident Mary Barr raised long-standing illegal dumping and neighborhood safety concerns along Shirley Caesar Court and Merrick Street. Council scrutinized Item 6, an interlocal agreement with GoTriangle for $78,000 in shared commuter-rail-related water line adjustments beneath the Gregson Street rail bridge, pulling the item to the General Business Agenda over transparency and cost-efficiency concerns, and received the 2021 Q4 Crime Report (highlighting 50 homicides in 2021) and Police Satisfaction Survey results before settling the March 7 agenda and entering closed session.

agenda_items.title: Announcements, McDougall Terrace Clarification & Ukraine Solidarity
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council marked Charlie Reece's final work session ahead of his March 7 resignation, expressed solidarity with residents and students impacted by Russia's invasion of Ukraine with a moment of silence, and pushed back against misleading news coverage by clarifying that Durham Housing Authority had no plans to tear down McDougall Terrace or displace its 300+ households.

agenda_items.title: City Manager & City Attorney Priority Items and Closed Session Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council accepted the City Manager's priority items updating Item 14's Police Satisfaction Survey attachment and adding Item 18 appointing Finance Officer Tim Flora, and accepted and approved the City Attorney's request to hold closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) on Vickers Land Co. and Darryl Howard.

agenda_items.title: Citizen Matters: Mary Barr on Shirley Caesar Court Dumping
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Homeowner Mary Barr described ten years of chronic illegal furniture and contractor dumping, drug paraphernalia, and safety hazards on the dead-end stretch of Merrick Street and Grant Street adjacent to Shirley Caesar Court. Council thanked Ms. Barr for bringing the chronic maintenance and enforcement concern to staff's attention.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 6: GoTriangle ILA for Commuter Rail Water Line Adjustments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan explained a $78,000 change order split 50/50 between Durham and GoTriangle to relocate a water line along West Main Street under the Gregson Street rail bridge in advance of potential Greater Triangle Commuter Rail service and granite curbing preservation. DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams questioned committing funds toward commuter rail after Durham's light rail experience, prompting Freeman to move Item 6 to the General Business Agenda.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 10: Emergency Watershed Protection (EWP) Streambank Stabilization Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Charlie Reece for clarification, Public Works staff confirmed that the amendment provides an NRCS-reimbursed stream bank stabilization extension along Ellerbe Creek near Northgate Park without unbudgeted net cost.

agenda_items.title: Item 13: 2021 Fourth Quarter Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Patrice Andrews presented year-end 2021 crime data showing 50 homicides (up 35% from 37 in 2020) alongside more than 100 fewer total shootings compared with 2020, highlighting officer staffing shortages (roughly 115-120 vacancies) and cross-jurisdictional gun violence trends. Council discussed recruitment, mental health calls, and ShotSpotter/crime-prevention context.

agenda_items.title: Item 14: 2021 Police Satisfaction Survey Results
agenda_items.discussion_summary: ETC Institute's Jason Morado presented results from 512 completed surveys (+/-4.2% margin of error) showing over 90% respect/trust in DPD officers overall alongside sharp racial disparities in perceptions of stops and discrimination (58% of Black residents vs 25% of Hispanic/White residents believing DPD stops certain racial groups disproportionately) and rising concern that Durham lacks sufficient officers (60% saying no, up from ~40%).

agenda_items.title: Settle Agenda for March 7, 2022 Regular Meeting & Recess to Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented the March 7 agenda placing Items 1-5, 7-12, and 18 on Consent, Item 6 on General Business Agenda, and Items 15 (Ellis Road PDR) and 16 (U Tower) as public hearings. With Charlie Reece having stepped away for travel, Council settled the agenda 5-0 and recessed to closed session.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (Item 14 Attachment Update & Item 18 Appointment of Finance Officer Tim Flora)
votes.notes: Javiera Caballero excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page submitted two priority additions: updating attachment two for Item 14 (Police Satisfaction Survey Results) and adding supplemental Item 18 (Appointment of Finance Officer Tim Flora). Approved unanimously by roll call with Javiera Caballero excused absent.

votes.item_title: Accept City Attorney's Priority Item (Closed Session Request)
votes.notes: Javiera Caballero excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: City Attorney Kim Rehberg requested adding a priority closed-session item under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation on City of Durham v. Vickers Land Co. LLC (19-CVS-2239) and Darryl Howard v. City of Durham et al. (17-CV-4777). Accepted 6-0.

votes.item_title: Hold Closed Session at Conclusion of Work Session
votes.notes: Javiera Caballero excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after accepting the City Attorney's priority item, Council voted 6-0 to hold the closed session at the end of the February 24 work session.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Feb, 24, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: GoTriangle Commuter Rail Water Line Adjustment ILA ($78,000 Split)
disagreements.summary: Council members questioned whether Durham should split $78,000 with GoTriangle for commuter-rail-related water line adjustments near Gregson Street given ongoing uncertainty around the Greater Triangle Commuter Rail project.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question or oppose spending $39,000 on commuter-rail-linked utility changes until commuter rail viability, public alignment, and preservation of historic granite curbing are better assured.
side_a_arguments: Following the collapse of the Durham-Orange Light Rail project, residents expect strict scrutiny before committing any funds tied to GoTriangle commuter rail.
Council needs clearer engineering justification and protection of historic West Main Street granite curbing before giving final consent.
disagreements.side_b_position: Proceed with co-locating the water line adjustment during existing American Tobacco water line replacement to avoid higher future reconstruction costs regardless of commuter rail's fate.
side_b_arguments: Transportation Director Sean Egan confirmed the pipe under the Gregson Street rail bridge requires replacement anyway, and performing the deeper depth work now saves taxpayers money over digging twice.
GoTriangle is reimbursing 50% of the $78,000 incremental change-order cost.
disagreements.resolution: DeDreana Freeman pulled Item 6 from Consent to the General Business Agenda for the March 7 regular meeting so members could weigh a formal separate vote.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb. 21, 2022 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: During the February 21, 2022 regular meeting (with Javiera Caballero excused absent and DeDreana Freeman joining shortly after roll call), Council Member Charlie Reece formally announced his resignation effective March 7, 2022, prompting Mayor Elaine O'Neal to task Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton and Jillian Johnson with establishing a seat-filling timetable through the Procedures Committee. Council proclaimed Black History Month, heard a divergence between Leonardo Williams urging faster easing of the indoor mask mandate to aid small businesses and Mayor O'Neal holding public-health review until around March 7, and approved the 25-item Consent Agenda 6-0—including the Student Loan Debt Cancellation Resolution and COVID-19 Relief Funds Performance Audit. The meeting concluded with a 90-minute public hearing on the FY 2022-23 HUD Annual Action Plan where community speakers urged $6M in ARPA rental relief, non-congregate shelter access, Longtime Homeowner Tax Assistance funding, DOST open-space staffing, and small-lot stormwater/tree adjustments.

agenda_items.title: Black History Month Proclamation, Resignation Announcement & Ceremonial Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted a Black History Month Proclamation read by Mark-Anthony Middleton and received by Gloria de los Santos. Charlie Reece formally announced his resignation effective March 7, 2022 due to a temporary family relocation to Europe; DeDreana Freeman honored late city employee Lester Smith; and Leonardo Williams urged reviewing the city indoor mask mandate on behalf of strained local restaurants while Mayor O'Neal maintained current orders pending March 7 public health consultations.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-25)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved all 25 consent items in a single 6-0 roll-call vote after Marielle Klein delivered public comment supporting Item 11 (Resolution Calling Upon the Federal Government to Cancel Student Loan Debt). Key consent items included Item 8 (COVID-19 Relief Funds Performance Audit), Item 22 (Durham YouthWorks 2021 Evaluation), and Items 24-25 (sidewalk construction contracts).

agenda_items.title: Item 26: FY 2022-2023 Annual Action Plan Needs Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Senior Planner Matthew Schnars introduced the FY 2022-23 Annual Action Plan public needs hearing covering projected HUD allocations (~$2.1M CDBG, ~$1.1M HOME, $174k ESG, $858k HOPWA). Over a dozen public speakers advocated allocating $6M in ARPA funds for eviction prevention, expanding non-congregate shelters, supporting longtime homeowner tax assistance and small-lot UDO Sec. 8.3.1B2 exemptions, adding a DOST Open Space FTE, improving Route 9 transit in Braggtown, and scrutinizing Fayette Place redevelopment.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb. 21, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Timeline for Lifting Durham's Indoor Mask Mandate
disagreements.summary: During Council announcements, Leonardo Williams called for expeditiously revisiting Durham's indoor mask mandate ahead of or aligned with North Carolina's March 7 shift, citing acute cashflow strain on restaurants, whereas Mayor Elaine O'Neal kept the emergency proclamation unchanged pending joint county public health review.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prepare immediately to ease the local indoor mask mandate so local restaurants and small businesses can recover foot traffic alongside state policy changes.
side_a_arguments: Governor Roy Cooper announced state-level mask guidance changes taking effect March 7.
Small restaurants face a 12-week operational survival window and risk losing patrons to neighboring municipalities without mask mandates.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain existing emergency public health orders until joint data review with Durham County Public Health Director Rod Jenkins and peer officials around March 7.
side_b_arguments: The city's indoor mask posture remains coordinated in lockstep with Durham County health metrics and expert guidance.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; Mayor O'Neal confirmed existing emergency orders remained in effect and scheduled further public-health consultation around March 7.

meetings.title: Day Two City Council Budget Retreats (Feb. 18, 2022)
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven council members attending Day Two of the FY23 Budget Retreat, Budget Director John Allore and Treasury Manager Mindy Taylor walked Council through FY23 General Fund projections showing an initial $8.3M deficit, $23M in unvetted departmental requests (~6 cents on the tax rate), over $2.6M in Council requests, and $53.3M in projected ending fund balance (~$13M above the 16.7% policy floor). Taylor detailed the 10-year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) debt model—including an 11.5-cent debt service tax rate, 10% pay-go cash target, $52.5M in General Fund CIP requests, and a dedicated half-cent Equitable and Green Infrastructure reserve—while clarifying to Mark-Anthony Middleton that 1.38 cents of the 3.38-cent housing tax covers the $95M housing bond debt while 2 cents remain programmatic. Equity & Inclusion Director Sharon Williams and budget analysts Christina Tookes and Mary Grace Stoneking then unveiled Durham's expanded racial-equity budget tools, scoring 88 budget requests across seven cross-departmental teams and locking equity weights (25.3 points out of 100) into CIP prioritization.

agenda_items.title: Welcome & Opening Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director John Allore and City Manager Wanda Page welcomed all seven council members to Day Two of the FY23 budget retreat, framing the shift from Day One's macro trends to concrete fiscal projections, capital debt modeling, and equity scoring.

agenda_items.title: FY23 Financial Projections & General Fund Budget Outlook
agenda_items.discussion_summary: John Allore reviewed FY22's $530M total budget and 55.17-cent property tax rate, highlighting strong sales and property tax collections while projecting an initial $8.3M FY23 General Fund shortfall driven by annualizing the ~$9.5M mid-year police/fire pay raise and restoring general staff merit increases. He noted $23M across 152 unvetted departmental requests, $2.6M+ in Council requests, and $13M in excess fund balance above the 16.7% target.

agenda_items.title: FY23 Capital Improvement Program (CIP) & 10-Year Debt Model
agenda_items.discussion_summary: John Allore and Treasury Manager Mindy Taylor introduced Durham's interactive CIP Project Viewer, $52.5M in new General Fund CIP requests across 62 projects, and $14.8M in fleet replacement requests. Responding to Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman, City Manager Page confirmed that within the 3.38-cent dedicated housing tax, only 1.38 cents service the $95M housing bond while 2 cents remain dedicated to programmatic affordable housing development and land acquisition.

agenda_items.title: Department of Equity & Inclusion Update & Racial Equity Commission
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Equity & Inclusion Director Sharon Williams briefed Council on GARE's 'Normalize, Organize, Operationalize' strategy, training over 2,300 city staff, onboarding FUSE Fellow Ann Phillips on racial equity data tracking, and preparing the joint 17-member City-County Racial Equity Commission to launch in April 2022.

agenda_items.title: Equity in the Budget & CIP Prioritization Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Christina Tookes and ICMA Fellow Mary Grace Stoneking detailed Durham's expanded Budget Equity Tool—scaling from 7 pilot items to 88 operating requests evaluated on a 0-40 scale by 22 staffers—and the locked 10-factor CIP scoring matrix allocating 25.3% weight to equity via Neighborhood Compass and HUD Qualified Census Tracts. Mark-Anthony Middleton urged developing contractor and developer primers so external partners understand how Durham operationalizes equity requirements.

meetings.title: Day One City Council Budget Retreats (Feb. 17, 2022)
meetings.executive_summary: Opening Durham City Council's four-part FY23 budget retreat series with all seven council members present, City Manager Wanda Page framed the fiscal landscape around five 'Wordle' themes—Needs, Wants, Wages, Taxes, and Money—and joined Budget Director John Allore in recognizing retiring Interim Finance Director David Hickman. ETC Institute's Jason Morado presented the 2021 Resident Satisfaction Survey (727 respondents, +/-3.6% margin of error), finding 84% positive ratings of Durham as a place to live and 69% customer-service satisfaction (28 points above the US average), while top resident investment priorities shifted to Police Protection (57%, #1), Public Schools (#2), Streets (#3), and Affordable Housing (#4), alongside 80% support for unarmed crisis response on welfare checks. Budget officials Andrew Holland and Sherry Metcalf unveiled Durham's interim two-year Strategic Plan distilled to 13 council-aligned initiatives, and NC State economist Dr. Michael Walden warned of 7.5% inflation, Federal Reserve tightening, and a 25% recession risk by late 2022.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order & City Manager's Budget Retreat Welcome
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called Day One of the FY23 budget retreat to order alongside all seven council members (formally confirming attendance via roll call at 00:12:12 at Charlie Reece's request). City Manager Wanda Page introduced five 'Wordle' themes—Needs, Wants, Wages, Taxes, and Money—highlighting restoring general employee step/merit increases alongside public safety adjustments.

agenda_items.title: 2021 City-County Resident Satisfaction Survey Results
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jason Morado (ETC Institute) presented the 12th Resident Satisfaction Survey (727 completed responses), noting 84% satisfaction with Durham overall, 79% neighborhood quality of life, and sharp declines in perceived personal safety pushing Police Protection to #1 resident priority (57%), followed by Public Schools, Streets, and Affordable Housing. Surveyed residents also showed 80% support for deploying unarmed behavioral-health crisis responders to welfare checks.

agenda_items.title: Strategic Plan Interim Update & Retiring Staff Tribute
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page honored retiring Interim Finance Director David Hickman before Assistant Budget Director Andrew Holland and Strategy Manager Sherry Metcalf presented the focused two-year interim Strategic Plan comprising 13 initiatives (including Forever Home Durham, Language Access, ARPA oversight, and Community Safety pilots) tracked every eight weeks via DSAP 2.0 ahead of a full FY24 refresh.

agenda_items.title: Economic Outlook Presentation by Dr. Michael Walden
agenda_items.discussion_summary: NC State Economist Dr. Michael Walden analyzed post-COVID economic recovery—noting Durham-Chapel Hill employment back at 100% of pre-pandemic peaks alongside persistent labor-force participation gaps from retirements and childcare—and examined how $5.5T in federal aid and supply-chain pressures pushed inflation to 7.5%. He advised city budget writers to monitor Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes closely and weighed a 25% risk of a mild two-quarter recession late in 2022.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Feb. 10, 2022 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal called the February 10, 2022 virtual Durham City Council work session to order with six members present and Leonardo Williams joining at 00:15:52. Council voted 6-0 to grant Javiera Caballero excused absences for February 21, February 24, March 3, and March 4, 2022, approved the City Manager's priority agenda changes 6-0, and authorized a closed session on three litigation matters 6-0. Under Citizen Matters, Emorywood Estates residents detailed heavy construction traffic, road damage, fire hydrant misuse, mailbox break-ins, and offensive street-naming linked to the Towns at Courtenay Creek development, while a Green New Deal for Durham Coalition speaker urged climate-justice investments. Council reviewed two pulled sidewalk contracts (SW-76 and Bragtown-focused SW-87C), received the 2021 Durham YouthWorks program evaluation report, resolved a 3-3-1 Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee nomination deadlock in favor of Andrew George after Mark-Anthony Middleton switched his vote, and unanimously settled the agenda 7-0 before moving into closed session.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Council Announcements, and Excused Absences for Javiera Caballero
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal opened the work session with six members present, noting Leonardo Williams would join shortly. Javiera Caballero announced her acceptance into a Latino elected official fellowship, requested excused absences for Feb. 21, Feb. 24, March 3, and March 4, 2022, proposed a March 10 work session discussion on prioritizing the first half of ARPA funds, and suggested a future Curamericas COVID-equity presentation; Jillian Johnson and DeDreana Freeman also flagged upcoming Women's History Month and Black History Month resolutions. Council unanimously approved Caballero's excused absences 6-0.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented three priority adjustments: scheduling a 10-minute presentation for the Durham YouthWorks 2021 program evaluation report (Item 20/22), updating Attachment 3 for Item 28 (Robert Desmarais), and adding Attachment 3 for Item 29 (Thelma White). Council approved the City Manager's priority items 6-0 on a roll-call vote.

agenda_items.title: City Attorney's Priority Item: Closed Session for Litigation Consultation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney requested a closed session pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation regarding three pending lawsuits: City of Durham v. J.E. Booth Farms, LLC et al. (21 CVS 1339), Oak Charter Academy, Inc. et al. v. City of Durham (21 CVS 2129), and Darryl Howard v. City of Durham et al. (17 CVS 477). Council approved the closed-session priority item 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Agenda Review and Item Pulls (Items 1-26)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal read through administrative consent Items 1-25 and noted Item 26 as a public hearing, during which Leonardo Williams joined the meeting (00:15:52). On Item 11 (resolution urging federal action to cancel student loan debt), DeDreana Freeman asked why federal House and Senate lawmakers were omitted and Charlie Reece agreed to add them alongside President Biden; Mark-Anthony Middleton pulled Items 24 and 25 for discussion.

agenda_items.title: Citizen Matters: Emorywood Estates / Towns at Courtenay Creek and Climate Justice
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Emorywood Estates residents Brenda Mares and HOA President Thelma Clegg-White (Item 29) presented a two-year update on impacts from Ryan Homes' Towns at Courtenay Creek development, citing logging and construction truck congestion on Kirby Street and Brandon, mud and debris, unfulfilled Highway 55 access promises, illegal hydrant water use, offensive 'Helms' street naming, mailbox break-ins, and rising home prices from $250,000 to $400,000. Christine Smith of the Green New Deal for Durham Coalition urged Council to direct ARPA, transit tax, and bond funding toward renewable energy, public transit, and affordable housing.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 24: Contract SW-76 Sidewalk Repairs 2021 Amendment No. 1
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned Public Works staff Tasha Johnson and Director Marvin Williams on whether PROWAG accessibility standards were statutorily mandated (staff clarified they are federal guidelines adopted locally as policy), how repair locations are selected (combining Durham One Call service heat maps and CIP priorities), and engineering recruitment and retention challenges. Williams explained that while the department was not requesting new FTEs yet, market competition from private firms and other cities made retaining trained engineers difficult.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 25: Contract SW-87C RFQ for Sidewalk Inspection and Ombudsman Services
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mark-Anthony Middleton and Charlie Reece commended Bragtown residents for persistent neighborhood advocacy that drove the sidewalk and upcoming road repair investments in Bragtown, and Middleton verified with E&I staff Eric Miller that subcontractor BRI and Associates is headquartered in Raleigh rather than Durham. Reece also thanked Tasha Johnson for six years of patient briefings on public works contracts.

agenda_items.title: Presentation — Item 22: Durham YouthWorks 2021 Program Evaluation Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Adrian Graham-Scott of the Office of Economic and Workforce Development presented RTI's 2021 evaluation via video featuring student Hayden Hill, consultant Jacob Dolan, and Durham Police Sgt. Butler (describing the program's sole in-person placement with the Police Athletic League). Graham-Scott highlighted 11 program providers, four Durham Tech/NCCU interns, wellness checks with DPS's trauma team, and onboarding and stipend-payment pain points ahead of the Feb. 21 interest form and Feb. 28 RFP, while Council members voiced unanimous support for expanding the program in the upcoming budget.

agenda_items.title: Boards, Committees, and Commissions Nominations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Clerk Diana Schreiber reported consensus nominations across several boards, confirmed re-advertising the Human Relations Commission 'other person' seat, and noted a 3-3-1 deadlock for the Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee at-large seat (three votes each for Andrew George and Paulette Jackson, and one vote from Mark-Anthony Middleton for Michael M. Bell). After Javiera Caballero advocated for Andrew George's climate justice and science background, Middleton switched his vote to George to reach consensus.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb 7, 2022 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, Durham City Council issued proclamations honoring Triangle Tribune editor Bonita Best and late fashion icon Andre Leon Talley, unanimously passed the revised Consent Agenda (7-0), and voted 7-0 to adopt Item 3—a $15,000 United Way / Walton Family Foundation subgrant for the Protecting Our Dignity (POD) coalition—after staff and advocate Idea Ortiz assured members the funds had no strings attached despite skepticism from Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson over Walton's school-privatization history. On Item 11 (Scannell Properties' NC 55 & Hobson consolidated annexation), Council split 5-2 across four motions (DeDreana Freeman and Charlie Reece dissenting) over direct-translation Industrial Light (IL) parcels lacking binding development-plan prohibited uses, before passing the consistency statement and Item 12 (3602 Westminster Avenue annexation) unanimously 7-0. After nearly two hours of testimony and scrutiny over missing written DPS proffers, uncertain unit counts (100 vs 147), and Ellis Road traffic on Item 13 (Bull City Townhomes), Council unanimously signaled by raised hands to refer the rezoning back to Planning staff for substantial revision.

agenda_items.title: Announcements & Proclamations (Bonita Best Day; Andre Leon Talley)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a moment of silence for 900,000 U.S. COVID-19 fatalities and late resident Erica Rojas/Eric Gutierrez, requested a briefing on Durham Police Department no-knock warrant policies after Amir Locke's killing in Minneapolis, and debated timelines for safely reopening City Hall and small businesses near the 5% positivity threshold. DeDreana Freeman presented the Bonita Best Day proclamation and Jillian Johnson presented a resolution honoring Andre Leon Talley received by his family.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 2, 4-8)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Item 3 held on the General Business Agenda, Council unanimously approved Consent Items 1, 2, and 4-8 (including the $50,000 County Community Intervention and Support Services ILA, Community Home Trust down-payment administrator contract, dump trucks purchase, CVS employee COVID testing extension, Welcoming America grant, and Connect & Protect grant).

agenda_items.title: Item 3: 2022 United Way of the Greater Triangle Grant Budget Ordinance ($15,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Protecting Our Dignity (POD) representative Idea Ortiz and Office on Youth manager Laura Khalil affirmed that the $15,000 United Way pass-through grant funded by the Walton Family Foundation imposed zero programmatic restrictions on local Black- and Latinx-led coalition partners. While Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson voiced ongoing concern about Walton's charter-school lobbying, all seven members trusted POD partners and passed the grant ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 11: Consolidated Annexation - NC 55 & Hobson (Scannell Properties #539 LLC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Scannell Properties attorney Patrick Byker presented an industrial annexation and rezoning request covering six direct-translation parcels (County IL to City IL, ~135 acres) plus four parcels rezoned with text-only commitments (IL-D, ~101 acres), opposed by neighbor Brenda Berry over traffic and environmental spillover. DeDreana Freeman and Charlie Reece opposed granting unconditioned City IL zoning without binding development-plan prohibited uses across all parcels, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and Leonardo Williams defended honoring Durham's direct-translation rules; the annexation and three UDO zoning motions passed 5-2, and the consistency statement passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 12: Consolidated Annexation - 3602 Westminster Avenue
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Michael Stock presented a contiguous 4.5-acre voluntary annexation and direct-translation zoning request (County RR/F/J-B to City RR/F/J-B) for a single-family home by applicant Joseph Francisco Mena (technical audio issues prevented attorney Michael Hudson from speaking, with Council inviting written comment). All three motions (annexation/UEA, zoning map change, and consistency statement) passed 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 13: Zoning Map Change - Bull City Townhomes (Z2100028)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Mark Bullock and attorney James Osler sought rezoning from RR to RSM-D for up to 147 townhomes (~$300k price point) off Ellis Road and Lindley Road after a 0-13 Planning Commission denial, facing neighbor opposition (Steve Devaris, Kellen Johnson) over Ellis Road traffic and neighborhood engagement. Council criticized discrepancies between verbal claims (~100 units, $6,000 verbal DPS proffer) and the submitted 147-unit plan without written commitments, reaching unanimous raised-hand consensus at 04:17:57 to refer the case back to Planning staff.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informal unanimous referral back to Planning staff

votes.item_title: Item 3: 2022 United Way of the Greater Triangle Grant Budget Ordinance ($15,000)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman and Leonardo Williams both called the motion; seconded by Mark-Anthony Middleton.
votes.discussion_detail: Leonardo Williams joined DeDreana Freeman in moving approval after Office on Youth confirmed no programmatic strings accompanied the Walton Family Foundation funds distributed via United Way to support the Protecting Our Dignity coalition.

votes.item_title: Item 11 Motion 1: Adopt Annexation Ordinance & Authorize Utility Extension Agreement (NC 55 & Hobson)
votes.notes: Tally announced 5-2 by Mayor O'Neal and City Clerk.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted ordinance annexing NC 55 & Hobson parcels effective March 31, 2022 and authorizing the utility extension agreement with Scannell Properties #539 LLC. Freeman and Reece voted no over lack of binding development-plan restrictions on the six IL parcels.

votes.notes: Tally announced 5-2; Freeman and Reece dissented.
votes.discussion_detail: Established direct-translation City Industrial Light (IL) zoning on the six parcels previously zoned County IL without a site-specific development plan.

votes.item_title: Item 11 Motion 3: UDO Zoning Map Change (County RR/CN F/J-B to City IL-D F/J-B)
votes.notes: Tally announced 5-2; Freeman and Reece dissented.
votes.discussion_detail: Rezoned parcel from County Residential Rural and Commercial Neighborhood (RR/CN) to City Industrial Light with Text-Only Development Plan (IL-D).

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted the statutory plan consistency statement following approval of the annexation and UDO map changes.

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted ordinance annexing 3602 Westminster Avenue effective March 31, 2022 and authorizing a utility extension agreement with Joseph Francisco Mena.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb 7, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: NC 55 & Hobson Direct-Translation IL Zoning Without Development Plan Commitments (Item 11)
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 on Scannell Properties' consolidated annexation and industrial rezoning along NC 55 and Hobson Road over whether allowing direct-translation City IL zoning on six parcels (~135 acres) without binding prohibited-use commitments created unacceptable community risk.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and both direct-translation IL and text-only IL-D zoning ordinances in keeping with Durham's existing UDO direct-translation rules.
side_a_arguments: UDO rules explicitly permit direct-translation annexation from County IL to City IL, and penalizing applicants for using an approved code pathway violates fair process.
The applicant committed text-only prohibited uses on the IL-D portion and engaged neighbors in the corridor.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose granting unrestricted City IL zoning without binding prohibited-use commitments or a concrete development plan across the full assemblage.
side_b_arguments: Without binding prohibited-use commitments or community benefits agreements, future property owners could build incompatible industrial uses adjacent to residents and Wake/Chatham county borders.
Councils regularly encourage applicants to submit binding commitments rather than relying on bare direct translation.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and all three zoning motions passed 5-2, followed by a 7-0 consistency statement.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb 7, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Accepting Walton Family Foundation Philanthropic Dollars via United Way (Item 3)
disagreements.summary: Members debated whether to accept a $15,000 United Way pass-through grant originating from the Walton Family Foundation to support the Protecting Our Dignity (POD) education coalition.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the unrestricted $15,000 grant and trust local Black- and Latinx-led coalition partners to guard community self-determination.
side_a_arguments: Staff and POD confirmed zero strings, no external agenda setting, and no Walton involvement at coalition tables.
Scrubbing every corporate or philanthropic foundation (such as Bloomberg or Aetna/CVS) would cripple needed youth funding.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain heightened skepticism and public scrutiny of funding tied to pro-privatization/charter education funders like the Walton Family Foundation.
side_b_arguments: National funders often advance long-term privatization agendas even through seemingly unrestricted general operating support.
Council must remain vigilant as public stewards even while ultimately trusting local groups on this grant.
disagreements.resolution: Following clarifications from Idea Ortiz and Laura Khalil, all members voted 7-0 to adopt the budget ordinance while emphasizing vigilance over future funder alignment.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 20, 2022 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Presided over by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton with Mayor Elaine O'Neal excused at the U.S. Conference of Mayors, Council opened by honoring late Durham native Andre Leon Talley, backing Jillian Johnson's upcoming federal Student Loan Debt Cancellation resolution, hearing DHA CEO Anthony Scott warn that 30-day eviction notices would go out unless delinquent residents applied for legal-aid rental assistance by February 12, and receiving an Ellerbe Creek Waterbird Colony Nature Preserve presentation. Council pulled four consent items for discussion—scrutinizing a $50,000 County Community Intervention and Support Services ILA, pulling Item 3 ($15,000 United Way / Walton Family Foundation grant) to the General Business Agenda over Walton privatization concerns, clarifying Community Home Trust's $450,000 down-payment administration contract, and reviewing CVS employee COVID testing extension costs (~$60 vs $130 retail). Community Safety Director Ryan Smith then unveiled plans for four HEART alternative crisis response pilots, sparking a sharp 3-3 policy clash when Charlie Reece, Jillian Johnson, and Javiera Caballero urged immediate analysis of deploying 15 frozen police vacancies mid-year while Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Leonardo Williams opposed bypassing the regular FY23 budget cycle.

agenda_items.title: Moment of Silence (Andre Leon Talley), Announcements & Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton remembered Andre Leon Talley, Jillian Johnson gained unanimous consent to bring a student-loan forgiveness resolution to the February work session and flagged a financing gap for 60-80% AMI units in DHA downtown redevelopment, and DHA CEO Anthony Scott urged residents facing $1.3M in arrears to apply for rental relief by February 12. Council unanimously approved accepting City Manager Wanda Page's three priority items.

agenda_items.title: Item 9: Ellerbe Creek Waterbird Colony Dedicated Nature Preserve Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Ellerbe Creek Watershed Association's Chris Dreps and NC Natural Heritage Program Director Misty Buchanan presented a proposal to designate city-owned bottomland forest along lower Ellerbe Creek as a state Dedicated Nature Preserve to permanently protect one of the Piedmont's rare great egret and great blue heron rookeries.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 2: ILA with Durham County for Community Intervention & Support Services ($50,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson and City Manager Wanda Page clarified that the $50,000 annual interlocal agreement allows both managers to jointly co-fund small community anti-violence grants (initially Campaign for Change at $20k city/$30k county and Hayti Reborn Justice Movement at $10k each) separately from Bull City United and Project BUILD. Council members asked for written project descriptions prior to February 7.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 3: 2022 United Way / Walton Family Foundation Grant ($15,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero questioned Office on Youth Manager Laura Khalil over accepting $15,000 originating from the Walton Family Foundation given its pro-charter education history, despite Khalil's assurance of zero strings attached and coalition stewardship by Spirit House, WE ARE, Village of Wisdom, and partner nonprofits. Caballero and Jillian Johnson insisted on moving the item to the General Business Agenda.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Items 4 & 6: Community Home Trust DPA Admin & CVS COVID-19 Testing Contract
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson confirmed Item 4's $450,000-$490,000 fee covers administration for ~180 down-payment loans (~$6M funded by HOME and Dedicated Housing Fund). On Item 6, City Manager Page and HR Assistant Director Drew Bullard reported 85.3% employee vaccination (~374 unvaccinated staff testing weekly) and noted city-contracted CVS clinics cut per-test self-insured plan costs from ~$130 retail to ~$60, with an upcoming July 1 health-plan surcharge.

agenda_items.title: Item 10: Community Safety Department Alternative Crisis Response (HEART) Pilots
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Safety Director Ryan Smith and Assistant Director Annisse Evans unveiled four pilots launching around June-July 2022—Crisis Call Diversion, Community Response Teams (CRT), Co-Response, and Care Navigation—informed by multi-agency planning, RTI partnership, and community feedback. Charlie Reece, Jillian Johnson, and Javiera Caballero urged having Smith examine deploying the 15 frozen DPD vacancies immediately, triggering extended debate with Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Leonardo Williams before deferring new requests to the FY23 budget process.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No consensus to direct mid-year study

agenda_items.title: Housing / Tenants Subcommittee Scheduling & Settle February 7 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jillian Johnson coordinated the four-member housing subcommittee (Johnson, Freeman, Caballero, Williams) to meet February 1 at 3:00 PM on NIS / Bull City Tenants United proposals, after which Council voted 6-0 to settle the February 7 regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 1, 2, 4-8; GBA Item 3; Public Hearings Items 11-13).

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (Items 8, 9 & 10 Scheduling Updates)
votes.notes: Mayor Elaine O'Neal excused absent (previously granted on Jan 18).
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted City Manager Wanda Page's priority updates to Item 8 (FY24 match memo clarification), Item 9 (Ellerbe Creek time-certain presentation), and Item 10 (Community Safety pilots presentation).

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 20, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Mid-Year Study/Transfer of 15 Frozen Police Vacancies to Community Safety Department (HEART)
disagreements.summary: Council divided evenly (3-3 with Mayor O'Neal absent) over whether to direct Community Safety Director Ryan Smith to come back before the FY23 budget with an operational plan to utilize the 15 frozen DPD positions to expand HEART crisis response pilots.
disagreements.side_a_position: Ask Director Smith to analyze how the 15 frozen DPD vacancies could accelerate and expand pilot hours, team capacity, or neighborhood coverage prior to waiting another fiscal year.
side_a_arguments: Last June's budget compromise froze the 15 positions explicitly for six-month review after Smith's January update rather than continuing unfilled DPD slots.
Residents and Community Safety & Wellness Task Force co-chairs support building robust crisis capacity immediately without adding net new budget dollars.
disagreements.side_b_position: Refrain from ordering a mid-year transfer of arbitrary vacant headcount before pilots even launch, and allow Smith to bring data-driven FTE asks through the imminent FY23 budget cycle.
side_b_arguments: Director Smith stated pilots will not reach the field until June-July 2022, could not guarantee filling additional positions before July, and made no mid-year FTE request.

Moving 15 unfilled police slots represents political theater rather than scientific budgeting; Council should fully fund Smith's actual budget requests in February-May without artificially dictating FTE sources.
disagreements.resolution: Charlie Reece acknowledged no Council majority existed to direct staff mid-year and agreed to defer additional Community Safety staffing requests to the regular FY23 budget process (with February 21 departmental submissions).

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 20, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Advancing or Pulling United Way / Walton Family Foundation Grant (Item 3)
disagreements.summary: Javiera Caballero and Jillian Johnson objected to approving a $15,000 United Way grant funded by the Walton Family Foundation on the Consent Agenda, prompting its transfer to the February 7 General Business Agenda.
disagreements.side_a_position: Pull Item 3 to the General Business Agenda to scrutinize the Walton Family Foundation's pro-privatization/charter-school objectives and document Coalition safeguards.
side_a_arguments: Even without overt contract strings, wealthy education-reform foundations strategically invest in local coalitions to advance charter and privatization interests.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep the $15,000 grant on Consent in trust of Office on Youth staff and established Black- and Latinx-led coalition partners.
side_b_arguments: The grant carries no strings attached, Walton sits at no planning tables, and doubting local nonprofit leaders' discernment risks paternalism.
disagreements.resolution: Per City Attorney guidance that Consent items lacking unanimity roll automatically to GBA, Mayor Pro Tem Middleton placed Item 3 on the February 7 General Business Agenda.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan. 18, 2022 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At a brisk 42-minute regular session presided over by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton while Mayor Elaine O'Neal attended the U.S. Conference of Mayors in Washington, D.C., City Council voted 6-0 to grant O'Neal an excused absence for January 18 and January 20. Charlie Reece delivered a Fred Korematsu Day of Civil Liberties and the Constitution proclamation received by Japan-America Society of NC representative David Otoji, and council members thanked crews for winter storm response while noting two recent officer-involved shootings and the Omicron surge. Council approved Consent Items 1-25 unanimously 6-0, then heard Interim HR Director JJ Scott explain that pulled Item 26 (~$4M mid-year Police and Fire compensation plan adjustment effective January 28) lifts base pay structures without retroactively restoring frozen prior step increases for three- and four-year firefighters before adopting Item 26 by a 6-0 vote.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence for Mayor Elaine O'Neal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Mayor Elaine O'Neal traveling to Washington, D.C. for the U.S. Conference of Mayors, Charlie Reece moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded granting an excused absence for both the January 18 regular meeting and January 20 work session.

agenda_items.title: Fred Korematsu Day Proclamation & Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Charlie Reece read a proclamation recognizing January 30 as Fred Korematsu Day of Civil Liberties and the Constitution, accepted by David Otoji of the Japan-America Society of North Carolina. During announcements, members praised city storm cleanup crews, noted DPD briefings on two officer-involved shootings (Circle K and Duke ER), and weighed Omicron vaccination/masking vigilance against keeping small restaurants afloat.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-25)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Item 26 pulled by Leonardo Williams for clarifying questions, Council passed Consent Items 1-25 unanimously 6-0, including the We Are the Ones grant, Bull City Tenants United staff response report receipt, sewer/lift-station contracts, and South Ellerbe Phase 2 restoration work.

agenda_items.title: Item 26: Police and Fire Compensation Plans Adjustment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Leonardo Williams, Interim HR Director JJ Scott clarified that while the mid-year structure adjustment increases base salaries for all sworn officers and firefighters (roughly $4M for FY22's remaining pay periods), there was no retroactive step restoration for three- and four-year firefighters affected by prior step freezes, which would be studied further in FY23 budgeting. Williams moved and Javiera Caballero seconded approval.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 6, 2022 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: In Mayor Elaine O'Neal's first work session presiding after 30 days in office, City Council marked the one-year anniversary of January 6 and urgent Omicron COVID-19 response by voting 7-0 to suspend its rules and immediately approve Item 27, an interlocal agreement with Durham County to open a third COVID-19 testing site at Wheels Fun Park. Council also approved restoring Council travel and expense allotments to pre-pandemic levels, permitted quasi-judicial Housing Appeals Board hearings to resume in person while keeping advisory boards under the 5% positivity threshold, and examined NIS's detailed response to Bull City Tenants United proposals—splitting over DeDreana Freeman's pitch to absorb tenants'-rights discussions into the Northeast Central Durham subcommittee versus forming a dedicated four-member housing subcommittee. Council heard Interim HR Director JJ Scott present the $4M mid-year Police and Fire compensation adjustment alongside firefighter union appeals regarding 56-hour living-wage parity and step compression, reached consensus on Dell R. Ruff for the City's final Racial Equity Commission seat, and settled the January 18 consent agenda 6-0 after Javiera Caballero departed.

agenda_items.title: Moment of Silence (January 6), Omicron Briefing & Manager Priority Items / Item 27 Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor O'Neal led a moment of silence commemorating the January 6 U.S. Capitol attack, Charlie Reece detailed an 18-fold surge in Durham COVID-19 cases (564/day), and Council voted 7-0 to accept City Manager priorities, suspend rules, and approve Item 27 (Durham County COVID-19 testing facility ILA at Wheels Fun Park). Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman urged renewed co-funding for lapsed community health ambassador contracts (Latin-19, African American COVID Task Force) and KN95 mask distribution.

agenda_items.title: City Clerk Priority Items: Council Expense Restoration & Virtual Board Rules
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 7-0 to accept City Clerk Diana Schreiber's priority items, reached consensus to administratively restore Council travel/expense budgets cut during COVID-19 so members could fulfill national municipal duties and board support, and agreed to allow the quasi-judicial Housing Appeals Board to meet in person while other appointed boards stayed remote until county positivity fell below 5%.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 15: NIS Response to Bull City Tenants United Proposals & Subcommittee Scope
agenda_items.discussion_summary: NIS Director Constance Stancil and Assistant Director Faith Gardner reviewed FY19-FY21 inspection totals (~13,000/yr, 81.6% compliance), plans to hire a bilingual code enforcement officer, housing code repairs (including owner-supplied stoves/refrigerators), and HUD requirements to add criminal history to the non-discrimination ordinance. Council members debated using DeDreana Freeman's existing Northeast Central Durham subcommittee versus establishing a dedicated four-member housing subcommittee to negotiate tenants-rights proposals.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Remained on Consent; standalone subcommittee dates to be scheduled via email

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 24: South Ellerbe Restoration Project Phase Two Demolition & Grading
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Megan Walsh, UBE Coordinator Eric Miller, and contractor Joel Miller (Buckeye Elm Contracting) addressed DeDreana Freeman's inquiry into the 11% MBE goal, explaining that while Buckeye Elm secured 19% WBE trucking participation and met good-faith outreach benchmarks, specialized soil-disposal subcontracting drew limited MBE bids.

agenda_items.title: Item 26: Police and Fire Compensation Plans Adjustment Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim HR Director JJ Scott and Compensation Manager Alisha Hardy presented market research across 13 peer cities showing DPD and DFD salaries trailing market averages by 12% and 10%, recommending a ~$4M mid-year structural pay adjustment (10.6% police recruit increase; 14.3% fire recruit increase) effective January 28 (~$9.5M annualized). Firefighter Meredith Carter and Union President Jimmy Wright praised the base adjustment while urging Council to fix 3rd/4th-year step compression and 56-hour living-wage parity; Jillian Johnson sought cost figures while City Manager Page warned restructuring 56-hour base pay mid-year would cause ~50k entry-pay ripple effects.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational at work session (scheduled for Jan 18 vote)

agenda_items.title: Boards & Commissions Nominations, Settle Jan 18 Agenda & NECD Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Clerk reported consensus on seven board appointments and a 3-3-1 deadlock on Durham's seventh Racial Equity Commission seat, which resolved in favor of Dell R. Ruff when Mark-Anthony Middleton shifted his vote to match Jillian Johnson's endorsement. Council settled the January 18 consent agenda 6-0 (Javiera Caballero having departed earlier), and DeDreana Freeman asked Council to formally consider disbanding the under-attended Northeast Central Durham subcommittee.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (Items 25, 26 & Rule-Suspension Request for Item 27)
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted supplemental Items 25 (Seaboard/st301 C Haven Services), 26 (Police & Fire Compensation Plans presentation), and 27 (Durham County COVID-19 Testing Facility ILA).

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules to Vote on Item 27 During Work Session
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended standard rules requiring a work-session delay so Council could immediately authorize Durham County's third COVID-19 testing location amid the Omicron surge.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Interlocal Agreement with Durham County for COVID-19 Testing Facility
votes.discussion_detail: Approved interlocal agreement allowing Durham County to establish a third community COVID-19 testing facility at Wheels Fun Park.

votes.item_title: Accept City Clerk's Priority Items (Council Expense Allotment & Board Meeting Format)
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted the Clerk's two priority discussion items regarding restoring Council's travel/expense accounts and virtual vs. in-person meeting guidance for appointed boards.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 6, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Northeast Central Durham Subcommittee vs. Dedicated Housing / Tenants Rights Subcommittee
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over DeDreana Freeman's proposal to hold Bull City Tenants United / housing subcommittee business under the existing Northeast Central Durham (NECD) subcommittee notice at 5:00 PM that evening versus convening a separate properly noticed subcommittee.
disagreements.side_a_position: Create or notice a standalone citywide Housing / Tenants Subcommittee rather than folding Bull City Tenants United negotiations into the NECD subcommittee without advance public notice.
side_a_arguments: NECD has a specific geographic charge and noticed agenda; co-opting it the same afternoon without public notice or Javiera Caballero present undermines open-meetings transparency.
Tenants' rights affects residents citywide and requires dedicated prioritization and Spanish-language representation.
disagreements.side_b_position: Leverage or disband/reformat the existing four-member NECD subcommittee notice to accelerate housing work without creating yet another committee structure.
side_b_arguments: NECD already holds a noticed four-member meeting at 5:00 PM that can immediately pick meeting dates and streamline staff workload, and NECD lacked three appointed colleagues.
disagreements.resolution: Mayor O'Neal directed Jillian Johnson to coordinate standalone housing-subcommittee dates via email with the four interested members and revisit disbanding NECD at a subsequent meeting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan. 6, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Firefighter Living-Wage Hourly Calculation (56-Hour Week) & Mid-Year Pay Scope
disagreements.summary: Following firefighter testimony over step compression and sub-living hourly effective pay across 56-hour shifts, Jillian Johnson pressed administration for cost estimates to bring firefighters to the living wage on a 56-hour basis, whereas Wanda Page and JJ Scott advised against altering the ordinance's annual-salary framework mid-year.
disagreements.side_a_position: Obtain updated cost calculations to pay firefighters Durham's minimum livable wage on their actual 56-hour workweek and seriously weigh tax/funding options.
side_a_arguments: Basing firefighters' salaries on a 40-hour formula when they work 56 hours leaves them below Durham's hourly living wage despite city living-wage commitments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Advance the $4M sworn structure increase now under the existing annual-salary ordinance and examine compression and broader pay equity during the regular FY23 budget.
side_b_arguments: Moving entry firefighter recruits to ~$50,000 for 56-hour living-wage parity would trigger severe upward compression across pay grades and ripple across other city pay plans.
No general employees received merit increases over the last two years, so full structural compression must be weighed holistically in FY23.
disagreements.resolution: Item 26 stayed on track for the January 18 vote while City Manager Page committed to updating the May cost-calculation memo as an agenda addendum without recommending immediate structural overhaul.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 3, 2022 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its first meeting of 2022, the Durham City Council issued proclamations for National Mentoring Month and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Day, reflected on recent gun violence (including a fatal shooting from celebratory gunfire) and COVID-19 mitigation, and unanimously passed the 15-item Consent Agenda (7-0) including eviction defense and DEAR expunction contracts with Legal Aid of North Carolina, Western Intake Partnership water infrastructure contracts, and public safety grants. Council unanimously approved (7-0 across three motions) the consolidated annexation, utility extension agreement, and Office & Institutional zoning (Z2100003) for 67 townhomes at 2211 Page Road after the applicant raised its affordable housing proffer from $16,750 to $20,100 ($300/unit) and added a $1,000-per-student DPS proffer. A contentious nearly two-hour debate followed on Item 19, Scannell Properties' 254.124-acre NC 55 and Hopson Road annexation and straight Light Industrial rezoning (Z2100009), which had been rejected 0-12 by the Planning Commission and prompted a late offer from the developer's attorneys to add a text-only list of prohibited uses. While Mark-Anthony Middleton and Leonardo Williams favored an immediate vote to secure projected jobs and tax base, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, and Elaine O'Neal insisted on staff review, and the public hearing was held open and continued by unanimous consent to February 7, 2022.

agenda_items.title: National Mentoring Month and Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Leonardo Williams read a proclamation designating January 2022 as National Mentoring Month, and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton read a proclamation honoring the life and legacy of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Mayor Elaine O'Neal presented both proclamations to Dewan K. Langley, Executive Director of the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation, who highlighted coalition mentoring organizations and January youth events.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements on COVID-19 Mitigation and Gun Violence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Javiera Caballero urged residents to continue following Durham's mask mandate, obtain COVID-19 boosters (including newly eligible youth ages 12 and older), and enroll Durham Public Schools students in free weekly testing. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council Members Leonardo Williams, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece, and Mayor Elaine O'Neal addressed fatal gun violence over the New Year weekend—including an elder killed by celebratory gunfire and a double homicide outside a hotel—calling for community-wide partnership alongside police and frontline staff.

agenda_items.title: City Manager, City Attorney, and City Clerk Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page reported one priority item: Attachment 8 was added to Agenda Item 6 (Legal Aid of North Carolina contract for the Durham Expunction and Restoration [DEAR] program) detailing how Durham residents use the program for expungement and driver's license restoration originating in other counties. City Attorney Kim Rehberg and the City Clerk reported no priority items, with the Clerk noting Council Member Javiera Caballero's presence for the roll.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Minutes, NIMS, Legal Aid Eviction & DEAR Contracts, Affordable Housing, Western Intake Partnership, Refuse Trucks, Parks, Public Safety Grants, VoIP)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal read the 15-item Consent Agenda, covering Council minutes, NIMS designation, Legal Aid of NC contracts for eviction defense and the DEAR program, Hardy Street Apartments, Lofts at Southside Phase III option contract, Jordan Lake Western Intake Partnership CIP and engineering contracts (Brown and Caldwell; CDM Smith), November 2021 bid report, five knuckleboom refuse trucks, C.M. Herndon Road Park soccer field change order, 2022 Blue Benevolence and 2021 DOJ JAG grants, and Cisco VoIP licensing. No items were pulled for separate discussion.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation, Utility Extension Agreement, and Zoning Map Change — 2211 Page Road (BDG2100007 / Z2100003)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a continued public hearing for 10.15 acres at 2211 Page Road by landowners Warren Mitchell and David Durham, requesting voluntary annexation (effective March 31, 2022), a utility extension agreement, and rezoning from Residential Rural (RR) to Office & Institutional with a development plan (OI(D)) for up to 67 townhomes, following a 7-5 unfavorable Planning Commission recommendation. During Council questioning on unit pricing, proffers, and process transparency (including an iLegislate packet visibility issue on Attachment 12), Mitchell increased the affordable housing proffer from $250/unit ($16,750) to $300/unit ($20,100) and added a $1,000-per-student proffer to Durham Public Schools for the estimated three students. Council approved the annexation/utility extension, zoning ordinance, and consistency statement in three consecutive unanimous roll-call votes.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation, Utility Extension Agreement, and Zoning Map Change — NC 55 and Hopson Road (BDG2100005 / Z2100009)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Sara Young recognized retiring planner Danny Cultra before Cultra presented Scannell Properties LLC's request to annex 254.124 acres across 10 parcels at NC 55 and South Alston Avenue and rezone four parcels from RR and CN to Industrial Light (IL) without a development plan, which the Planning Commission rejected 0-12 on October 12, 2021. Proponents cited ~$67 million in tax base and 1,000-2,000 living-wage jobs near RTP and offered during the hearing to submit a text-only development plan prohibiting uses such as electronic gaming/internet cafes and payday lenders, while speakers Jackie Wagstaff and Lee Weaver raised concerns about internet cafes, neighborhood compatibility, and lack of a binding plan or Chatham/Wake utility connections. Following sharp Council debate between members favoring an immediate vote and members supporting Planning staff's request for review time, Mayor O'Neal held the public hearing open and continued the item for two cycles to February 7, 2022 by unanimous consent.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Continued to Feb 7, 2022 by unanimous consent (No formal vote)

votes.item_title: Item 17 (Motion 1): Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement — 2211 Page Road (BDG2100007)
votes.notes: Public hearing had been opened on December 6, 2021 and continued to January 3, 2022.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted the ordinance annexing 10.15 acres at 2211 Page Road into the City of Durham effective March 31, 2022 and authorized the City Manager to enter into a utility extension agreement with Warren D. Mitchell and David Durham.

votes.item_title: Item 17 (Motion 2): Zoning Map Change Ordinance — 2211 Page Road (Z2100003)
votes.notes: Planning Commission had given an unfavorable recommendation (7-5) on October 12, 2021; staff supported the OI(D) proposal.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 3, 2022 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: NC 55 and Hopson Road Rezoning (Item 19): Immediate Vote vs. Referral/Continuance for Binding Text Commitments
disagreements.summary: Council divided sharply over Scannell Properties' straight Industrial Light rezoning request (Z2100009) after the Planning Commission voted 0-12 against it and the applicant's attorneys offered a last-minute slide prohibiting certain commercial uses (such as internet cafes and payday lenders) during the public hearing without prior staff review.
disagreements.side_a_position: Proceed to a vote tonight on the straight Industrial Light rezoning without further delay to secure jobs and tax base.
side_a_arguments: Scannell Properties has an established track record in Durham (PowerSecure, Pfizer, Candle Science) and 135 adjacent acres are already zoned IL without a development plan.
The 235-acre industrial park is projected to generate 1,000-2,000 living-wage jobs accessible without a graduate degree and ~$67 million in city tax base near RTP and Apple.
Creating non-degree career opportunities helps address root causes of gun violence and youth inactivity, whereas bureaucratic delays push investment to neighboring Wake, Chatham, and Cary.
Requiring a development plan or formal text commitments for economic outcomes should not be applied reflexively, and the applicant's public commitment against internet cafes is sufficient.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not vote on unvetted last-minute commitments; require formal staff review and binding text commitments before taking final action.
side_b_arguments: The Planning Commission rejected the proposal 0-12 in October, yet the developer made zero changes before the Council hearing and ambushed staff at the dais with an unverified text-only plan.
Projected job counts, wages, and tax base increases are not legally binding in a straight rezoning without text commitments or a development plan.

Allowing applicants to circumvent Planning staff review disrespects staff and the Planning Commission; Planning Director Sara Young requested time to rewrite the ordinance, rerun traffic numbers, and update the staff report.

Broader community impacts—including prohibited uses (electronic gaming/internet cafes), open space, transportation, and neighboring Chatham/Wake County utility coordination—require formal documentation.
disagreements.resolution: After Planning Director Sara Young confirmed staff could process a text-only development plan limiting prohibited uses in two cycles if no other changes were made (and the applicant agreed), Mayor Elaine O'Neal held the public hearing open and continued Item 19 to February 7, 2022 by unanimous consent.
